questions.q: \(\mathrm{CH}_{3}  \mathrm{OC}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{5}\) and \(\left(\mathrm{CH}_{3}\right)_3  \mathrm{C}-\mathrm{OCH}_{3}\) are treated with hydroiodic acid. The fragments after reactions obtained are
questions.solution: When mixed ethers are used, the alkyl iodide produced depends on the nature of alkyl groups. If one group is Me and the other a pri- or sec-alkyl group, then methyl iodide is produced. Here reaction occurs via \(\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}}2\) mechanism and because of the steric effect of the larger group, \(\mathrm{I}^{-}\)attacks the smaller (Me) group. \(\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{OC}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{5}+ \mathrm{HI} \rightarrow \mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{I}+\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{5} \mathrm{OH}\) When the substrate is a methyl \(t\)-alkyl ether, the products are \(t-R \mathrm{I}\) and \(\mathrm{MeOH}\). Here reaction occurs by \(\mathrm{S}_{\mathrm{N}}1\) mechanism and formation of products is controlled by the stability of carbocation. Since carbocation stability order is \(3^{{}^{\circ}} > 2^{{}^{\circ}} > 1^{{}^{\circ}} > \stackrel{\oplus}{\mathrm{CH}_{3}}\). \(\therefore \quad\) Alkyl halide is always derived from tert-alkyl group.

questions.q:
Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their acidic strength :
i. m-nitrophenol
ii. m-cresol
iii. phenol
iv. m-chlorophenol
questions.solution:
Nitro group has both \( -R \) effect and \( -1 \) effect; but \( -R \) effect predominates. Due to stronger electron withdrawing nature of
\( $\mathrm{NO}_{2}$\) group, phenoxide ion is stabilized. Hence, m-nitrophenol is more acidic than phenol. Methyl group destabilizes the
phenoxide ion by \( +I \) effect and hyperconjugation. Hence m-cresol is weaker acid than phenol. Chlorine have both +R
and \( -1 \) effect but \( -1 \) effect predominates
Hence m-chlorophenol is more acidic than phenol. \( -R \) effect of nitro group is stronger than \( -1 \) effect of chlorine hence, m-
nitrophenol is more acidic than m-chlorophenol.
Therefore, the correct order of acidic strength is \( m \)-nitrophenol \( \gt m \)-chlorophenol \( \gt p h e n o l \gt m \)-cresol.

questions.q: Which of the following vitamins cannot be stored in the body?
questions.solution:
Vitamins are classified into two groups depending upon their solubility in water or fat.

Fat soluble vitamins: Vitamins which are soluble in fat and oils but insoluble in water are kept in this group. These are vitamins $A, D, E$ and $K$. They are stored in liver and adipose (fat storing) tissues.

Water soluble vitamins: $B$ group vitamins and vitamin $C$ are soluble in water. Water soluble vitamins must be supplied regularly in diet because they are readily excreted in urine and cannot be stored (except vitamin ${B}_{12}$) in our body.

Observe the following statements.
I. Sucrose has glycosidic linkage.
II. Cellulose is present in both plants and animals.
III. Lactose contains D-galactose and D-glucose units.
Which of the following statements are correct?
questions.solution: Let's evaluate each statement to determine which are correct. - Statement I: Sucrose has a glycosidic linkage. This is correct. Sucrose is a disaccharide formed by a glycosidic linkage between a glucose unit and a fructose unit. - Statement II: Cellulose is present in both plants and animals. This is incorrect. Cellulose is the main structural component of the primary cell wall of green plants, but it's not present in animals. Animals lack the enzyme cellulase to break down cellulose. - Statement III: Lactose contains D-galactose and D-glucose units. This is correct. Lactose is a disaccharide commonly known as milk sugar. It's composed of one molecule of Dgalactose and one molecule of D-glucose, joined by a \(\beta\)-1,4-glycosidic linkage. Therefore, the correct statements are I and III. The correct option is (4).

options: a-normal enzyme reaction, b-competitive inhibition, c-non-competitive inhibition
a-enzyme with an allosteric modulator added, b-normal enzyme activity, c-competitive inhibition
a-enzyme with an allosteric stimulator, b-competitive inhibition added c-normal enzyme reaction
a-normal enzyme reaction, b-non-competitive inhibitor added c-allosteric inhibitor added
questions.solution: Enzymes or biocatalysts are proteinaceous substance that are capable of catalysing chemical reactions of biological systems without themselves undergoing any change. In the graph $a$ shows normal enzyme reaction, graph $b$ shows competitive inhibition and graph $c$ shows non competitive inhibition. In competitive inhibition the inhibitor, which is a substrate analogue, combines reversibly to the free enzyme at the active site. In non competitive inhibition, the inhibitor binds to enzyme at a place other than substrate binding site. It results in destruction of enzyme activity.

questions.q: The $F - Br - F$ bond angles in $Br{F}_{5}$ and the $Cl - P - Cl$ bond angles in $PC{l}_{5}$, respectively, are
questions.solution:
The geometry of $Br{F}_{5}$ is square pyramidal.

Here, the lone pair occupies the axial position and hence axial bonds will suffer more repulsion than equatorial bonds. Thus, the axial $Br - F$ bond length will be different from equatorial $Br - F$.

The geometry of $PC{l}_{5}$ is triangular pyramidal.

The axial bonds suffer more repulsions than equatorial bonds, so they are larger in bond length.

questions.q: Stability of the species ${Li}_{2} \text{,} {Li}_{2}^{-} \text{and} {Li}_{2}^{+}$& increases in the order of
questions.solution:
$ {Li}_{2}^{-} < {Li}_{2}^{+} < {Li}_{2}$
Bond order $∝$ stability of species
${Li}_{2} = \sigma1s^{2} < \overset{*}{σ}1s^{2} < \sigma2s^{2}; B. O = \dfrac{4 - 2}{2} = 1$
${Li}_{2}^{−} = \sigma1s^{2} < \overset{*}{σ}1s^{2} < \sigma2s^{2} < \overset{*}{σ}2s^{1}; B. O = \dfrac{4 - 3}{2} = 0.5$
${Li}_{2}^{+} = \sigma1s^{2} < \overset{*}{σ}1s^{2} < \sigma2s^{1}; B. O = \dfrac{3 - 2}{2} = 0.5$
${Li}_{2}^{+}$ and ${Li}_{2}^{-}$ both have same bond order, but ${Li}_{2}^{-}$& has more number of electron in anti-bonding molecular orbitals (experience more inter electronic repulsion) and hence least stable among three species.

Bond length of $\mathrm{HCl}=1.3 Å$ and $\mathrm{HI}=1.6 Å$. The ratio of fraction of electric charge, $\delta$, existing on each atom in $\mathrm{HCl}$ and $\mathrm{HI}$ is
questions.solution:
From the definition of dipole moment,
$\mu=\delta \times d$
where, $\delta=$ magnitude of electric charge
$d=$ distance between particles (here bond length)
$\begin{array}{rlrl}\therefore& \delta =\frac{\mu}{d}\\ \text{ or, } \quad \frac{\delta_{\mathrm{HCl}}}{\delta_{\mathrm{HI}}} =\frac{\mu_{\mathrm{HCl}}}{d_{\mathrm{HCl}}} \times \frac{d_{\mathrm{HI}}}{\mu_{\mathrm{HI}}}\\  =\frac{1.03 \times 1.6}{1.3 \times 0.38}=3.3: 1\end{array}$

questions.q: Four diatomic species are listed below. Identify the correct order in which the bond order is increasing in them.
questions.solution:
Bond order $=\frac{N_b-N_a}{2}$
In NO, total electrons $=7+8=15\therefore$ Configuration of $\mathrm{NO} \begin{aligned}& =K K, \sigma\left(2 s²\right), \stackrel{*}{\sigma}\left(2 s²\right), \sigma\left(2 p_z^2\right), \pi\left(2 p_x^2\right) \\
& \approx \pi\left(2 p_y^2\right) \stackrel{*}{\pi}\left(2 p_x^1\right) \\
&
\end{aligned}

$\therefore$ Bond order $=$\frac{8-3}{2}=\frac{5}{2}=2.5$
In $\mathrm{O}_2^{-}$$, total electrons $=16+1=17
$$\begin{aligned}& \therefore \text{ Configuration of } \mathrm{O}_{2}^{-} \\
& =K K, \sigma\left(2 s^2\right), \stackrel{*}{\sigma}\left(2 s^2\right), \sigma\left(2 p_z^2\right), \pi \left(2 p_x^2\right) \\
& \approx \pi\left(2 p_y^2\right), \pi\left(2 p_x^2\right)\approx \pi\left(2 p_y^1\right) \\
& \therefore \text{ Bond order }=\f frac{8-5}{2}=\frac{3}{2}=1.5 \\
& \text{ In } \mathrm{C}_{2}^{2-} \text{, total electrons }=12+2=14 \\
& \therefore \text{ Configuration of } \mathrm{C}_{2}^{2-}\\
& =K K, \sigma\left(2 s^2\right), \stackrel{*}{\s sigma}\left(2 s²\right), \sigma\left(2 p_z^2\right), \approx \pi\left(2 p_x^2\right), \pi\left(2 p_y^2\right) \\
& \therefore \quad \text{ Bond order }=\frac{8-2}{2}\\
& =\frac{6}{2}=3 \\
& \text{ In } \mathrm{He}_2^{+} \text{, total electrons }=4-1=3 \\
& \therefore \text{ Configuration of } \mathrm{He}_2^{+}=\sigma\left(1 s²\right), \stackrel{*}{\ssigma}\left(1 s^1\right) \\
& \therefore \quad \text{ Bond order }=\frac{2-1}{2}\\
& =\frac{1}{2}= 0.5 \\
&
\end{aligned}$$

Hence, correct order of bond order is

$\mathrm{He}_{2}^{+}$<  $\mathrm{O}_{2}^{-}$$ < $$\mathrm{NO}$$ <  $$\mathrm{C}_{2}^{2-}$

questions.q: Match each of the diatomic molecules in Column I with its property/properties in Column II.
questions.solution:
- A. \(B_2\) : Has two unpaired electrons, making it p. Paramagnetic. The close energy levels of \(2 s\) and \(2 p\) orbitals lead to \($\mathrm{t.s - p}$\) mixing.
- B. \(\boldsymbol{N}_{\mathrm{2}$}$\) : Has a bond order of \($\mathrm{3}$\), so its bond order is \($\mathrm{s}$\). \($\mathrm{\geq 2}$\). It also has \($\mathrm{t . s - p}$\) mixing and can gain electrons, so it r. Undergoes reduction.
- C. \(O_2\) : Has two unpaired electrons, making it p. Paramagnetic. Its bond order is 2 , so it's \($\mathrm{s}$\). \(\geq\) 2. With electrons in antibonding orbitals, it can lose electrons, thus q. Undergoing oxidation.
- D. \(O_2^{-}\): Has one unpaired electron, making it p. Paramagnetic. It can both gain and lose electrons, so it q. Undergoes oxidation and r. Undergoes reduction.
The correct option is (3).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: In the equilibrium, $A B \rightleftharpoons A+B$, if the equilibrium concentration of $A$ is double, then equilibrium concentration of $B$ will be
questions.solution:
For the equilibrium reaction $AB \rightleftharpoons A + B$, the equilibrium constant $K_{eq}$ is given by the expression:

$K_{eq} = \dfrac{[A][B]}{[AB]}$

Since $K_{eq}$ is a constant at a fixed temperature, the product of the concentrations of the products divided by the concentration of the reactant remains constant. Let the initial equilibrium concentrations be $[A]_1$, $[B]_1$, and $[AB]_1$. Then $K_{eq} = \dfrac{[A]_1 [B]_1}{[AB]_1}$.

If the equilibrium concentration of $A$ is doubled, let the new concentration be $[A]_2 = 2[A]_1$. Assuming the concentration of the reactant $[AB]$ remains effectively constant or the system adjusts such that the ratio is maintained, we have:

$\dfrac{[A]_1 [B]_1}{[AB]} = \dfrac{[A]_2 [B]_2}{[AB]}$

$[A]_1 [B]_1 = (2[A]_1) [B]_2$

$[B]_2 = \dfrac{[A]_1 [B]_1}{2[A]_1} = \dfrac{1}{2} [B]_1$

Therefore, the equilibrium concentration of $B$ becomes half of its original value.

Answer: half

questions.q: For the equilibrium, $2 \mathrm{NOCl}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NO}(g)+\mathrm{Cl}_{2}(g)$, the value of the equilibrium constant, $K_{C}$ is $3.75 \times 10^{-6}$ at $1069 \mathrm{ K}$. The value of $K_{p}$ for the reaction at this temperature will be
questions.solution:
The relationship between the equilibrium constants $K_{p}$ and $K_{c}$ is given by the equation $K_{p} = K_{c}(RT)^{\Delta n_{g}}$.

For the reaction $2 \mathrm{NOCl}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{NO}(g) + \mathrm{Cl}_{2}(g)$, the change in the number of moles of gaseous species is calculated as $\Delta n_{g} = (2 + 1) - 2 = 1$.

Given values are $K_{c} = 3.75 \times 10^{-6}$, $R = 0.0821 \text{ L atm K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$, and $T = 1069 \text{ K}$.

Substituting these values into the formula:

$K_{p} = (3.75 \times 10^{-6}) \times (0.0821 \times 1069)^{1}$

$K_{p} = 3.75 \times 10^{-6} \times 87.7649$

$K_{p} \approx 0.000329118$

Rounding to the appropriate precision, $K_{p} \approx 0.00033$.

Answer: $0.00033$

If the equilil rium concentration of benzene is $0.5 \mathrm{ mol}^{-1}$ than what is the value of concentration of ethylene?
questions.solution:
The chemical equation for the reaction is $3 \mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{2}(\mathrm{g}) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{6}(\mathrm{g})$.

The expression for the equilibrium constant $K_{C}$ is given by:

$K_{C} = \dfrac{[\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{6}]}{[\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{2}]^{3}}$

Given $K_{C} = 4 \mathrm{ L}^{2} \mathrm{ mol}^{-2}$ and $[\mathrm{C}_{6} \mathrm{H}_{6}] = 0.5 \mathrm{ mol} \mathrm{ L}^{-1}$.

Substituting the values into the expression:

$4 = \dfrac{0.5}{[\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{2}]^{3}}$

$[\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{2}]^{3} = \dfrac{0.5}{4} = 0.125$

$[\mathrm{C}_{2} \mathrm{H}_{2}] = (0.125)^{1/3} = (0.5^{3})^{1/3} = 0.5 \mathrm{ mol} \mathrm{ L}^{-1}$.

Answer: $0.5 \mathrm{ mol} / \mathrm{L}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: For the reaction $2 \mathrm{ N}_2 \mathrm{O}_5 \longrightarrow 4 \mathrm{NO}_2+\mathrm{O}_2$. If inital pressure is $100 \mathrm{ atm}$ and rate constant $k$ is $3.38 \times 10^{-5} \mathrm{ s}^{-1}$. After $20 \mathrm{ min}$ the final pressure of $\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}_5$ will be
questions.solution:
The reaction $2 \mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}_5 \rightarrow 4 \mathrm{NO}_2 + \mathrm{O}_2$ is a first-order reaction. The rate equation for a first-order reaction is given by $P_t = P_0 e^{-kt}$, where $P_0$ is the initial pressure and $P_t$ is the pressure at time $t$.

Given values are:
$P_0 = 100 \text{ atm}$
$k = 3.38 \times 10^{-5} \text{ s}^{-1}$
$t = 20 \text{ min} = 20 \times 60 \text{ s} = 1200 \text{ s}$

Substituting these values into the equation:
$P_t = 100 \times e^{-(3.38 \times 10^{-5}) \times 1200}$

Calculate the exponent:
$-(3.38 \times 10^{-5}) \times 1200 = -0.04056$

Now calculate $P_t$:
$P_t = 100 \times e^{-0.04056}$
Using the approximation $e^{-x} \approx 1 - x$ for small $x$:
$P_t \approx 100 \times (1 - 0.04056) = 100 \times 0.95944 = 95.944 \text{ atm}$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we get $96 \text{ atm}$.

Answer: $96 \mathrm{ atm}$

questions.q: The equilibrium constants \(K_{P 1}\) and \(K_{P 2}\) for the reaction \(X \rightleftharpoons2 Y\) and \(Z $\rightleftharpoons$P+Q\), respectively are in the ratio of \(1:\) 9. If the degree of dissociation of \(X\) and \(Z\) be equal then the ratio of total pressure at these equilibria is:
questions.solution:
$\text{X}( \text{g} ) ⇌ \text{2Y}( \text{g} )$

& & & & & & & & & & & 1 & & & & & & & & 0&

At equilibrium & & $1 - \text{x}$ & & & & $\text{2x}$

Total no. of moles = $1 + \text{x}$

${K}_{{p}_{1}} \text{=}\dfrac{{\left[\dfrac{\text{2x}}{\text{1+x}} {\text{.p}_{1}\right]}^{2}}{\left(\dfrac{\text{1} - \text{x}}{\text{1+x}}\right){\text{.p}_{1}} \text{=}\dfrac{{\text{4x}^{2}}{\left(\text{1} - \text{x}\right)} \dfrac{{p}_{1}}{\left(\text{1+x}\right)} \text{=}\dfrac{{\text{4x}^{2} {p}_{1}}{\left(\text{1} - x^{2}\right)}$

$\text{Z}( \text{g} ) ⇌ \text{P}( \text{g} )\text{+Q}( \text{g} )$

& & & & & & & & & & & 1 & & & & & & & & & & & & & & 0 & & & & & & 0

At equilibrium & $1 - \text{x}$ & & & & & & $\text{x}$ & & $\text{x}$

Similarly, ${K}_{{p}_{2}} \text{=}\dfrac{x^{2}}{\left(\text{1} - \text{x}\right)} \dfrac{{p}_{2}}{\left(\text{1+x}\right)} \text{=}\dfrac{x^{2} {p}_{2}}{\left(\text{1} - x^{2}\right)}$

$∴ \dfrac{{K}_{\text{p1}}}{{K}_{\text{p2}}} \text{=}\dfrac{1}{9}$

So, $\dfrac{\text{4}\text{\times}{p}_{1}}{{p}_{2}} \text{=}\dfrac{1}{9}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{p}_{1}}{{p}_{2}} \text{=}\dfrac{1}{\text{36}}$

questions.q:
The following equilibrium constants are given:

${N}_{2} + 3 {H}_{2} ⇌ 2 {NH}_{3} \text{;} {\text{K} ⁡}_{1}$

${N}_{2} + {O}_{2} ⇌ 2 \text{NO} \text{;} {\text{K} ⁡}_{2}$

${H}_{2} + {1 / 2 \text{O}_{2} ⇌ {H}_{2} \text{O} \text{;} {\text{K} ⁡}_{3}$

The equilibrium constant for the oxidation of $2$ mole ${\text{NH}_{3}$ by oxygen to give $\text{NO}$ is
questions.solution:
${N}_{2} + 3{H}_{2} ⇌ {\text{2NH}_{3}$

${K}_{1} = \dfrac{{ \left[{$$\text{NH}_{3}$\right]}^{2}}{ $\left[{N}_{2}\right]${ $\left[{H}_{2}\right]$}^{3}} \ldots $\left($\text{i}$\right)$

${N}_{2} ${$\text{+O}_{2}$$⇌$2$\text{NO}$\text{;}{$K}_{2} = $\dfrac{{ $\left[$\text{NO}$\right]$$}^{2}}{ $$\left[{N}_{2}\right]$\left[{O}_{2}\right]$} \ldots $$\left($\text{ii}$\right)$$

${H}_{2} + 1 / 2{O}_{2} ⇌ {H}_{2} $\text{$O}$\text{;}${K}_{3} = $\dfrac{ $$\left[{H}_{2} $\text{O}$\right]$$}${ $\left[{H}_{2}\right]${ $\left[{O}_{2}\right]$}^{1 / 2}}$ \ldots $$\left($\text{iii}$\right)$$

For the reaction, $2 {NH}_{3} + $\dfrac{5}{2}$ {O}_{2}$⇌ 2 $$\text{NO}$ +$3 {H}_{2} $$\text{O}$$

$$\text{K}$⁡ = \dfrac{{$\left[$\text{NO}$\right]$$}^{2} {$$\left[{H}_{2} $\text{O}$\right]$$}^{3}}{{ $$\left[{NH}_{3}\right]$}^{2} {$\left[{O}_{2}\right]$$}^{5 / 2}}$

$= $\dfrac{{$\left[$\text{NO}$\right]$}^{2}}${$$\left[{N}_{2}\right]$$\left[{O}_{2}\right]$} \times \dfrac{{ \left[{H}_{2} $\text{O}\right]}^{3}}{{ \left[{H}_{2}\right]$}^{3} { $\left[{O}_{2}\right]}^{3 / 2}} \times \dfrac{ \left[{N}_{2}\right]${ $\left[{H}_{2}\right]$}^{3}}{{ $\left[{NH}_{3}\right]$}^{2}}$

$= $\dfrac{{K}_{2} \times {K}_{3}^{3}}{{K}_{1}}$

\(18.4 \mathrm{ g} \mathrm{ N}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}\) was placed in \(1 \mathrm{ L}\) vessel at \(400 \mathrm{ K}\) and allowed to attain the following equilibrium $\mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}($ g) \rightleftharpoons2 $\mathrm{NO}_{2}($ g)\).
If the total pressure at equilibrium was 10.64 bar, approximate \(K_p\) is \((R=0.083 \mathrm{ L}\) bar \(\mathrm{K}^{-1} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1}\) ) (Assume \( \mathrm{N}_{2} \mathrm{O}_{4}, \mathrm{NO}_{2}\) as ideal gases)
questions.solution:
From ideal gas equation, \$(\begin{aligned}$p V & =n R T \\ $p_{\mathrm{N}_2$} $\mathrm{O}}_{4}} \times \mathrm{l}& =\frac{18.4}{92} \times0.083 \times400 \\ p_{\mathrm{N}_2} \mathrm{O}$}_{4}} & =6.64 $\text{ bar } \end{aligned}$\) For the equilibrium reaction,
\$(\begin{aligned}$p_T & =p-p_i+2 p_i \\ p_T & =p+p_i \Rightarrow p_i=p_T-p \\ p_i & =10.64-6.64 \\ & =4.00 $\mathrm{bar} \end{aligned}\) At equilibrium, \$(\begin{aligned} \therefore \quad$p_{\mathrm{N}_2$} $\mathrm{O}}_{4}} & =p-p_i=6.64-4 \\ & =2.64 \mathrm{bar}\\ p_{\mathrm{NO}_2} & =2 p_i=2 \times4 \\ & =8 \mathrm{bar}\\ \therefore \quad K_p $$=\frac{$\left[p_{\mathrm{NO}_2}\right]$^2}{$\left[p_{\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}_4}\right]$}$\\ $$=\frac{[8]^2}{2.64}=$24.29 \end{aligned}\)

questions.q:
Using the data provided, find the value of equilibrium constant for the following reaction at $298K$ and $1$ atm pressure. ${NO}_{( g )} + \dfrac{1}{2}{O}_{2} ( g ) ⇌ {NO}_{2} ( g )$
${\Delta}_{f}{H}^{0}\left({NO}_{( g )}\right) = 90 .4 kJ . {mol}^{- 1}$

${\Delta}_{f}{H}^{0}\left({NO}_{2} ( g )\right) = 32 .48 kJ ⋅ {mol}^{- 1}$

${\Delta S}^{∘} @ 298K = - 70 .8 J ⋅ {K}^{- 1} ⋅ {mol}^{- 1}$

$antilog ⁡ ( 0 .50 ) = 3162$
questions.solution:
The given reaction is

${NO}_{( g )} + \dfrac{1}{2}{O}_{2} ( g ) ⇌ {NO}_{2} ( g )$

The enthalpy of the above reaction given by the difference of enthalpies of reactant side and product side.

Therefore,

${∆}_{c}H = {∆}_{f}H\left({NO}_{2}\right) - \left[{∆}_{f}H\left(NO\right) + \dfrac{1}{2}{∆}_{f}H\left({O}_{2}\right)\right]{∆}_{c}H = 32 . 8 - \left[90 . 4 + \dfrac{1}{2}\left(0\right)\right]{∆}_{c}H = - 57 . 6{KJmol}^{- 1}$

Also, we know that Gibb's free energy can be determined by

$∆ G = ∆ H - T ∆ S ∆ G = 57600{Jmol}^{- 1} - 298 \times \left(- 70 . 8\right){JK}^{- 1}{mol}^{- 1} ∆ G = - 36501 . 5{Jmol}^{- 1}$

Again, Using relation of Gibb's free energy with equilibrium constant i.e.

$∆ G = - 2 . 303 \times 8 . 31 \times 298logk = - 36501 . 5{Jmol}^{- 1}K = 3 . 162 \times {10}^{6}$

500 mL of 0.150 M AgNO3 solution were added in 500 mL of 1.09 M Fe2+ solution and the reaction is allowed to reach an equilibrium at $2 {5}^{∘} \text{C}$.

${\text{Ag}}^{+} \left(\text{aq}\right) + {\text{Fe}}^{2 +} \left(\text{aq}\right) ⇌ {\text{Fe}}^{3 +} \left(\text{aq}\right) + \text{Ag} \left(\text{s}\right)$

For 25 mL of the solution, 30 mL of 0.0832 M KMnO4 were required for oxidation. Calculate equilibrium constant (M-1) of the reaction at $2 {5}^{∘} \text{C}$.
[Report your answer by rounding it upto nearset whole number]
questions.explanation:
$\begin{cases} & {\text{Ag}}^{+} \left(\text{aq}\right) & + & {\text{Fe}}^{2 +} \left(\text{aq}\right) & ⇌ & {\text{Fe}}^{3 +} \left(\text{aq}\right) & + & \text{Ag} \left(\text{s}\right) \\ \text{Initial} & 7 5 \text{mM} & & 5 4 5 \text{mM} & & 0 & & 0 \\ \text{Reaction} & - 4 6 \text{mM} & & - 4 6 \text{mM} & & + 4 6 \text{mM} & & + 4 6 \text{mM} \\ & \text{---------------} & & \text{---------------} & & \text{---------------} & & \text{---------------} \\ \text{Final} & 2 9 \text{mM} & & 4 9 9 \text{mM} & & 4 6 \text{mM} & & 4 6 \text{mM}\end{cases}$

m.eqs of ${\text{KMnO}_{4} = 3 0 \times 0 \cdot 0 8 3 2 \times 5 = 1 2 \cdot 4 8 \text{m.eqs}$
(Z factor =5)

m.eqs of ${\text{Fe}}^{2 +}$ $= 12\cdot48 \text{Meqs} = 12\cdot48 \text{mM}$
(Z factor= 1)

Total mM of ${\text{Fe}}^{2 +}$ left $= 12 \cdot 48 \times 4 0 = 4 9 9 \text{mM}$

At Equilibrium concentrations

$\left[{\text{Ag}}^{+}\right] = \dfrac{2 9 \text{mM}}{1 0 0 0 \text{mL}} = 0 \cdot 0 2 9 \text{M}$

$\left[{\text{Fe}}^{2 +}\right] = \dfrac{4 9 9 \text{mM}}{1 0 0 0 \text{mL}} = 0 \cdot 4 9 9 \text{M}$

$\left[{\text{Fe}}^{3 +}\right] = \dfrac{4 6 \text{mM}}{1 0 0 0 \text{mL}} = 0 \cdot 0 4 6 \text{M}$

${\text{K}}_{\text{C}} = \dfrac{\left[{\text{Fe}}^{3 +}\right]}{\left[{\text{Ag}}^{+}\right]\left[{\text{Fe}}^{2 +}\right]} = \dfrac{0 \cdot 046}{0 \cdot 499 \times 0 \cdot 029} = 3.18{\text{M}}^{- 1}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Consider the reaction $A ⇌ B$ at $1000K$. At time ${t}^{'}$, the temperature of the system was increased to $2000K$ and the system was allowed to reach equilibrium. Throughout this experiment the partial pressure of $A$ was maintained at $1$ bar. Given below is the plot of the partial pressure of $B$ with time. What is the ratio of the standard Gibbs energy of the reaction at $1000K$ to that at $2000K$?
questions.solution:
Use $\Delta G ° = - RTlnKP$ at equilibrium

${\Delta G}_{1}^{∘} = - {RT}_{1}ln{\text{K}}_{{\text{P}}_{1}}$ ...... $( 1 )$

${\Delta G}_{2}^{∘} = - {RT}_{2}ln{\text{K}}_{\text{P}2}$ ..... $( 2 )$

${\Delta G}_{1}^{∘}{\Delta G}_{2}^{∘} = \dfrac{{\text{T}}_{1}}{{\text{T}}_{2}} \times \dfrac{{lnK}_{{\text{P}}_{1}}}{{lnK}_{{\text{P}}_{2}}}$

$= \begin{array}{ll}1000 \\ 2000\end{array} \times \begin{array}{ll}ln ( 10 ) \\ ln ( 100 )\end{array}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0 . 25$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
For the gaseous reactions (I) and (II), the equilibrium constants are $X$ and $Y$ respectively.
I. $\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{ N}_2(g)+\mathrm{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NO}_2(g)$
II. $2 \mathrm{NO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}_4(g)$
Using the above reactions the equilibrium constant $Z$ for the reaction (III) given below is
III. $\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}_4(g) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{N}_2(g)+2 \mathrm{O}_2(g)$
questions.solution: For reaction $\begin{aligned} \frac{1}{2} \mathrm{ N}_2(g)+\mathrm{O}_2(g) & \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NO}_2(g) \\ X & =K_{C_1}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{NO}_2\right]}{\left[\mathrm{N}_2\right]^{1 / 2}\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]} \end{aligned}$ $\begin{aligned} & \text{$ For $} 2 \mathrm{NO}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}_4(g) \\ & Y=K_{C_2}=\frac{\left[\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}_4\right]}{\left[\mathrm{NO}_2\right]^2}\end{aligned}$ For reaction $\mathrm{N}_2 \mathrm{O}_4(g) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{N}_2(g)+2 \mathrm{O}_2$ Substituting values from equation (i) and (ii) in equation (iii) we get. $\begin{aligned} & Z=\left(\frac{\left[\mathrm{NO}_2\right]}{X}\right)^2 / Y\left[\mathrm{NO}_2\right]^2 \\ & Z=\frac{\left[\mathrm{NO}_2\right]^2}{X^2 Y\left[\mathrm{NO}_2\right]^2}=\frac{1}{X^2 Y} \end{aligned}$

questions.q:
The stepwise stability constants of a complex are given below. What is its overall reaction stability constant $(\left(\beta_4\right)\) ?
\begin{aligned}& M+L $\rightleftharpoons$M L ; K_1=1.0 \times10^4 \\
 \text{$ and }  M L+L\rightleftharpoons$M L_2 ; K_2=1.0 \times10^3 \\
 \text{$ and }  M L_2+L\rightleftharpoons$M L_3 ; K_3=1.0 \times10^3 \\
 \text{$ and }  M L_3+L\rightleftharpoons$M L_4 ; K_4=1.0 \times10^2
\end{aligned}\)
(Overall$ reaction : \(M+4 L\rightleftharpoons$M L_4\) )$
questions.solution:
Given,
$\begin{gathered} M+L \rightleftharpoons$ M L ; K_1=1.0 $\times10^4 \\
M L+L \rightleftharpoons$ M L_2 ; K_2=1.0 $\times10^3 \\
M L_2+L \rightleftharpoons$ M L_3 ; K_3=1.0 $\times10^3 \\
M L_3+L \rightleftharpoons$ M L_4 ; K_4=1.0 $\times10^2
\end{gathered}\)
Overall reaction,
\(M+4 L \rightleftharpoons M L_4\)$ The $overall stability constant,
\begin{aligned}
\beta_4 & =K_1 \times K_2 \times K_3 \times K_4 \\
\beta_4 & =1.0 \times10^4 \times1.0 \times10^3 \times1 \times10^3 \times1 \times10^2 \\
& =1 \times10^{12}
\end{aligned}\)$

questions.q:
At $800 ° C$, the following equilibrium is established as
${F}_{2} \left(\text{g}\right)⇌ 2 \text{F}\left(\text{g}\right)$
The composition of equilibrium may be determined by measuring the rate of effusion of the mixture through a pin hole. It is found that $800 ° C$ and $1atm$ mixture effuses $1.6$ times as fast as ${SO}_{2}$ effuses under the similar conditions. (At. wt. of $F = 19$). What is the value of ${K}_{p} (in atm) ?$
questions.solution:
According to Graham's law of effusion
$r ∝ \dfrac{1}{M}$

$\dfrac{{r}_{mix}}{{r}_{\text{SO} 2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{{M}_{\text{SO} 2}}{{M}_{mix}}}$

$⇒ \text{2.56} = \dfrac{6 4}{{M}_{mix}}$

$⇒ {M}_{mixture} = 2 5$

Let mole fraction of ${F}_{2}$ is x. Therefore, mole fraction of $F$ will be $\left(1 - x\right)$

$2 5 = \dfrac{3 8 \times \text{x} + \left(1 - \text{x}\right) \times 1 9}{1}$

$\text{x} = 0.315$ ;

$⇒ {K}_{p} = \dfrac{{P}_F^{2}}{{P}_{\text{F} 2}} = \dfrac{{\left(\text{0.685P}\right)}^{2}}{\left(\text{0.315P}\right)} ≃ \text{1.49 atm}$

questions.q: For the equilibrium $AB ( g ) ⇌ A ( g ) + B ( g )$ , at a given temperature $\dfrac{1}{3}rd$ of AB is dissociated then $\dfrac{P}{{K}_{p}}$ will be numerically equal to
questions.solution:
$Σn = \dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{2}{3} + \dfrac{1}{3} = \dfrac{4}{3}$
${K}_{p} = \dfrac{{n}_{A} \times {n}_{B}}{{n}_{AB}} \times {\left(\dfrac{P}{Σn}\right)}^{\Delta{n}_{g}}$
$= \left[\dfrac{\dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{3}}{\dfrac{2}{3}}\right] \times {\left[\dfrac{P}{\dfrac{4}{3}}\right]}^{1}$
$= \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{3P}{4} = \dfrac{P}{8}$
So, $\dfrac{P}{{K}_{p}} = 8$

questions.q: Equilibrium constants for the following reactions at $1200 \mathrm{K}$ are given $2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{H}_{2}(g)+\mathrm{O}_{2}(g)K_{1}=6.4 \times 10^{-8}2 \mathrm{CO}_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{CO}(g)+\mathrm{O}_{2}(g)K_{2}=1.6 \times 10^{-6}$ The equilibrium constant for the reaction? $\mathrm{H}_{2}(g)+\mathrm{CO}_{2}(g) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CO}(g)+\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}(g)$ at $1200 \mathrm{K}$ will be
questions.solution: For the given reactions, $2 \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{H}_{2}+\mathrm{O}_{2}, K_{1}=6.4 \times 10^{-8}$ or, $\mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_{2}+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_{2}, K_{1}^{\prime}=\sqrt{K_{1}}$ or $\mathrm{H}_{2}+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_{2}, \longrightarrow \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{O}, K_{1}^{\prime \prime \prime}=1 / \sqrt{K_{1}} \ldots2 \mathrm{CO}_{2} \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{CO}+\mathrm{O}_{2}, K_{2}=1.6 \times 10^{-6}$ or $\mathrm{CO}_{2} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CO}+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_{2}, K_{2}^{\prime}=\sqrt{K_{2}}$ From (i) and (ii) [on adding] $K=\frac{\sqrt{K_{2}}}{\sqrt{K_{1}}}=\frac{\sqrt{1.6 \times 10^{-6}}}{\sqrt{6.4 \times 10^{-8}}}K=\sqrt{\frac{10^{2}}{4}}=\sqrt{25}=5$

questions.q:
The equilibrium constant for the reaction
$\mathrm{SO}_2(g)+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{SO}_3(g)$ is $5 \times 10^{-2}$ atm.
The equilibrium constant of the reaction
$2 \mathrm{SO}_3(g) \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{SO}_2(g)+\mathrm{O}_2(g)$ would be
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} \mathrm{SO}_2+\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{O}_2 & \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{SO}_3 \\ K_1 & =\frac{\left[\mathrm{SO}_3\right]}{\left[\mathrm{SO}_2\right]\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]^{1 / 2}} \\ 2 \mathrm{SO}_3 & \rightleftharpoons 2 \mathrm{SO}_2+\mathrm{O}_2 \\ \mathrm{ K}_2 & =\frac{\left[\mathrm{SO}_2\right]^2\left[\mathrm{O}_2\right]}{\left[\mathrm{SO}_3\right]^2}\end{aligned}$
From Eqs. (i) and (ii)
$\begin{aligned} K_2 & =\frac{1}{K_1^2} \\ K_2 & =\frac{1}{\left(5 \times 10^{-2}\right)^2}=\frac{1}{25 \times 10^{-4}} \\ & =\frac{100 \times 10^2}{25} \\ & =4 \times 10^2 \mathrm{ atm}\end{aligned}$

(Given: \text{R} =0.082{\text{LatmK}$}^{- 1} ${\text{mol}$}^{- 1}, $\text{R} =8.314{\text{JK}$}^{- 1} ${\text{mol}$}^{- 1},$ ln\text{x} =2.303{log}_{10} \text{x})$ If your answer is K, mark 2K as answer after rounding off to nearest integer.
questions.solution:
${M}_{avg} = \dfrac{ρ \text{RT}}{\text{P}} = \dfrac{4. 8 \times 0. 0 8 2 \times 5 0 0}{1} = 1 9 6. 8$

\begin{cases}{PCl}_{5} $\left(\text{g}\right)$& ⇌ & {PCl}_{3} $\left(\text{g}\right)$& + & {Cl}_{2} $\left(\text{g}\right)$& \\ 1 - \alpha & & \alpha & & \alpha & $\left(\text{Total moles} = 1 + \alpha\right)\end{cases}$

${M}_{avg} = \dfrac{{M}_{\text{PCl} 5}}{1 + \alpha} = 1 9 6. 8 = \dfrac{2 0 8. 5}{1 + \alpha}$

$∴ \alpha = 0. 0 6$

${K}_{P} = \dfrac{{α}^{2}}{1 - {α}^{2}} \text{P} = \dfrac{{\left(0.06\right)}^{2}}{1 - {\left(0.06\right)}^{2}} = 3.6 \times {10}^{- 3}$

$\Delta G^{∘} = - \text{RT} \text\ln \text{K}$

& $= - 8. 3 1 4 \times 5 0 0 \times 2. 303 \text\log \left(3. 6 \times1 {0}^{- 3}\right)$

& $= 23.4\text{kJ}$

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: Ammonium sulphide and ammonium selenide on heating dissociates as (NH_{4})_{2}S(s) $⇌ 2NH_{3}(g)+ H_{2}S(g); K_{p1}=9 × 10^{-3} atm^{3} (NH_{4})_{2}Se(s) $⇌$ 2NH_{3}(g) + H_{2}Se(g); K_{p2}=4.5 × 10^{-3} atm^{3} The total pressure over the solid mixture at equilibrium is$
questions.solution:
$\begin{array}{ll}{\left({\text{NH}_{4}\right)}_{2} \text{S}\left(\text{s}\right) ⇌ {\text{2NH}_{3} \left(\text{g}\right) + {H}_{2} \text{S}\left(\text{g}\right) \\ \text{2p}\text{p}\end{array}$

$\begin{array}{ll}{\left({\text{NH}_{4}\right)}_{2} \text{Se}\left(\text{s}\right) ⇌ {\text{2NH}_{3} \left(\text{g}\right) + {H}_{2} \text{Se}\left(\text{g}\right) \\ \text{2q}\text{q}\end{array}$

${K}_{\text{p} 1} = {\left({p}_{\text{NH} 3}\right)}^{2} \cdot {p}_{{H}_{2} \text{S}} = {\left(2 \text{p} + 2 \text{q}\right)}^{2} \cdot \text{p} = \text{9.0} \times {10}^{- 3}$

${K}_{\text{p} \text{2}} = {\left({p}_{\text{NH} 3}\right)}^{2} \cdot {p}_{{H}_{2} \text{S} \text{e}} = {\left(2 \text{p} + 2 \text{q}\right)}^{2} \cdot \text{q} = \text{4.5} \times {10}^{- 3}$

$∴ \dfrac{\text{p}}{\text{q}} = 2 ⇒ \text{p} = 2 \text{q}$

y &=0
\end{aligned}

Hence,$ the rate of equation is\text{ Rate }=$k[A]^{2}[B]^{0}

Order of reaction $=2$

Usually, the first step is the slow step since it has the highest activation energy.

questions.q: Paragraph: Carbon-14 is used to determine the age of organic material. The procedure is based on the formation of ${ }^{14} \mathrm{C}$ by neutron capture in the upper atmosphere. { }_7^{14} $\mathrm{~N}+{ }_$0^1 n \longrightarrow{ }_6^{14} $\mathrm{C}+{ }_$1 n¹ ${ }^{14} \mathrm{C}$ is absorbed by living organisms during photosynthesis. The ${ }^{14} \mathrm{C}$ content is constant in living organism once the plant or animal dies, the uptake of carbon dioxide by it ceases and the level of ${ }^{14} \mathrm{C}$ in the dead being, falls to the decay which ${ }^{14} \mathrm{C}$ undergoes. { }_6^{14} $\mathrm{C} \longrightarrow{ }_$7^{14} $\mathrm{~N}+\beta^{-}$The half life period of ${ }^{14} \mathrm{C}$ is 5770 years. questions.q: The correct decreasing order of negative electron gain enthalpy for $\mathrm{C}, \mathrm{Ca}, \mathrm{Al}, \mathrm{F}$ and $\mathrm{O}$ is
questions.solution:
The electron gain enthalpy is the energy released when an electron is added to a neutral gaseous atom. Generally, it becomes more negative (higher magnitude) across a period from left to right and decreases down a group.

The elements given are $\mathrm{F}$ (Group 17, Period 2), $\mathrm{O}$ (Group 16, Period 2), $\mathrm{C}$ (Group 14, Period 2), $\mathrm{Al}$ (Group 13, Period 3), and $\mathrm{Ca}$ (Group 2, Period 4).

Comparing the magnitudes of electron gain enthalpy:
1. $\mathrm{F}$ has the highest negative electron gain enthalpy among these due to its small size and high effective nuclear charge, although it is slightly less than $\mathrm{Cl}$ due to inter-electronic repulsion.
2. $\mathrm{O}$ follows $\mathrm{F}$ in the same period.
3. $\mathrm{C}$ has a lower negative electron gain enthalpy than $\mathrm{O}$.
4. $\mathrm{Al}$ is a metal with a low tendency to gain electrons, but it is more electronegative than $\mathrm{Ca}$.
5. $\mathrm{Ca}$ is an alkaline earth metal with a stable $ns^2$ configuration, making its electron gain enthalpy very low (near zero or positive).

The order of magnitude of negative electron gain enthalpy is $\mathrm{F} > \mathrm{O} > \mathrm{C} > \mathrm{Al} > \mathrm{Ca}$.

Answer: $\mathrm{F}> \mathrm{O}> \mathrm{C}> \mathrm{Al}> \mathrm{Ca}$

The periodic table consists of 18 groups. An isotope of copper, on bombardment with protons, undergoes a nuclear reaction yielding element $X$ as shown below. To which group, element $X$ belongs in the periodic table?

${ }_{29}^{63} \mathrm{Cu}+{ }_{1}^{1} \mathrm{H} \rightarrow 6_{0}^{1} n+{ }_{2}^{4} \alpha+2{ }_{1}^{1} \mathrm{H}+\mathrm{X}$
questions.solution:
${ }_{29}^{63} \mathrm{Cu}+{ }_{1}^{1} \mathrm{H} \rightarrow 6{ }_{0}^{1} n+{ }_{2}^{4} \mathrm{He}+2{ }_{1}^{1} \mathrm{H}+{ }_{Z}^{A} X$

Balancing the atomic mass and atomic number

$63+1=(6 \times 1)+4+2+A \Rightarrow A=52$

$29+1=(6 \times 0)+2+2+Z \Rightarrow Z=26$

Thus ${ }_{Z}^{A} X={ }_{26}^{52} X$ or ${ }_{26}^{52} \mathrm{Fe}$

Hence, $X$ belongs to group 8 in the periodic table.

questions.q: Geometrical shapes of the complexes formed by the reaction of ${Ni}^{2 +}withCl^{-}, CN^{-}and{H}_{2}O$ , respectively, are
questions.solution:
$Ni^{2 +} + 4CN^{-} \to {\left[Ni{\left(CN\right)}_{4}\right]}^{2 -}$

Here $Ni^{2 +}$ has $d^{8}$ -configuration with $CN^{-}$ as strong ligand.



$d^{8}$ -configuration in strong ligand field gives ${\text{dsp}^{2}$ hybridisation, hence square planar geometry.
$Ni^{2 +} + 4Cl^{-} \to {\left[NiC{l}_{4}\right]}^{2 -}$
Here $Ni^{2 +}$ has $d^{8}$ -configuration with $Cl^{-}$ as weak ligand.



$d^{8}$-configuration in weak ligand field gives $sp^{3}$hybridisation, hence tetrahedral geometry.
$Ni^{2 +}$ with ${H}_{2}O$ forms ${\left[Ni{\left({H}_{2}O\right)}_{6}\right]}^{2 +}$ complex and ${H}_{2}O$ is a weak ligand.



Therefore, ${\left[Ni{\left({H}_{2}O\right)}_{6}\right]}^{2 +}$ has octahedral geometry.
In octahedral complexes with $d^{8}$ configuration, there is always ${\text{sp}^{3} d^{2}$ hybridisation (outer orbital complex) irrespective of strong ligand field or weak ligand field.

&
& Catalyst & Process

B. $PdC{l}_{2}$ ii. Ziegler − Natta polymerisation

options: $A \to iii, B \to i, C \to ii, D \to iv$

questions.solution:

In the Deacon's process, the reaction takes place at about $400to{450}^{o}C$ in the presence of a variety of catalysts, which include& copper chloride $( {CuCl}_{2} )$.

In Ziegler-Natta polymerisation,& homogenous catalysts, usually based on complexes of $Ti, ZrorHf$,& are used. They are usually used in combination with different catalysts.

questions.q: The oxidation number of $\mathrm{Cr}$ in $\mathrm{CrO}_{5}$ which has the following structure, is
questions.solution:
The structure of $\mathrm{CrO}_{5}$ is a butterfly structure where the central chromium atom is bonded to one oxygen atom via a double bond and to four oxygen atoms via two peroxo linkages.

In the peroxo linkage, the oxidation state of each oxygen atom is $-1$.

Let the oxidation number of $\mathrm{Cr}$ be $x$. The molecule contains one oxo group (O^{2-}$) and two peroxo groups (O_{2}^{2-}$).

The sum of oxidation states in a neutral molecule is zero:

$x + 1(-2) + 2(-2) = 0$

$x - 2 - 4 = 0$

$x = +6$

Answer: $+6$

The basic character of the transition metal monoxides follows the order:
(Atomic nos. $\mathrm{Ti}=22, \mathrm{ V}=23, \mathrm{Cr}=24, \mathrm{Fe}=26$ )
questions.solution:
As we move from left side to right side in the first transition series atomic number of elements increases and no. of electrons also increases. Size of elements on moving left to right decreases because effective nuclear charge of nucleus on the outermost shell electron increases. It means electronegativity of atoms increases from left to right, then the power of donation of electrons decreases which means the basicity of that element decreases.
Caution
Students get confused on the order of size of elements in the series, because order of size of elements is not regular in the periods and groups. In periods of increasing atomic number size decreases and on the groups with the increase of atomic number size also increases.

questions.solution:
The balanced chemical equation for the oxidation of the complex is as given below

$\text{Mn}{\text{O}_{4}^{-} + 5 [ \text{Fe}\left({H}_{2}O\right){\left({C}_{2}{O}_{4}{)}_{2}\right]}^{2 -} + \text{8}{\text{H}^{+} \to 5{\left[\text{Fe}\left({H}_{2}O\right){\left({C}_{2}{O}_{4}\right)}_{2}\right]}^{-} + \text{M}{\text{n}^{2 +} + \text{4}{\text{H}_{2}O$

$\dfrac{\dfrac{d}{dt}\left[H^{+}\right]}{\dfrac{d}{dt} \left[Mn{O}_{4}^{-}\right]}$ =$8$

Rate of change of $\left[H^{+}\right]$ is 8 times the rate of change of $\left[Mn{O}_{4}^{-}\right]$.

questions.q:
Identify all the correct statements for Lanthanide contraction.
(A) The covalent properties of the Lanthanide metal hydroxides increases from $\mathrm{La}$ to $\mathrm{Lu}$.
(B) The chemical reactivity decreases from $\mathrm{La}$ to $\mathrm{Lu}$.
(C) $\mathrm{La}(\mathrm{OH})_3$ is more basic than $\mathrm{Lu}(\mathrm{OH})_3$
(D) Zr and Hf have about the same radius.
(E) Separation of Lanthanides from one another is easy
questions.solution: The change in ionic radii is Lanthanide series is very small, their chemical properties are small. Thus, the separation of Lanthanide is difficult due to consequence of Lanthanide contraction. The ionic radii of same positive charge of $\mathrm{La}$ to $\mathrm{Lu}$ decreases. So, the polarizing power towards hydroxyl group increases. Therefore the covalent character increases. Thus, $\mathrm{La}(\mathrm{OH})_3$ is more basic than $\mathrm{Lu}(\mathrm{OH})_3$. $\mathrm{Zr}$ and $\mathrm{Hf}$ have the almost same radius as the electrons in the elements after $\mathrm{Zr}$ are added into the deep seated $4 \mathrm{f}$ orbitals which do not take part in the chemical reaction.

questions.q: If ' $A$ ' is the reactant and ' $P$ ' is the product, which one of the following is the correct form of Nernst equation?

According to $Nernst equation :
\begin{aligned} & E=E^{{}^{\circ}}-\frac{R T}{n F} \ln \frac{[\text{ Product }]}{[\text{ Reactant }]} \\ & \text{ or, } \quad E=E^{{}^{\circ}}-\frac{R T}{n F} \ln \frac{[P]}{[A]} \\ & \text{ or, } \quad E-E^{{}^{\circ}}=-\frac{R T}{n F} \ln \left[\frac{P}{A}\right] \\ & \text{ or, } \quad\left[\frac{A}{P}\right]=e^{\left[\frac{n F}{R T}\left(E-E^{{}^{\circ}}\right)\right]} \\ & \text{$ or $} \quad \frac{[A]}{[P]}=\exp ^{\left[\frac{n F}{R T}\left(E-E^{{}^{\circ}}\right)\right]} \\ & \end{aligned}$
Hence, option (b) is the correct answer.

questions.solution:
The principle of conductometric titration is based on the fact that during the titration one of the ions is replaced by other and invariably these two ions differ in the ionic conductivity.

In the conductometric titration of $0. 05M{H}_{2}{SO}_{4}$ with $0. 1M{NH}_{4}OH$, initially the fast moving $H^{+}$ ion get neutralised as ${H}_{2}O$ and is replaced by slow moving ${NH}_{4}^{+}$ ion up to neutralisation point. After neutralisation point, weak electrolyte ${NH}_{4}OH$ is added gradually, which do not affect the conductance.

questions.q: Salts of $A$ (atomic weight $8$), $B$ (atomic weight $18$) and $C$ (atomic weight $50$) were electrolysed under identical conditions using the same quantity of electricity. It was found that $2. 4g$ of $A$ was deposited, the weight of $B$ and $C$ deposited are $1. 8g$ and $7. 5g$ respectively. The valences of $A, B$ and $C$ are, respectively,
questions.solution:
According to the Faraday's law of electrolysis,

$W = ZQ = \dfrac{E}{96500}Q$

For the compound $A$,

Equivalent mass of $A$ = $\dfrac{Atomicmass}{Valency} = \dfrac{8}{x}$

$x$ is the valency factor for compound $A$.

So, $W = \dfrac{E}{96500}Q = \dfrac{\dfrac{8}{x}}{96500}Qx = \dfrac{7}{2 . 4 \times 96500}Q$

For compound $B$,

Equivalent mass of $B$=$\dfrac{Atomicmass}{Valency} = \dfrac{18}{y}$

$y$ is the valency factor for compound $B$.

So, $W = \dfrac{E}{96500}Q = \dfrac{\dfrac{18}{y}}{96500}Qy = \dfrac{27}{1 . 8 \times 96500}Q$

For compound $C$,

Equivalent mass of $C$ = $\dfrac{Atomicmass}{Valency} = \dfrac{50}{z}$

$z$ is the valency factor for compound $C$.

So, $W = \dfrac{E}{96500}Q = \dfrac{\dfrac{50}{z}}{96500}Qz = \dfrac{50}{7 . 5 \times 96500}Q$

Hence, $x: y: z = \dfrac{8}{2 . 4}: \dfrac{18}{1 . 8}: \dfrac{50}{7 . 5} = 3 . 33: 10: 6 . 66x: y: z = 1: 3: 2$

Hence, the valencies of $A, B$ and $C$ respectively are $1, 3, 2$.

questions.q: Which of the following compound is not aromatic?
questions.solution:
Aromatic compounds satisfy $(4 n+2) \pi$ Huckel rule. (a) 1,3 -cyclobutene
Number of $\pi$ electrons $=4$ $\because$ It is not equal to $4 n+2$ $\therefore$ It is not an aromatic compound (b) Pyridine
Number of $\pi$ electrons $=6(=4 n+2)$ (Here lone pair of electrons of N does not evolve in delocalisation) (c) Furane
Number of $\pi$ electrons $=4+2=6(=4 n+2)$ (d) Thiophene
Number of $\pi$ electrons $=6(=4 n+2)$ Thus, except 1,3 -cyclobutene, all species are aromatic in nature.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q: According to Cahn-Ingold-Prelog sequence rules, the correct order of priority for the given groups is
questions.solution:
According to Cahn-Ingold-Prelog sequence rules, the priority of groups is decided by the atomic number of their atoms. When the atom (which is directly attached to the asymmetric carbon atom) of a group has higher atomic number, then the group gets higher priority. Groups with atoms of comparable atomic number having double or triple bond, have high priority than those have single bond.
Hence, the order of priority of groups is -$\mathrm{OH}$>-$\mathrm{COOH}$>-$\mathrm{CHO}$>-$\mathrm{CH}_{2} \mathrm{OH}$

C. meta-nitrophenol
D. para nitrophenol
the acidity order is
questions.solution:
An electron withdrawing group (-I showing group like $\left.-\mathrm{NO}_2,-\mathrm{CN}\right)$ stabilises the phenoxide ion, thus when present, increases the acidity of phenol. On the other hand electron releasing groups ($+I$ showing group like $-\mathrm{CH}_3,-\mathrm{C}_2 \mathrm{H}_5$), when present, decrease the acidity of phenol by destabilising phenoxide ion. Hence, the correct order of acidity of given compounds is
\(\underset{(D)}{\text{p-nitrophenol}}  \gt  \underset{(C)}{\text{m-nitrophenol}}  \gt  \underset{(A)}{\text{phenol}}  \gt  \underset{(B)}{\text{methyl phenol}}\)
(due to intermolecular H -bonding)

inhibits the incoming nucleophile which decrease the rate of reaction, therefore, alkyl halides having bulkier substituents
or higher degree alkyl halides preferably react through \( S N_{1} \) path. The order of reactivity for \( S_{N} 1 \) path is \( 1^{{}^{\circ}} > 2^{{}^{\circ}} > 3 \)

questions.q: The decreasing order of reactivity towards electrophilic substitution of the following compounds is
questions.solution:
Due to $+I$-effect of $-\mathrm{CH}_{3}$ group (4) has higher electron density, than benzene (1). Due to strong $-I$-effect of - Cl group and strong $-I$ and $-M$-effect of $-\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ group, both (2) and (3) have lower electron density, than benzene (l).
As - I-effect of -Cl group is weaker, than that of $-\mathrm{NO}_{2}$ (3) has much lower electron density than (2).
Hence, nitrobenzene will have high reactivity towards electrophilic substitution due to lower electron density on benzene ring.
Thus, the overall reactivity order towards electrophilic substitution is $4 > 1 > 2 > 3$.

questions.q: $20 \mathrm{ml}$ of $0.1 \mathrm{M}$ acetic acid is mixed with $50 \mathrm{ mL}$ of potassium acetate. $\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{a}}$ of acetic acid $=1.8 \times 10^{-5}$ at $27^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}.$ Calculate concentration of potassium acetate if $\mathrm{pH}$ of the mixture is $4.8$.
questions.solution:
Let the concentration of potassium acetate is $x$. According to Henderson's equation,

$\begin{array}{l}\mathrm{pH}=\mathrm{pK}_{\mathrm{a}}+\log \frac{[\mathrm{salt}]}{[\mathrm{acid}]}\\
4.8=-\log \left(1.8 \times10^{-5}\right)+\log \frac{x \times 50}{20 \times 0.1 \mathrm{M}}\\
4.8=4.74+\log 25 x \\
\text{ or } \log25 x=0.06
\end{array} \begin{array}{l}25 x=1.148 \\
\therefore x=0.045 \mathrm{M}
\end{array}$

For the indicator, HIn; the ratio& $\dfrac{\left[{In}^{-}\right]}{\left[\text{HIn}\right]}$ is $7 .0$ at pH of $4 .3$. ${K}_{\text{In}}$ for the indicator is

[ Given: $log7 = 0 .845$ and Antilog $( - 3.455 ) = 3.5 \times {10}^{- 4}$ ]
questions.solution:
For weak organic acid indicators

$\text{pH} = {\text{pK}_{\text{In}} + \text\log\dfrac{\left[{\text{In}^{−}\right]}{\left[\text{HIn}\right]}$

$\text{4}\text{.3} = {\text{pK}_{\text{In}} + \text{log 7}$

${\text{pK}_{\text{In}} = 4.3 - 0.845 = 3.455$

${\text{pK}_{\text{In}} = - {\text\log}_{\text{10}} {K}_{\text{In}}$

${K}_{\text{In}} = \text{Antilog} \left(- {\text{pK}_{\text{In}}\right)$

${K}_{\text{In}$}$ = \text{Antilog} \left(-3.455\right)$

$= 3.5 \times {10}^{- 4}$

questions.q: The first and second dissociation constants of an acid $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{A}$ are $1.0 \times 10^{-5}$ and $5.0 \times 10^{-10}$ respectively. The overall dissociation constant of the acid will be
questions.solution:
$\begin{array}{ll}\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{A} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{HA}^{-}+\mathrmH^{+} & \mathrm{K}_1=\frac{\left[\mathrm{HA}^{-}\right]\left[\mathrmH^{+}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{A}\right]} \quad \dots (1)\\ \mathrm{HA}^{-} \rightleftharpoons \mathrmH^{+}+\mathrmA^{2-} & \mathrm{K}_2=\frac{\left[\mathrmH^{+}\right]\left[\mathrmA^{2-}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{HA}^{-}\right]}\quad \dots(2)\end{array}
For the reaction \begin{aligned}& \mathrm{H}_{2} \mathrm{A} \rightleftharpoons2 \mathrmH^{+}+\mathrmA^{2-} \\
& \mathrm{K}=\frac{\left[\mathrmH^{+}\right]^2\left[\mathrm{ A}^{2-}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{A}\right]}=\mathrm{K}_{1} \times \mathrm{K}_{2} \\
& =1 \times10^{-5} \times5 \times10^{-10} \\
& =5 \times10^{-15}
\end{aligned}$
Hence, (C) is correct.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
In an aqueous solution, the ionization constants for carbonic acid are

${K}_{1} = \text{4.2} \times 1 {0}^{- 7}$ and ${ K}_{2} = \text{4.8} \times 1 {0}^{- 11}$

Select the correct statement for a saturated $\text{0.034 M}$ solution of the carbonic acid:
options: The concentration of $H^{+}$ is double that of ${CO}_{3}^{2 -}$.
The concentration of ${CO}_{3}^{2 -}$ is greater than that of ${HCO}_{3}^{-}$.
The concentration of $H^{+}$ and ${HCO}_{3}^{-}$ are approximately equal.
questions.solution:
$\begin{cases}{H}_{2} {CO}_{3} & ⇌ & H^{+} & + & {HCO}_{3}^{-} \text{;} & {K}_{1} & = & \text{4.2} \times 1 {0}^{- 7} \\ {HCO}_{3}^{-} & ⇌ & H^{+} & + & {CO}_{3}^{2 -} \text{;} & {K}_{2} & = & \text{4.8} \times 1 {0}^{- 1 1}\end{cases}$

$∵ {K}_{1} ≫ {K}_{2}$, so ${H}_{2} {CO}_{3}$ ionises more than ${HCO}_{3}^{-}$ and hence, contribution of $H^{+}$ is mostly due to ionization of carbonic acid. Thus, the concentrations of $H^{+}$ and ${HCO}_{3}^{-}$ are approximately equal.

Let the volume of $\mathrm{KCN}$ solution required be $V \mathrm{ mL}\therefore \quad[\mathrm{KCN}]=\frac{5 \times V}{V+10}$ and $[\mathrm{HCN}]=\frac{10 \times 2}{V+10}$
Now from eqn. (i),

On solving, $V=1.99 \approx 2 \mathrm{ mL}$

Given, that $\mathrm{pH}=5.74, \mathrm{pK}_{a}=4.74$

From Henderson equation,

$\mathrm{pH}=\mathrm{p}K_{\mathrm{a}$}+$\log\frac{[\mathrm{Salt}]}{[\mathrm{Acid}]}$ or, $\mathrm{pH}-\mathrm{p}$ K_{$\mathrm{a}$}=$\log \frac{\left[\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COONa}\right]$}{$\left[\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}\right]$}$

or $\frac{\left.\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COONa}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}\right]}=10$
or $\frac{\left[\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COOH}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{CH}_{3} \mathrm{COONa}\right]}=\frac{1}{10}=\frac{\frac{x+y}{0.1 \mathrm{y}}}{\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{y}}$
Thus, $\frac{x}{y}=\frac{1}{10}$

questions.q: The standard half-cell reduction potential for $\mathrm{Ag}^{+} \mid \mathrm{Ag}$ is $0.7991 \mathrm{ V}$ at $25^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$. Given the experimental value $K_{s p}=1.56 \times 10^{-10}$ for $\mathrm{AgCl}$, calculate the standard half-cell reduction potential for the $\mathrm{Ag} \mid \mathrm{AgCl}$ electrode.
questions.solution:
For the desired reaction, $\mathrm{AgCl}+1 e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag}+\mathrm{Cl}^{-}, \quad$ E^{{}^{\circ}}=$\frac{-\Delta_r G^{{}^{\circ}}}{(1) F}$ The needed $\Delta_r G^{{}^{\circ}}$ can be obtained by adding the values of $\Delta_r G^{{}^{\circ}}$ for the reactions $\begin{aligned}& \mathrm{Ag}^{+}+1 e^{-} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag}; \Delta G^{{}^{\circ}}=-n F E^{{}^{\circ}} \\
& \mathrm{AgCl} \rightarrow \mathrm{Ag}^{+}+\mathrm{Cl}^{-}; \Delta G^{{}^{\circ}}=-R T \ln K_{s p}, \text{ giving }\\
& \Delta_r G^{{}^{\circ}}=-(1 \mathrm{ mol})\left(9.648 \times10^4 \mathrm{ J} \mathrm{ mol}{ }^{-1} \mathrm{ V}^{-1}\right)(0.7991 \mathrm{ V})\\
& \quad-\left(8.314 \mathrm{JK}^{-1} \mathrm{ mol}^{-1}\right)(298 \mathrm{ K}) \ln \left(1.56 \times10^{-10}\right) \\
& =-77.10 \mathrm{ kJ}+55.95 \mathrm{ kJ}=-21.15 \mathrm{ kJ}
\end{aligned}$ The potential is $E^{{}^{\circ}$}=$\frac{-(-21.15)}{(1)(96.485)}=+0.2192 \mathrm{ V}.$

questions.solution:
Given the solubility of ${Ca}_{3}\left({PO}_{4}\right)2$ is $Wg / 100mL$. The solubility in $mol / L$ is $S = \dfrac{W}{M} \times \dfrac{1000}{100}mol / L$.

The equilibrium reaction of calcium phosphate is

$\begin{cases} & {Ca}_{3}\left({PO}_{4}\right)2 & \overset{}{⇌} & 3{Ca}^{2 +} & + & 2{PO}_{4}^{3 -} \\ Atequilibrium & & & 3S & & 2S\end{cases}$

Now, ${K}_{sp} = \left[{Ca}^{2 +}\right]3\left[{PO}_{4}^{3 -}\right]2$

$⇒ {K}_{sp} = \left(3S\right)3\left(2S\right)2 = 108 \times S^{5}$

$⇒ {K}_{sp} = 108 \times \left(\dfrac{W}{M} \times 10\right)5 ⇒ {K}_{sp} = 108 \times {10}^{5} \times \left(\dfrac{W}{M}\right)5$

$= 1 . 08 \times {10}^{7}\left(\dfrac{W}{M}\right)5$

questions.q: In qualitative analysis, the metals of group I can be separated from other ions by precipitating them as chloride salts. \therefore \quad\left[\mathrm{Pb}^{2+}\right]& =\frac{1.7 \times 10^{-5}}{10^{-1} \times 10^{-1}}\\

\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
Identify the correct statement for ${B}_{2}{H}_{6}$ from those given below.

(A) In ${B}_{2}{H}_{6}$, all $B - H$ bonds are equivalent.

(B) In ${B}_{2}{H}_{6}$, there are four $3$-centre- $2$-electron bonds.

(C) ${B}_{2}{H}_{6}$ is a Lewis acid.

(D) ${B}_{2}{H}_{6}$ can be synthesized from both ${BF}_{3}$ and ${NaBH}_{4}$.

(E) ${B}_{2}{H}_{6}$ is a planar molecule.

Choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :
questions.solution:
${B}_{2}{H}_{6}$ have $four2c - 2e$ bonds and $two3c - 2e$ bonds. Bridging bonds have larger bond length than terminal bonds. Angle between terminal bonds is more than angle between bridging bonds if all $4$ terminal bonds are in one plane then bridging bonds are in perpendicular plane.

$3{NaBH}_{4} + 4{BF}_{3}\mathop{⟶ ether}_{450K}3{NaBF}_{4} + 2{B}_{2}{H}_{6}$

Therefore we can say that only statement (C) and (D) are correct.&

$\mathrm{B}(\mathrm{OH})_3+\mathrm{NaOH} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NaBO}_2+\mathrm{Na}\left[\mathrm{B}(\mathrm{OH})_4\right]+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{O}$.
How can this reaction is made to proceed in forward direction?
questions.solution:
This reaction is reversible reaction because sodium metaborate, $\mathrm{Na}^{+}\left[\mathrm{B}(\mathrm{OH})_4\right]^{-}$ formed by the reaction between $\mathrm{B}(\mathrm{OH})_3$ and $\mathrm{NaOH}$ gets hydrolysed to regenerate $\mathrm{B}(\mathrm{OH})_3$ and $\mathrm{NaOH}$
If, some quantity of polyhydroxy compound like cis-1, 3-diol, catechol, glycerol etc. is added to the reaction mixture. The $\mathrm{B}(\mathrm{OH})_3$ combines with such polyhydroxy compound to give chelated complex compound. Due to complex compound formation, stability increases and due to higher stability of complex, reaction moves in forward direction.

questions.q: The elements with the highest and the lowest enthalpy of atomisation respectively, for first row transition elements are:
questions.solution:
The enthalpy of atomisation is the enthalpy change that accompanies the total separation of all atoms in a chemical substance.

The extent of metallic bonding an element undergoes decides the enthalpy of atomization. The more extensive the metallic bonding of an element, the more will be its enthalpy of atomisation.

$Sc$ has the& lowest enthalpy of atomisation, for& first row of transition elements& and $Zn ( 4d^{10}5s^{2} )$ has completely filled $d -$orbital and has no unpaired electron to take part in the formation of metallic bonds. So, the metallic bonding in zinc& is the weakest and it has the least& enthalpy of atomisation.

questions.q: A compound contains three elements X, Y and Z. The oxidation number of X, Y and Z are $+ 3, + 5$ and $- 2$ respectively. The possible formula of the compound is
questions.solution:
The sum of all oxidation values must be equal to zero. Let, number of atoms of X, Y and Z are respectively a, b and c.

Then, $( + 3 ) ext{a} + ( + 5 ) ext{b} + ( - 2 ) ext{c} = 0$

Or

$3 ext{a} + 5 ext{b} - 2 ext{c} = 0$

Now, putting values of a, b and c for all the given options, which will give sum equal to zero, will be our formula.

(a) For, ${ ext{X}_{2} ext{Y} ext{Z}$

$ ext{a} = 2$

$ ext{b} = 1$

$ ext{c} = 1$

Thus, $3 ext{a} + 5 ext{b} - 2 ext{c} = 0$

$3 imes 2 + 5 - 2 e 0$

(b) For, $ ext{X} ext{Y}{ ext{Z}_{3}$

$ ext{a} = 1, ext{b} = 1, ext{c} = 3$

$3 ext{a} + 5 ext{b} - 2 ext{c} = 0$

$3 + 5 - 6 e 0$

(c) ${ ext{X}_{3}{( ext{Y}{ ext{Z}_{4} )}_{3}$

$ ext{a} = 3, ext{b} = 3, ext{c} = 12$

$3 ext{a} + 5 ext{b} - 2 ext{c} = 0$

$( 3 imes 3 + 5 imes 3 ) - ( 2 imes 12 ) = 0$

$9 + 15 - 24$

$24 - 24 = 0$

(d) ${ ext{X}_{2}{ ext{Y}_{2} ext{Z}$

$ ext{a} = 2, ext{b} = 2, ext{c} = 1$

$3 ext{a} + 5 ext{b} - 2 ext{c} = 0$

$( 3 imes 2 ) + ( 5 imes 2 ) - ( 2 imes 1 ) = 0$

$6 + 10 - 2 e 0$

Hence, option (c) is the correct answer.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
From the given reactions identify the disproportionation reaction
i) ${Cl}_{2} ( g ) + 2KI ( aq ) ⟶ 2KCl ( aq ) + {I}_{2} ( s )$
ii) ${Cl}_{2} ( g ) + 2{OH}^{-} ( aq ) ⟶ {ClO}^{-} ( aq ) + {Cl}^{-} ( aq ) + {H}_{2}O ( l )$
iii) $Mg ( s ) + 2HCl ( aq ) ⟶ {MgCl}_{2} ( aq ) + {H}_{2} ( g )$
iv) $2{H}_{2}{O}_{2} ( aq ) ⟶ 2{H}_{2}O ( l ) + {O}_{2} ( g )$
questions.solution:
The reaction in which one reactant gets oxidized, and the same reactant gets reduced is known as disproportionation reaction.&

$\overset{0}{Cl}2 ( g ) + 2K\overset{- 1}{I} ( aq ) ⟶ 2K\overset{0}{C}l ( aq ) + \overset{- 1}{I}2 ( s )$

In the above reaction different elements undergoing oxidation and reduction. Hence, It is not a disproportionation reaction.&

$\overset{0}{Cl}2 ( g ) + 2{OH}^{-} ( aq ) ⟶ \overset{+ 1}{Cl}O^{-} ( aq ) + {Cl}^{-} ( aq ) + {H}_{2}O ( l )$

In the above reaction chlorine is undergoing oxidation as well as reduction. Hence, It is a disproportionation reaction.&

$\overset{0}{Mg} ( s ) + 2\overset{+ 1}{H}Cl ( aq ) ⟶ \overset{+ 2}{Mg}{Cl}_{2} ( aq ) + \overset{0}{H}2 ( g )$

In the above reaction magnesium is undergoing oxidation and hydrogen ion undergoing reduction. Hence, It is not a& disproportionation reaction.&

$2{H}_{2}\overset{- 1}{O}2 ( aq ) ⟶ 2{H}_{2}\overset{- 2}{O} ( l ) + \overset{0}{O}2 ( g )$

In the above reaction peroxide is undergoing oxidation as well as reduction.& Hence, It is a disproportionation reaction.&

questions.q:
What will be the value of x, y and $z$ in the following equation?
${H}_{2}{C}_{2}{O}_{4} + x{H}_{2}{O}_{2} \to yC{O}_{2} + z{H}_{2}O$
questions.solution:
(i) The half reaction for oxidation is,
${H}_{2}{C}_{2}{O}_{4} \to C{O}_{2}$
Balancing carbon atoms on both sides, ${H}_{2}{C}_{2}{O}_{4} \to 2C{O}_{2}$
Balancing hydrogen atoms on both sides, ${H}_{2}{C}_{2}{O}_{4} \to 2C{O}_{2} + 2H^{+}$
Balancing the charge on both sides,
${H}_{2}{C}_{2}{O}_{4} \to 2C{O}_{2} + 2H^{+} + 2e^{-}$...(i)
(ii) The half reaction for reduction is‐ ${H}_{2} {O}_{2} \to {H}_{2} \text{O}$
Balancing oxygen atoms on both sides, ${H}_{2}{O}_{2} \to 2{H}_{2}O$
Balancing hydrogen atoms, ${H}_{2}{O}_{2} + 2H^{+} \to 2{H}_{2}O$
Balancing the charge,
${H}_{2}{O}_{2} + 2H^{+} + 2e^{-} \to 2{H}_{2}O$...(ii)
Now, adding both equations, ${H}_{2}{C}_{2}{O}_{4} + {H}_{2}{O}_{2} \to 2C{O}_{2} + 2{H}_{2}O$
This is balanced equation so x, y, z are 1,2,2 respectively.

In titration at equivalence& point, number of equivalents of both reactants must be same.

$∴ {N}_{1}{V}_{1} = {N}_{2}{V}_{2}$

$N$ (normality) of ${FeCl}_{2} = \dfrac{\left(N \times V\right)of{K}_{2}{Cr}_{2}{O}_{7}}{Vof{FeCl}_{2}}$

$N$ (normality) of ${K}_{2}{Cr}_{2}{O}_{7} = \dfrac{Mass \times 1000}{Equivalentmass \times Volumeofsolutionprepared}$

Equivalent mass $= \dfrac{Molarmass}{nfactor}$

$= \dfrac{294}{6}$

$= 49g / equi.$

(${K}_{2}{Cr}_{2}{O}_{7}$ as oxidising agent is reduced to $2{Cr}^{3 +}$).

Oxidation state of $2Cr$ atoms change from $+ 6$ to $+ 3$.

Total change is$3 \times 2 = 6$, ($∴ n$-factor $= 6$)

$∴ N$ (of ${K}_{2}{Cr}_{2}{O}_{7}$) $= \dfrac{1225 \times 1000}{49 \times 250} = 0. 1N$

$∴ N$ (of ${FeCl}_{2}$) $= \dfrac{0. 1 \times 25}{10}$

$= 0. 25N$

questions.q: A mixture of two miscible liquids $A$ and $B$ is distilled under equilibrium conditions at $1 \mathrm{ atm}$ pressure. The mole fraction of $A$ in solution and vapour phase are 0.30 and 0.60 respectively. Assuming ideal behaviour of the solution and the vapour, calculate the ratio of the vapour pressure of pure $A$ to that of pure $B$
questions.solution:
In solution, $x_A=0.30 ; x_B=0.70$
In vapour phase, $x_A^{\prime}=0.60 ; x_B^{\prime}=0.40$
Using Dalton's law and Raoult's law
$\begin{aligned} & x_A^{\prime}=0.60=\frac{p_A}{P}=\frac{p_A}{p_A+p_B}=\frac{0.30 p_A^{{}^{\circ}}}{0.30 p_A^{{}^{\circ}}+0.70 p_B^{{}^{\circ}}} \\ & x_B^{\prime}=0.40=\frac{p_B}{P}=\frac{p_B}{p_A+p_B}=\frac{0.70 p_B^{{}^{\circ}}}{0.30 p_A^{{}^{\circ}}+0.70 p_B^{{}^{\circ}}} \\ & \frac{x_A^{\prime}}{x_B^{\prime}}=\frac{0.60}{0.40}=\frac{0.30 p_A^{{}^{\circ}}}{0.70 p_B^{{}^{\circ}}} \\ & \frac{p_A^{{}^{\circ}}}{p_B^{{}^{\circ}}}=\frac{0.60 \times 0.70}{0.40 \times 0.30}=\frac{7}{2}=3.5\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
A solution contains non-volatile solute of molecular mass $M_2$. Which of the following can be used to calculate the molecular mass of the solute in terms of the osmotic pressure?
Note: $m_2$ is the mass of the solute, $\mathrm{V}$ is the volume of the solution and $\pi$ is the osmotic pressure.
questions.solution:
For dilute solution, the $van't Hoff equation is:
\begin{aligned}
\pi & =\frac{n}{\mathrm{ V}} \mathrm{RT} \\
\pi \mathrm{V} & =\frac{m_2}{\mathrm{M}} \mathrm{RT} \\
\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{M} & =\frac{m_2 \mathrm{RT}}{\pi \mathrm{V}}
\end{aligned}$
Van't Hoff explained that when solutes are dissolved in a solvent they dissociate into ions. Since colligative properties depend only on the number of solute particles, the dissociation of solute molecules into ions results in an increase in the number of particles and hence affects the colligative properties.

An electrolyte \(\mathrm{MX}_{2}\) undergoes dissociation as follows :-

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|}

\end{array}$$\)
Thus from the above condition we can say that,
\(\mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{sp}}=\mathrm{s} \times(2  \mathrm{ s})^2=4 \times(\mathrm{s})^3\)

\(\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \mathrm{K}_{\mathrm{sp}}=4 \times\left(0.5 \times10^{-4}\right)^3 \\

The relation between temperature and vapor pressure is given by the Clausius-Clapeyron equation.

Case $II$, at ${X}_{X} = 1$

${p}_{T} = {p}_X^{0}

One of its examples is the use of ethylene glycol and water mixture as anti-freezing liquid in the radiator automobiles. A solution $M$ is prepared by mixing ethanol and water. The mole fraction of ethanol in the mixtrue is $0.9$ Given Freezing point depression constant of water $\left(k^{\text{water }}\right)=1.86 \mathrm{~K} \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ Freezing point depression constant of ethanol $\left(k_f^{\text{ethanol }}\right)=2.0 \mathrm{Kkg} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ Boiling point elevation constant of water $\left(k_b^{\text{water }}\right)=0.52 \mathrm{Kkg} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ Boiling point elevation constant of ethanol $\left(k_b^{\text{ethanol }}\right)=1.2 \mathrm{Kkg} \mathrm{mol}^{-1}$ Standard freezing point of water $=273 \mathrm{~K}$ Standard freezing point of ethanol $=155.7 \mathrm{~K}$ Standard boiling point of water $=373 \mathrm{~K}$ Standard boiling point of ethanol $=351.5 \mathrm{~K}$ Vapour pressure of pure water $=328 \mathrm{~mm} of \mathrm{Hg}$ Vapour pressure of pure ethanol $=40 \mathrm{~mm} of \mathrm{Hg}$ Molecular weight of water $=18 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ Molecular weight of ethanol $=46 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~mol}^{-1}$ In answering the following questions, consider the solutions to be ideal dilute solutions and solutes to be non-volatile and non-dissociative.Question: The freezing point of the solution $M$ is

Solution $M$ is mixture of ethanol and water.

questions.q:
Formation of a solution from two components can be considered as:
(i) Pure solvent → separated solvent molecules $\Delta \mathrm{H}_1$
(ii) Pure solute → separated solute molecules, $\Delta \mathrm{H}_2$
(iii) Separated solvent and solute molecules → solution, $\Delta \mathrm{H}_3$
Solution so formed will be ideal of:
questions.solution: So the enthalpy of solution can either be endothermic, exothermic or neither $(\Delta$ Hsolution $=0)$, depending on how much heat is required or release in each step. If $\Delta Hsolution $= 0 , then the solution is called an ideal solution and if $\Delta Hsolution > 0 or $\Delta Hsolution$< 0$, then these solutions are called non-ideal solutions. Related Theory The enthalpy of solution depends on the strengths of intermolecular forces of the solute and solvent. If the solution is ideal, and $\Delta \mathrm{H}  solution $=0$, then  \begin{aligned} & \Delta H_{\text{solution }}=$\Delta H_1+\Delta H_2+\Delta H_3=0 \\ & \Delta H_1+\Delta H_2=-\Delta H_3 \end{aligned}

At $30^{{}^{\circ}} \mathrm{C}$, the total vapour pressure of a solution containing $1 \mathrm{ mol}$ of A and $2 \mathrm{ mol}$ of B is $250 \mathrm{ mm} \mathrm{Hg}$. The total vapour pressure becomes $300 \mathrm{ mm} \mathrm{Hg}$ when 1 more mol of $\mathrm{A}$ is added to the first solution. questions.solution:
Let vapour pressure of $A=P_A^0$
Vapour pressure of $B=P_B^0$
In first solution,
Mole fraction of $A\left(x_A\right)=\frac{1}{1+2}=\frac{1}{3}$
Mole fraction of $B\left(x_B\right)=\frac{2}{1+2}=\frac{2}{3}$
According to Raoult's law,
Total vapour pressure $\begin{aligned}$& =250=P_A^0 x_A+P_B^0 x_B \\
& 250=$\frac{1}{3}$ P_A^0+$\frac{2}{3}$P_B^0
\end{aligned}$ In second solution
Mole fraction of A\left(x_A\right)=\frac{2}{2+2}=\frac{2}{4}=\frac{1}{2}$
Mole fraction of $B\left(x_B\right)=\frac{2}{4}=\frac{1}{2}\therefore$ Total vapour pressure $\begin{aligned}$& =300=P_A^0 x_A+P_B^0 x_B \\
& 300=$\frac{1}{2}$ P_A^0+$\frac{1}{2}$ P_B^0
\end{aligned} Multiplying equation (i) by $\frac{1}{2}$ and equation (ii) by $\frac{1}{3} \begin{aligned}$& $\frac{1}{6}$ P_A^0+$\frac{2}{6}$ P_B^0=125 \\
& $\frac{1}{6}$ P_A^0+$\frac{1}{6}$ P_B^0=100 \\
& $\frac{1}{6}$ P_B^0=25 \\
& P_B^0=25 $\times6=150 \mathrm{ mm} \mathrm{Hg}
\end{aligned}$ On substituting value of $P_B^0$ in equation
(ii) we get $\begin{aligned}$& 300=P_A^0 $\times \frac{1}{2}+150 \times \frac{1}{2}$\\
& P_A^0=450 $\mathrm{ mm} \mathrm{Hg}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: The mole fraction of a solute in a binary solution is $0.1 .$ At $298 \mathrm{~K}$, molarity of this solution is same as as its molality. Density of this solution at $298 \mathrm{~K}$ is $2.0 \mathrm{~g} \mathrm{~cm}^{-3}$. The ratio of molecular weights of the solute and the solvent $\left(\mathrm{M}_{\text{solute }} / \mathrm{M}_{\text{solvent }}\right)$ is
questions.solution: $\mathrm{X}_{2}=0.1 \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{n}_{2}}{\mathrm{n}_{2}+\mathrm{n}_{1}}=0.1\ldots(1)\mathrm{M}=\frac{\mathrm{W}_{2} \times 1000}{\mathrm{M}_{2} \times \mathrm{W}} \times \mathrm{d}\ldots(2)\mathrm{m}=\frac{\mathrm{W}_{2} \times 1000}{\mathrm{M}_{2} \times \mathrm{W}_{1}(\mathrm{ g})}\ldots(3)\mathrm{d}=2 \mathrm{ g} / \mathrm{cc}\ldots(4)$ Given M = m (numerically) $\begin{array}{l} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{W}_{2} \times 1000}{\mathrm{M}_{2} \times\left(\mathrm{W}_{2}+\mathrm{W}_{1}\right)} \times \mathrm{d}=\frac{\mathrm{W}_{2} \times 1000}{\mathrm{M}_{2} \times \mathrm{W}_{1}(\mathrm{ g})} \\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{W}_{2}+\mathrm{W}_{1}=\mathrm{W}_{1} \times \mathrm{d}=2 \mathrm{ W}_{1} \\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{W}_{2}=\mathrm{W}_{1} \end{array} Now, \frac{n_{2}}{n_{2}+n_{1}}=0.1 \Rightarrow \frac{\frac{w_{2}}{M_{2}}}{\frac{W_{2}}{M_{2}}+\frac{W_{1}}{M_{1}}}=0.1 \Rightarrow \frac{\frac{W_{2}}{M_{2}}}{W_{2}\left(\frac{1}{M_{2}}+\frac{1}{M_{1}}\right)}=0.1\Rightarrow \frac{\frac{1}{\mathrm{M}_{2}}}{\frac{\mathrm{M}_{1}+\mathrm{M}_{2}}{\mathrm{M}_{1} \mathrm{M}_{2}}}=0.1 \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{M}_{1}}{\mathrm{M}_{1}+\mathrm{M}_{2}}=\frac{1}{10} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{M}_{1}}{\mathrm{M}_{1}+\mathrm{M}_{2}-\mathrm{M}_{1}}=\frac{1}{10-1} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{M}_{1}}{\mathrm{M}_{2}}=\frac{1}{9} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{M}_{2}}{\mathrm{M}_{1}}=9$

questions.q: Calculate the molality of KI if the density of 20% (mass/mass) aqueous KI is 1.202 gmL<sup>-1</sup>. Report your final answer by rounding off the molality correct upto one place of decimal and then multiplying it by 10.
questions.solution:
Weight of KI in 100g of water = 20 g

Weight of water in the solution = 100 - 20 = 80 g= 0.08 kg

Molar mass of KI = 39 + 127 = 166 g mol-1

$\text{Molality of the solution (m)} = \dfrac{\text{Number of moles of KI}}{\text{Mass of water in kg}}$

$= \dfrac{\left(2 0 \text{g}\right) / \left(1 6 6 \text{g} {\text{mol}}^{- 1}\right)}{\left(0 \cdot 0 8 \text{kg}\right)}$

= 1.506 mol kg-1 = 1.506 m

By rounding off to one place, we get the molality as 1.5 and by further multiplying it with 10, we get "15" as the final answer.

$\dfrac{{M}_{solute}}{{M}_{solvent}} = 9$

questions.q: An unknown compound A ${C}_{8}{H}_{10}{O}_{3}$ on acetylation with $C{H}_{3}COCl / Py$ forms acetyl derivative of A whose MW is 280. A on treat with $C{H}_{2}{N}_{2}$ gives methyl ether of B having MW 182. If the number of phenolic hydroxyls and alcoholic hydroxyls in the compound A are X and Y respectively. Find the sum of X + Y here?
questions.solution:
Number of hydroxyl group by acetylation method $\text{=}\dfrac{\text{280} - \text{MW}\text{of}{\text{C}}_{\text{8}} {\text{H}}_{\text{10}} {\text{O}}_{\text{3}}}{\text{42}}$
$= \dfrac{280 - 154}{42} = \dfrac{126}{42} = 3$
Number of phenolic hydroxyl $\text{=}\dfrac{\text{MW}\text{of}\text{methyl}\text{ether} - \text{MW}}{\text{14}}$
$= \dfrac{182 - 154}{14} = \dfrac{28}{14} = 2$
Hence, X = 2
Number of alcoholic $- OH$ groups $= 3 - 2 = 1$
Hence, Y = 1
So X + Y = 2 + 1 = 3.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
What mass of $95 %$ pure ${CaCO}_{3}$ will be required to neutralise $50mL of 0. 5MHCl$ solution according to the following reaction?

${CaCO}_{3\left(s\right)} + 2HCl \left(aq\right) \to {CaCl}_{2 \left(aq\right)} + ${CO}_{2$\left(g\right)$} +2{H}_{2}O$\left(l\right)$

[Calculate upto second place of decimal point]
questions.solution:
\(\$underset{(s)}{\mathrm{CaCO}_3}+\underset{50  \mathrm{ mL},0.5 $\mathrm{M}$}${2  \mathrm{HCl}(\mathrm{aq})$} \longrightarrow \underset{(\m$mathrm{aq})}{\mathrm{CaCl}_2}+\$underset{(g)}{$\mathrm{CO}_2$}+\underset{(l)}{2 \mathrm{H}}_{2} $\mathrm{O}$}\)
the number of moles of HCl taken \(=0.5 \times0.05\)
\(=0.025\) moles
As we can see that from the above balanced equation is one mole of \($\mathrm{CaCO}$}_{3}(s)\) requires 2 moles of \(\mathrm{HCl}(\mathrm{aq})\) therefore, for 0.025 moles of \(\mathrm{HCl}(\mathrm{aq}),$0.0125\) moles of \(\mathrm{CaCO}}_{3}(s)\) will be required.
Mass of 0.0125 moles of \($\mathrm{CaCO}$}_{3}(s)=0.0125 \times\) molar mass of \(\mathrm{CaCO}}_{3}\)
\$(\begin{aligned}$& =0.0125 \times100 \\
& =1.25 $\mathrm{ g}$
\end{aligned}\)
But purity of \($\mathrm{CaCO}$}_{3}(s)\) is \(95 \%\). Therefore, the actual amount of \( $\mathrm{CaCO}$}_{3}(s)\) required is
Percentage purity \$(=\frac{\text{ weight of pure substance }}{\text{ weight of impure sample }} \times$100\)
\$(95=\frac{1.25}{\text{ weight of impure sample }} \times$100\)
weight of impure sample \$=\frac{1.25 \times 100}{95}$
\(=1.32 $\mathrm{ g}$\)
Hence. option 1 is correct.

${\left(C^{3 +}\right)}_{2} \to 2C^{4 +} + 2e$
$Mn^{7 +} + 5e \to Mn^{2 +}$
$\text{Meq}\text{.}\text{of}\text{CaO}\text{=}\text{Meq}\text{.}\text{of}{\text{CaCO}_{3} \text{=}\text{Meq}\text{.}\text{of}{H}_{2} {C}_{2} {O}_{4}$
$\text{=}\text{Meq}\text{.}\text{of}{\text{CaC}_{2} {O}_{4} \text{=}\text{Meq}\text{.}\text{of}{\text{KMnO}_{4}$
Hence $\text{Meq}\text{.}\text{of}\text{CaO}\text{=}\text{Meq}\text{.}\text{of}{\text{KMnO}_{4}$
$\left[w / ( 56 / 2 )\right] \times 1000 = 45 \times 0.2$
So $\text{wt}\text{.}\text{of}\text{CaO}\text{=}\text{0}\text{.252}\text{g}$
Here % of $CaO$ in lime stone = $\left(\dfrac{0.252}{0.256}\right) \times 100 = 45%$

Mol. wt. of $C{H}_{4} = 16$

Solutions having same osmotic pressure, at a given temperature, have same concentration. Concentration of compound $=$ concentration of glucose

Related Theory
Moderators are used to slow down the neutrons produced from fission. questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.q:
An element undergoes a reaction as shown :

$\text{X} + 2 e^{-} \to X^{2 -}$, energy released $= 30.87 eV / atom$. If the energy released is used to dissociate $4gms$ of ${H}_{2}$ molecules, equally into $H^{+}$ and $H^{*}$, where $H^{*}$ is excited state of $H$ atoms where the electron travels in orbit whose circumference equal to four times its de Broglie's wavelength. Determine the least moles of $X$ that would be required:

Given: I.E. of $H = 13.6 eV / atom$ bond energy of ${H}_{2} = 4.526 eV / molecule$.
questions.solution:
Total energy requirement per molecule of ${H}_{2}$:

Binding energy $\text{=4}\text{.526 eV}$

$\text{I}\text{.E}\text{=}\text{13}\text{.60}\text{eV}$

According to de Broglie's explanation of Bohr's orbit-

${\text{2 \pi r}}_{n} = \text{n \lambda}$

As per question, $\text{2 \pi r} = \text{4 \lambda}$

Thus, electron is excited to the 4th Bohr orbit

Excitation energy~$= {E}_{4} - {E}_{1} = - 0 .85 - \left(- 13 .60\right) = 12 .75 eV$~

Thus, total eenergy requirement per molecule $= 13 .60 + 12 .75 + 4 .526 ≅ 30 .87 eV$

Thus, $\text{1}$ molecule of ${H}_{2}$ will be dissociated by $\text{1}$ atom of $\text{X}$

Therefore, $\left(4{gH}_{2}\right) ≡ 2$~moles of ${H}_{2}$ molecules will be dissociated by $2$ moles of $X$.

An electron beam can undergo diffraction by crystals. The potential of 'V' volt should a beam of electrons be accelerated so that its wavelength becomes equal to $1.0Å$ . The value of 'V' is

We know that

questions.q: According to Bohr's theory $E_n=$ Total energy, $K_n=$ Kinetic energy, $V_n=$ Potential energy, $r_n=$ Radius of $n$th orbit
questions.solution:
According to Bohr's theory,
Total energy is $E_n=K_n+V_n$
Kinetic energy $=K_n=\frac{1}{8 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{Z e^2}{r}$
Potential energy $=V_n=\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{Z e^2}{r}\therefore \quad E_n=\frac{1}{8 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{Z e^2}{r}-\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{Z e^2}{r}$
Radius of $n$th orbit $\left(r_n\right)=\frac{n^2 h^2 \varepsilon_0}{\pi m Z e^2}$ E_n=-$\frac{m e^4}{8 \varepsilon_0^2 h^2} \times \frac{1}{n^2}  ($A) $\frac{V_n}{K_n}=\frac{-\frac{1}{4 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{Z e^2}{r}}{\frac{1}{8 \pi \varepsilon_0} \cdot \frac{Z e^2}{r}}=-2$
Hence, $(A)$ match with $(R)$.
(B) $E_n \propto \frac{1}{n^2}$ or $E_n \propto \frac{1}{r_n}$
Radius of $n$th orbit $r_n \propto E_n^x\therefore \quad x=-1Hence, (B) match$ with (Q).
(C) Angular momentum =$\frac{h}{2 \pi}$ \sqrt{l(l+1) l}=0,1,2, \ldots$
For the lower orbit $n=1\therefore \quad l=0 and m=0
Hence, angular momentum of $lowest orbit =\frac{h}{2 \pi} \sqrt{0(0 H)}=0$
(C) match with (P)
(D) $\frac{1}{r^n} \propto Z^y$ as $r_n \propto \frac{1}{Z} \therefore y=1$
Hence, (D) match with (S).

questions.solution:
The entropy change for a process, when $T$ and $P$ are the variables is given by

For an isobaric process $P_1=P_2$. Hence the above equation reduces to
$C_P \ln \frac{T_2}{T_1}=\Delta S$
or $\Delta S=2.303 C_P \log \frac{T_2}{T_1}$.

questions.q: One mole of a monatomic gas at pressure $\text{2}\text{atm,}\text{279}\text{K}$ taken to final pressure $\text{4}\text{atm}$ by a reversible path described by $P / V =$ constant. Calculate the magnitude of~$\dfrac{\Delta \text{E}}{\text{w}}$ for the process.
questions.solution:
$\text{dE} = \text{dq} + \text{dw}$ (F L T)
${\text{P}_{1} = {\text{K}}^{′} {\text{V}_{1}$ and ${\text{P}_{2} = {\text{K}}^{′} {\text{V}_{2}$ Also ${\text{V}_{1} = \dfrac{{\text{P}_{1}}{{\text{K}}^{′}} \text{,} {\text{V}_{2} = \dfrac{{\text{P}_{2}}{{\text{K}}^{′}}$
${\text{T}_{2} = {\text{T}_{1} \left(\dfrac{{\text{P}_{2} {\text{V}_{2}}{{\text{P}_{1} {\text{V}_{1}}\right) = {\text{T}_{1} \left(\dfrac{{\text{P}_{2} {\text{P}_{2} / {\text{K}}^{′}}{{\text{P}_{1} {\text{P}_{1} / {\text{K}}^{′}}\right) = {\text{T}_{1} \dfrac{{\text{P}_{2}^{2}}{{\text{P}_{1}^{2}}$
${\text{T}_{2} = {\text{T}_{1} \dfrac{{4}^{2}}{{2}^{2}} = 4 {\text{T}_{1}$
$\Delta \text{E} = {\text{C}}_{\text{v}} \left(\Delta \text{T}\right) = {\text{C}}_{\text{v}} \left(4 {\text{T}_{1} - {\text{T}_{1}\right) = 3 {\text{C}}_{\text{v}} {\text{T}_{1}$
$= 3 \dfrac{3}{2} \text{R} {\text{T}_{1} = 9 \dfrac{\text{R} {\text{T}_{1}}{2}$
$\text{w} = - \mathop{∫}_{{\text{v}_{1}}^{{\text{v}_{2}} \text{pdv} = - \mathop{∫}_{{\text{v}_{1}}^{{\text{v}_{2}} {\text{K}}^{′} \text{v} \text{dv} = - {\left|\dfrac{{\text{K}}^{′} {\text{v}}^{2}}{2}\right|}_{{\text{v}_{1}}^{{\text{v}_{2}}$
$\left({\text{K}}^{′} {\text{v}}^{2} = {\text{K}}^{′} \text{v} \text{v} = \text{P} \text{v} = \text{RT}\right)$
$\text{w} = - {\left|\dfrac{\text{RT}}{2}\right|}_{{\text{T}_{1}}^{{\text{T}_{2}} = - \dfrac{\text{R}}{2} \left({\text{T}_{2} - {\text{T}_{1}\right) = - \dfrac{\text{R}}{2} 3 {\text{T}_{1}$
$\dfrac{\Delta \text{E}}{\text{w}} = \dfrac{9 \text{R} {\text{T}_{1} / 2}{- 3 \text{R} {\text{T}_{1} / 2} = - 3$

Given, $f(x)=x^{25}(1-x)^{75}
\begin{aligned}

&=25 x^{24}(1-x)^{74}(1-4 x) \\
\therefore \quad f^{\prime}(x) &=0 \\
\Rightarrow \quad x &=0,1,1 / 4
\end{aligned} If $ x < 1 / 4$, then f^{\prime}(x)=25 x^{24}(1-x)^{74}(1-4 x)>0.$ and if x > 1 / 4$, then f^{\prime}(x)=25 x^{24}(1-x)^{74}(1-4 x) < 0. Thus, $ f^{\prime}(x)$ changes its sign from positive to negative as $x$ passes through 1 / 4$ from left to right. Hence, $f(x)$ attains its maximum at $x=1 / 4$.

& \therefore(3 a)^2-32 b < 0 \Rightarrow \frac{3 a^2}{32} < b \\

questions.solution:
Given curve is
$\begin{aligned}
& x y+\mathrm{a} x+\mathrm{b} y=0 \\
\therefore \quad & \text{ Slope }=2=\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x} \\
\therefore \quad & x y+\mathrm{a} x+\mathrm{b} y=0
\end{aligned}$
Differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\begin{aligned}
& x \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}+y+\mathrm{a}+\mathrm{b} \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}=0 \\
& \therefore \quad(x+\mathrm{b}) \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}=-(y+\mathrm{a}) \\
& \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}=\frac{-(y+\mathrm{a})}{x+\mathrm{b}} \\
& \therefore \quad\left(\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}\right)_{(1,1)}=2 \\
& \therefore \quad 2=\frac{-(1+\mathrm{a})}{1+\mathrm{b}} \\
& \therefore \quad \mathrm{a}+2 \mathrm{ b}=-3 ... (i)
\end{aligned}$
Since $(1,1)$ lies on $x y+a x+b y=0$, we get $\mathbf{a}+\mathbf{b}=-1$ ... (ii)
Solving (i), (ii), we get
$\begin{aligned}
& a=1, b=-2 \\
\therefore \quad & a-b=1-(-2)=3
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If the curves $x^2+p y^2=1$ and $q x^2+y^2=1$ are orthogonal to each other, then
questions.solution:
Given curves are

$\begin{aligned}$& x²+p y²=1 \\
& q x²+y²=1
\end{aligned}$ and On differentiating Eq. (i), w.r.t.,x$ we get

$\begin{gathered}$2 x+2 y p $\frac{d y}{d x}=$0 \\
\Rightarrow \quad $\frac{d y}{d x}=$m_1=-$\frac{x}{p y}
\end{gathered}On differentiating Eq. (ii), w.r.t.$ to x$, we get

$\begin{array}{r}2 q x+2 y $\frac{d y}{d x}-$0 \\
\Rightarrow \quad $\frac{d y}{d x}=$m_2=$\frac{-q x}{y}$
\end{array}$Since, both the $curves are orthogonal to each other,
Then,

\Rightarrow \quad $\frac{-x}{p y} \cdot \frac{-q x}{y}=-$1

$\Rightarrow \quad q x^2=-p y^2\Rightarrow \quad q\left(1-p y^2\right)=-p y^2$
[from Eq. (i)]
$\Rightarrow \quad q-p q y^2=-p y^2\Rightarrow \quad q=(p q-p)=y^2\therefore \quad y^2=\frac{q}{p q-p}$
and

x²=$\frac{-p}{p q-p}On putting $x^2 and y^2$ in Eq. (ii) we get

$\begin{array}{cc}& -$\frac{p q}{p q-q}+\frac{q}{p q=p}=$1 \\
\Rightarrow & -p q+q=p q-p \Rightarrow p+q=2 p q \\
\Rightarrow & $\frac{1}{p}+\frac{1}{q}=$2
\end{array}

questions.q: The number of values of $a$ for which the curves $4{x}^{2} + {a}^{2}{y}^{2} = 4{a}^{2}$ and ${y}^{2} = 16x$ are orthogonal is
questions.solution:
Given curves are

$4{x}^{2} + {a}^{2}{y}^{2} = 4{a}^{2}$ ...(i)

and ${y}^{2} = 16x$ ...(ii)

If the curves intersect at $P\left(\alpha, \beta\right)$, then

$\dfrac{{\alpha}^{2}}{{a}^{2}} + \dfrac{{\beta}^{2}}{4} = 1$ and ${\beta}^{2} = 16\alpha .$

On differentiating equation (i), we get,
$\dfrac{2x}{{a}^{2}} + \dfrac{2y}{4}{y}^{'} = 0$
$⇒ {y}^{′} = - \dfrac{4x}{{a}^{2} y}$
$⇒ {m}_{1} = \dfrac{- 4\alpha}{{a}^{2}\beta}$

On differentiating equation (ii), we get,
$2y{y}^{'} = 16$
$⇒ {m}_{2} = \dfrac{8}{\beta}$

For curves to be orthogonal,
${m}_{1}{m}_{2} = - 1$

i.e. $\left(- \dfrac{4\alpha}{{a}^{2}\beta}\right)\left(\dfrac{8}{\beta}\right) = - 1$
$⇒ 32\alpha = {a}^{2}{\beta}^{2}$
$⇒ 2{\beta}^{2} = {a}^{2}{\beta}^{2}$
$⇒ {a}^{2} = 2$
$⇒ a = \pm \sqrt{2}$
Hence, two values of $a$

questions.q: If the relation $p$ (subnormal length) $=q$ (subtangent length) ${ }^2$ holds true for the curve $b y^2=(x+a)^3$, then the value of $\frac{p}{q}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given curve,
$b y^2=(x+a)^3$
On differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get
$2 b y \frac{d y}{d x}=3(x+a)^2\begin{aligned} & \text{ Length of subnormal }=y \frac{d y}{d x}=y\left(\frac{3(x+a)^2}{2 b y}\right) \\ & \text{ Length of subtanget }=y \frac{d x}{d y}=y\left(\frac{2 b y}{3(x+a)^2}\right)\end{aligned}$
Given, $P($ Subnormal length $)=q($ subtangent length) ${ }^2\Rightarrow \quad P\left(y \frac{d y}{d x}\right)=q\left(y \frac{d x}{d y}\right)^2 \Rightarrow \frac{P}{q}=y\left(\frac{d x}{d y}\right)^3\Rightarrow \quad \frac{P}{q}=y\left(\frac{2 b y}{3(x+a)^2}\right)^3=\frac{8 y^4}{27} \frac{b^3}{\left((x+a)^3\right]^2}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{P}{q}=\frac{8 b}{27}\left(\frac{b y^2}{(x+a)^3}\right)^2\Rightarrow \quad \frac{P}{q}=\frac{8 b}{27}  \left[\becauseby^2=(x+a)^3\right]$
