questions.q: The points on the curve $y^2=x+\sin x$ at which the normal is parallel to the Y-axis lie on
options: a circle with centre at origin
a pair of lines bisecting the angle between the coordinate axes
questions.solution:
The given curve is $y^2=x+\sin x$...(i)
$\Rightarrow \frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{1+\cos x}{2 y}$
Now, slope of the normal is
$m=-\frac{1}{\left(\frac{d y}{d x}\right)}=-\frac{2 y}{1+\cos x}\therefore \quad$ Normal is parallel to $y$-axis
$\therefore \quad m=\frac{1}{0}\begin{aligned} & \Rightarrow-\frac{2 y}{1+\cos x}=\frac{1}{0} \Rightarrow 1+\cos x=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \cos x=-1 \Rightarrow \sin x=\sqrt{1-(-1)^2}=\sqrt{1-1}=0\end{aligned}\Rightarrow \sin x=0$...(ii)
From eqns. (i) and (ii) :
$y^2=x+0 \Rightarrow y^2=x$ which is a parabola.

(ii) in (1). we get (x-2)^{2}=x \Rightarrow x^{2}+4-4 x=x \Rightarrow \quad x^{2}-5 x+4=0\Rightarrow x^{2}-4 x-x+4=0\Rightarrow \quad x(x-4)-1(x-4)=0\Rightarrow \quad(x-1)(x-4)=0$ or $x=1,4$ then from is (ii) $y=2,5\therefore$ Required area $=\int_{1}^{4}\left\{(x+1)-\left(x^{2}-4 x+5\right)\right\} d x=\int_{1}^{4}\left(-x^{2}+5 x-4\right) d x=\left[\frac{-x^{3}}{3}+\frac{5 x^{2}}{2}-4 x\right]_{1}^{4}=\left[-\frac{64}{3}+40-16+\frac{1}{3}-\frac{5}{2}+4\right]=\left(-21-\frac{3}{2}+28\right)=\frac{9}{2}$

questions.q: What is the area of a loop of the curve $\mathrm{r}=\operatorname{asin} 3 \theta$ ?
questions.solution:
If curve $\mathrm{r}=\mathrm{a} \sin 3 \theta$ To trace the curve, we consider the following table : $\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline$3 $\theta=$& 0 & $\frac{\pi}{2}$& $\pi$& $\frac{3 \pi}{2}$& 2 $\pi$& $\frac{5 \pi}{2}$& 3 $\pi$\\ \hline$\theta=$& 0 & $\frac{\pi}{6}$& $\frac{\pi}{3}$& $\frac{\pi}{2}$& $\frac{2 \pi}{3}$& $\frac{5 \pi}{6}$& $\pi$\\ \hline $\mathrm{r}=$& 0 & $\mathrm{a}$& 0 & -$\mathrm{a}$& 0 & $\mathrm{a}$& 0 \\ \hline \end{array} Thus there is a loop between $\theta=0 \& \theta=\frac{\pi}{3}$ as r varies from $\mathrm{r}=0$ to $\mathrm{r}=0$.
Hence, the area of the loop lying in the $\text{ positive quadrant }=\frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}}$r^{2} $\mathrm{~d} \theta =\frac{1}{2} \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{3}} \sin ^{2} \phi \cdot \frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~d} \phi\left[\right.$ On putting, $\left.3 \theta=\phi \Rightarrow \mathrm{d} \theta=\frac{1}{3} \mathrm{~d} \phi\right]$ $\begin{array}{c} =$$\frac{a^{2}}{6} \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \sin ^{2} \phi \mathrm{d} \phi$\\ =$\frac{\mathrma^{2}}{6} \cdot \int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}} \frac{1-\cos 2 \phi}{2} \mathrm{~d} \phi\left[\because \cos$2 $\theta=$1-2 \sin ^{2} $\theta\right] \end{array}=\frac{\mathrma^{2}}{12} \cdot\left[\phi+\frac{\sin 2 \phi}{2}\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{2}}=\frac{\mathrma^{2}}{12} \cdot\left[\frac{\pi}{2}+\sin \pi\right]=\frac{\mathrma^{2} \pi}{24}$

Let $n \ge 2$ be a natural number and $f: \left[0, 1\right] \to \mathbb{R}$ be the function defined by

$f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}n\left(1 - 2nx\right) & if & 0 \le x \le \dfrac{1}{2n} \\ 2n\left(2nx - 1\right) & if & \dfrac{1}{2n} \le x \le \dfrac{3}{4n} \\ 4n\left(1 - nx\right) & if & \dfrac{3}{4n} \le x \le \dfrac{1}{n} \\ \dfrac{n}{n - 1}\left(nx - 1\right) & if & \dfrac{1}{n} \le x \le 1\end{cases}\right$

If $n$ is such that the area of the region bounded by the curves $x = 0, x = 1, y = 0$ and $y = f\left(x\right)$ is $4$, then the maximum value of the function $f$ is
questions.solution:
Given,

$f\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll}n\left(1 - 2nx\right), 0 \le x\right$

Here, $x \in \left[0, 1\right]$

Now $f\left(x\right) = n - 2{n}^{2}x$ is decreasing in $\left[0, \dfrac{1}{2n}\right]$

And $f\left(x\right) = 4{n}^{2}x - 4n$ increasing in $\left[\dfrac{1}{2n}, \dfrac{3}{4n}\right]$

And $f\left(x\right) = 4n - 4{n}^{2}x$ decreasing in $\left[\dfrac{3}{4n}, \dfrac{1}{n}\right]$

And $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{n}^{2}x - n}{n - 1}$ increasing in $\left[\dfrac{1}{n}, 1\right]$

Now plotting the graph of above function we get,

Also, $f\left(x\right) \in \left[0, n\right]$

Now from above diagram area will be,

$A = \dfrac{1}{4} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{n - 1}{2} = 4$ $\left\{\text{as}n \ge 2\right\}$

$⇒ \dfrac{1}{2} + \dfrac{n - 1}{2} = 4$

$⇒ \dfrac{n}{2} = 4$

$⇒ n = 8$

So, $f{\left(x\right)}_{max} = n = 8$

questions.q: The coefficient of $x^{20}$ in the expansion of $\left(1+3 x+3 x^2+x^3\right)^{20}$ is
questions.solution:
The given expression is $(1 + 3x + 3x^2 + x^3)^{20}$.

Observe that $1 + 3x + 3x^2 + x^3 = (1 + x)^3$.

Substituting this into the expression, we get $((1 + x)^3)^{20} = (1 + x)^{60}$.

The general term in the binomial expansion of $(1 + x)^{60}$ is given by ^{60}C_{r} x^{r}$.

To find the coefficient of $x^{20}$, we set $r = 20$.

The coefficient is ^{60}C_{20}$.

Using the property ^{n}C_{r} = ^{n}C_{n-r}$, we have ^{60}C_{20} = ^{60}C_{60-20} = ^{60}C_{40}$.

Answer: $\binom{60}{40}$

questions.q: In the expansion of $\left(1+3 x+3 x^2+x^3\right)^{2 n}$, the term which has greatest binomial coefficient, is
questions.solution:
The given expression is $\left(1+3x+3x^2+x^3\right)^{2n}$.

Recognizing the binomial expansion, $1+3x+3x^2+x^3 = (1+x)^3$.

Substituting this into the expression, we get $((1+x)^3)^{2n} = (1+x)^{6n}$.

The expansion of $(1+x)^{6n}$ is given by $\sum_{r=0}^{6n} {^{6n}C_{r}} x^r$.

The binomial coefficients are of the form ${^{6n}C_{r}}$. The greatest binomial coefficient in the expansion of $(1+x)^N$ occurs at the middle term. For $N=6n$, the middle term is at $r = \dfrac{6n}{2} = 3n$.

The general term $T_{r+1}$ in the expansion of $(1+x)^{6n}$ is ${^{6n}C_{r}} x^r$.

For $r=3n$, the term is $T_{3n+1} = {^{6n}C_{3n}} x^{3n}$.

Thus, the greatest binomial coefficient occurs at the $(3n+1)$ th term.

Answer: $(3 n+1)$ th term

In the expansion of $(1+x)^{2 n}$, middle term is ${ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n x^n$. Since, middle term is the greatest term.
$\therefore{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n x^n > { }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n-1} x^{n-1}\text{ and }{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_r x^n > { }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n+1} x^{n+1}\begin{aligned}
& \Rightarrow \quad x > \frac{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n-1}}{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n} \text{ and } x < \frac{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n}{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n+1}} \\
& \text{ Hence, } x \in\left(\frac{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n}{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n+1}}, \frac{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n}{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n+1}}\right)
\end{aligned}$
Hence, $x \in\left(\frac{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n}{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n+1}}, \frac{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_n}{{ }^{2 n} \mathrm{C}_{n+1}}\right)\begin{aligned}
& x \in\left($\begin{array}{c}
$\frac{(2 n) !}{(n-1) !(2 n-n+1)}$ \times $\frac{n !(2 n-n) !}{(2 n) !}$ \\
$\frac{(2 n) !}{n !(2 n-n) !}$ \times $\frac{(n-1) !(2 n-n+1)}{(2 n) !}$
\end{array}$\right) \\
& x \in\left(\frac{n(n-1) ! n !}{n(n-1) !(n+1) n !}, \frac{(n+1) n !(n-1) !}{n(n-1) ! n !}\right) \\
& \therefore \quad x \in\left(\frac{n}{n+1}, \frac{n+1}{n}\right)
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If $0 < y < 2^{1 / 3}$ and $x\left(y^3-1\right)=1$, then $\frac{2}{x}+\frac{2}{3 x^3}+\frac{2}{5 x^5}+\ldots$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
We have,
$x\left(y^3-1\right)=1 \Rightarrow x=\frac{1}{y^3-1}=\frac{1}{k} \text{ (say) }\Rightarrow \quad k=\frac{1}{x}$
Then, $\frac{2}{x}+\frac{2}{3 x^3}+\frac{2}{5 x^5}+\ldots=2 k+\frac{2}{3} k^3+\frac{2}{5} k^5+\ldots=\log \frac{1+k}{1-k}=\log \left\{\frac{1+y^3-1}{1-y^3+1}\right\}=\log \frac{y^3}{2-y^3}$

$\begin{aligned} & {\left[\frac{(x+1)}{\left(x^{2 / 3}-x^{1 / 3}+1\right)}-\frac{(x-1)}{(x-\sqrt{x})}\right]^{10}} \\ & \quad=\left[\frac{\left(x^{1 / 3}\right)^3+1^3}{\left(x^{2 / 3}-x^{1 / 3}+1\right)}-\frac{\left\{(\sqrt{x})^2-1\right\}}{\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-1)}\right]^{10} \\ & \quad=\left[\frac{\left(x^{1 / 3}+1\right)\left(x^{2 / 3}-x^{1 / 3}+1\right)}{\left(x^{2 / 3}-x^{1 / 3}+1\right)}-\frac{\left\{(\sqrt{x})^2-1\right\}}{\sqrt{x}(\sqrt{x}-1)}\right]^{10} \\ & \quad=\left[\left(x^{1 / 3}+1\right)-\frac{(\sqrt{x}+1)}{\sqrt{x}}\right]^{10}=\left(x^{1 / 3}-x^{-1 / 2}\right)^{10}\end{aligned}$
The general term is $\begin{aligned} T_{r+1} & { }^{10} C_r\left( x^{1 / 3}\right)^{10-r}\left(- x^{-1 / 2}\right)^r \\
& ={ }^{10} C_r(-1)^r \cdot x^{\frac{10-r}{3}-\frac{r}{2}}

\Rightarrow & 20-2 r-3 r=0 \\

\therefore & T_5={ }^{10} C_4=$\frac{10 \times 9 \times 8 \times 7}{4 \times 3 \times 2 \times 1}=$210
\end{array}

Coefficient of $(2 r+1)$ th term $=$ co-efficient of $(r+2)$ th term

& =\frac{3 n}{2} \cdot{ }^{2 n} C_n-{ }^{2 n} C_n={ }^{2 n} C_n\left(\frac{3 n}{2}-1\right) \\

questions.solution:
Let the coefficients of the middle terms in the expansion of $\left(\dfrac{1}{6} + \betax\right)4, \left(1 - 3\betax\right)2$ and $\left(1 - \dfrac{β}{2}x\right)6, \beta > 0$, respectively form the first three terms of an A.P. If $d$~is the common difference of this A.P., then $50 - \dfrac{2d}{\beta2}$ is equal to _____ .

Given,

Coefficients of middle terms of given expansions $\left(\dfrac{1}{6} + \betax\right)4$,~$\left(1 - 3\betax\right)2$~and$\left(1 - \dfrac{β}{2}x\right)6$~are& $C2 4 \dfrac{1}{6}{β}^{2}, C1 2 \left(- 3\beta\right) & C3 6 \left(\dfrac{- \beta}{2}\right)3$~respectively,

Now it is given that middle terms are forming an& $A . P$

So,~$2 C1 2 \left(- 3\beta\right) = C3 6 \left(\dfrac{- \beta}{2}\right)3 + C2 4 \dfrac{1}{6}{β}^{2}$

$⇒ 2 . 2\left(- 3\beta\right) = {β}^{2} - \dfrac{5{β}^{3}}{2}$

$⇒ - 24 = 2\beta - 5{β}^{2}$

$⇒ 5{β}^{2} - 2\beta - 24 = 0$

$⇒ 5{β}^{2} - 12\beta + 10\beta - 24 = 0$

$⇒ \beta\left(5\beta - 12\right) + 2\left(5\beta - 12\right) = 0$

$⇒ \left(\beta + 2\right)\left(5\beta - 12\right) = 0$

So,~$\beta = \dfrac{12}{5}$~and& $\beta = - 2$~{which is not possible as $\beta > 0$}

Now~$d = C1 2 \left(- 3\beta\right) - C2 4 \dfrac{1}{6}{β}^{2} = - 6\beta - {β}^{2}$

Now putting the value of~$\beta & d$~in& $50 - \dfrac{2d}{\beta2}$~we get,

$50 - \dfrac{2d}{\beta2} = 50 - 2\left(- 6\beta - {β}^{2}\right){β}^{2} = 50 + \dfrac{12}{β} + 2 = 57$

Let $P \left(t, \frac{4 t-20}{5}\right) be a point on$ the line
4 x-5 y=20. Then the chord of contact of tangents drawn from $P$ to the circle $x^2+y²=9$ is
$t x+\left(\frac{4 t-20}{5}\right)$ y=9\quad \quad \dots(i)$
Let \theta($ h, k)$ be the mid-point of this chord of contact, then its equation is also $h x+k y=h²+k²\quad \quad \dots(ii) $\left[\right.$ using $\left.T=S^{\prime}\right]$
Clearly Eqs. (i) and (ii) represent the same line
$\begin{aligned}
& \therefore \frac{t}{h}=\frac{4 t-20}{5 k}=\frac{9}{h^2+k^2} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{t}{h}=\frac{9}{h^2+k^2} \text{ and } \frac{t}{h}=\frac{4 t-20}{5 k} \\
& \Rightarrow t=\frac{9 h}{h^2+k^2} \text{ and } t=\frac{20 h}{4 h-5 k} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{9 h}{h^2+k^2}=\frac{20 h}{4 h-5 k} \\
& \Rightarrow  h\left\{20\left(h^2+k^2\right)-36 h+45 k\right\}=0 \\
& x=0, \text{ or }\left[20\left(x^2+y^2\right)-36 x+45 y\right]=0
\end{aligned}$

questions.question: For how many values of $p$, the circle ${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + 2x + 4y - p = 0$ and the coordinate axes have exactly three common points?

We shall consider 3 cases.

Case I: When p = 0

(i.e., circle passes through origin)

Now, equation of circle becomes

${x}^{2} + {y}^{2} + 2x + 4y = 0$

Case II: When circle intersect x-axis at 2 distinct points and touches y-axis.

${g}^{2} - c > 0$ and ${f}^{2} = c$

$1 + p > 0$ and $p = - 4$ so, this case is not possible

Case III: When circle intersect y-axis at 2 distinct points and touches x-axis

Now, ${g}^{2} - c = 0$  and ${f}^{2} - c > 0$

$⇒ 1 - \left(- p\right) = 0$ and $4 - \left(- p\right) > 0$

$⇒ p = - 1$  and, $p > - 4$

$∴ p = - 1$ is possible.

$∴$   Finally, we conclude that $p = 0, - 1$.

$⇒$Two possible values of p.

questions.solution:
Let the centre be $(\alpha, \beta)\because$ It cut the circle $\mathrm{x}^2+\mathrm{y}^2=\mathrm{p}^2$ orthogonally
$2(-\alpha) \times 0+2(-\beta) \times 0=c_1-p^2\mathrm{c}_1=\mathrm{p}^2$
Let equation of circle is $x^2+y^2-2 \alpha x-2 \beta y+p^2=0$
It pass through $(a, b) \Rightarrow a^2+b^2-2 \alpha a-2 \beta b+p^2=0$
Locus $\therefore 2 a x+2 b y-\left(a^2+b^2+p^2\right)=0$

questions.q: If the derivative of the function $f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cc}b x^2+a x+4 ; & x \geq-1 \\ a x^2+b ; & x < -1\end{array}\right.$ is everywhere continuous, then
questions.solution:
The function $f(x)$ is defined as $f(x) = bx^2 + ax + 4$ for $x \geq -1$ and $f(x) = ax^2 + b$ for $x < -1$.

For the derivative $f'(x)$ to be continuous everywhere, $f(x)$ must be continuous at $x = -1$. Thus, $\lim_{x \to -1^{-}} f(x) = \lim_{x \to -1^{+}} f(x) = f(-1)$.

Calculating the limits: $\lim_{x \to -1^{-}} (ax^2 + b) = a + b$ and $\lim_{x \to -1^{+}} (bx^2 + ax + 4) = b - a + 4$.

Equating these, $a + b = b - a + 4$, which simplifies to $2a = 4$, so $a = 2$.

Now, consider the derivative $f'(x) = \left\{\begin{array}{cc} 2bx + a; & x > -1 \\ 2ax; & x < -1 \end{array}\right\}$.

For $f'(x)$ to be continuous at $x = -1$, the left-hand derivative and right-hand derivative must be equal: $\lim_{x \to -1^{-}} f'(x) = \lim_{x \to -1^{+}} f'(x)$.

Substituting $a = 2$: $\lim_{x \to -1^{-}} (2ax) = 2(2)(-1) = -4$.

The right-hand derivative is $\lim_{x \to -1^{+}} (2bx + a) = 2b(-1) + 2 = -2b + 2$.

Equating these, $-4 = -2b + 2$, which gives $2b = 6$, so $b = 3$.

Thus, $a = 2$ and $b = 3$.

Answer: $a=2, b=3$

questions.q:
Let $f:[1,3] \rightarrow R$ be a function satisfying $\frac{x}{[x]} \leq f(x) \leq \sqrt{6-x}$, for all $x \neq 2$ and $f(2)=1$, where $R$ is the set of all real numbers and $[x]$ denotes the largest integer less than or equal to $x$.
Statement 1: $\lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{-}} f(x)$ exists.
Statement 2: $f$ is continuous at $x=2$.
options: Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is a correct explanation for Statement 1.
Statement 1 is false, Statement 2 is true.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is not a correct explanation for Statement 1.
Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is false.
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned} \text{ Consider } \frac{x}{[x]} \leq f(x) \leq \sqrt{6-x}\\
& \Rightarrow \lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{-}} \frac{x}{[x]}=\frac{2}{1}=2
\end{aligned} \begin{aligned}& \Rightarrow \lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{-}} \sqrt{6-x}=2 \\ \text{$ and $} \therefore \lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{-}} f(x)=2
\end{aligned} [By Sandwich theorem]
Now \lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{+}} \frac{x}{[x]}=1, \lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{+}} \sqrt{6-x}=2$
Hence by Sandwich theorem $\lim _{x \rightarrow 2^{+}} f(x)$ does not exists.
Therefore $f$ is not continuous at $x=2$. Thus statement-1 is true but statement- 2 is not true

(i) ${f}_{1} \left(x\right) = sin ⁡ \left(\sqrt{1 - e^{- x^{2}}}\right)
(ii) ${f}_{2}( x ) = \left$\{\begin{cases} \left|sinx\right|\tan^{- 1}\left(x\right) & , x \ne 0 \\ 1 & , x = 0\end{cases}\right$ , where the inverse trigonometric function $\tan^{- 1} x$ assumes values in $( - \dfrac{\pi}{2} , \dfrac{\pi}{2} )
(iii) ${f}_{3} ( x ) = [ sin( \log_${\mathrm{e}}$ ( x + 2 ) ) ]$ , where, for $t \in $\mathbb{R}$, [ t ]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $t$ ,
(iv) ${f}_{4}$\left( x\right)$ = \left$\{ \begin{cases}x^{2}sin\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)& , x \ne 0 \\ 0 & , x = 0\end{cases} \right$
List-I List-II
A. the function ${f}_{1}$ is$ P. NOT continuous at $x = 0$
B. The function ${f}_{2}$ is$ Q. continuous at $x = 0$ and NOT differentiable at $x = 0$
C. The function ${f}_{3}$ is$ R. differentiable at $x = 0$ and its derivative is NOT continuous at $x = 0$
D. The function ${f}_{4}$ is$ S. differentiable at $x = 0$ and its derivative is continuous at $x = 0$
The correct option is :
questions.solution:
(i) ${f}_{1}\left(x\right) = sin\sqrt{1 - e^{- x^{2}}}$. Clearly ${f}_{1} ( x )$ is continuous at x = 0 and $f\left(0\right) = 0$
${f}_{1}^{′}\left(0\right) = \lim_{x \to 0}\dfrac{sin\sqrt{1 - e^{- x^{2}}}}{1 - e^{- x^{2}}} \cdot \sqrt{\dfrac{1 - e^{- x^{2}}}{x2}} \cdot \left|x\right|x$

$= 1 \cdot 1 \cdot \lim_{x \to 0}\left|x\right|x$, which does not exist. So it is not differentiable at $x = 0$.
So, $P \to 2$
(ii) ${f}_{2}\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}\left|sinx\right|\tan^{-1}x, & x \ne 0 \\ 0 & x = 0\end{cases}\right$
$\lim_{x \to {0}^{+}}\dfrac{sinx}{x}\dfrac{x}{\tan^{-1}x} = 1$ and $\lim_{x \to {0}^{−}} - \dfrac{sinx}{x} \times \dfrac{x}{\tan^{-1} x} = - 1$
$⇒{f}_{2} \left(x\right)$ is not continuous at $x = 0$
So $Q \to 1$
(iii) In the close neighborhood of $x = 0$ given function ${f}_{3} ( x ) = 0$ hence $f^{′} 3 ( x ) = 0$ also $f^{′} 3 ( x )$ is continuous at $x = 0$
So, $R \to 4$
(iv) ${f}_{4}\left(x\right) = \left\{\begin{cases}x^{2}sin ⁡ \dfrac{1}{x},& x \ne 0 \\ 0, & x = 0\end{cases}\right$

Although ${f}_{4} ' \left(0\right) =0due$ to sandwich theorem, but \lim_{x \to 0}{f}_{4} '$\left(x\right)$ does not exist because$cos \left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right) oscillates infinitely many times near $x = 0$.
So $S \to 3$

and $f^{'}\left({0}^{-}\right) = \lim_{h \to $0}\d$ dfrac{f\left(0 - h\right) - f\left(0\right)}{- h}$

$∴ f^{'} $\left({0}^{+}\right)$ =$f^{'} \left({0}^{-}\right)

Statement $2 f^{\prime}(0)=g(0)$.
options: Statement 1 is true, Statement 2 is true, Statement 2 is a correct explanation for Statement 1.

Statement 2. $f^{\prime}(x)=g^{\prime}(x) \sin x+g(x) \cos x

questions.solution:
Given,&

$f\left(x\right) + f\left(x + k\right) = n$....(i)

Replacing $x \to x + k$ in above equation we get,

$f\left(x + k\right) + f\left(x + 2k\right) = n$.....(ii)

Subtraction equation (i) from equation (ii) we get,

$⇒ f \left(x\right) = f \left(x + 2k\right)$

$f \left(x\right)$ is periodic with period $2k$

Now, ${I}_{1} = {∫}_{0}^{4nk}f\left(x\right)dx = 2n{∫}_{0}^{2k}f\left(x\right)dx$

${I}_{2} = {∫}_{- k}^{3k}f\left(x\right)dx = 2{∫}_{0}^{2k}f\left(x\right)dx$

Now integrating both side of $f\left(x\right) + f\left(x + k\right) = n$ with limit ${∫}_{0}^{k}$ we get,

$⇒ {∫}_{0}^{k}f\left(x\right)dx + {∫}_{0}^{k}f\left(x + k\right)dx = nk$

$⇒ {∫}_{0}^{k}f\left(x\right)dx + {∫}_k^{2k}f\left(x\right)dx = nk$

$⇒ {∫}_{0}^{2k}f\left(x\right)dx = nk$

$⇒ {I}_{1} = 2n^{2}k, {I}_{2} = 2nk$

$⇒ {I}_{1} + n{I}_{2} = 4n^{2}k$

questions.solution:
The system of equations are

$\begin{array}{l}x+3 y+5 z=\alpha x \\
5 x+y+3 z=\alpha y \\
3 x+5 y+z=\alpha z \\
(1-\alpha)x+3 y+5 z=0 \\
5 x+(1-\alpha)y+3 z=0 \\
3 x+5 y+(1-\alpha)z=0
\end{array}$

For infinite number of solutions, we must have $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1-\alpha & 3 & 5 \\ 5 & 1-\alpha & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & 1-\alpha\end{array}\right|=0\Rightarrow \quad\left|\begin{array}{ccc}9-\alpha & 3 & 5 \\ 9-\alpha & 1-\alpha & 3 \\ 9-\alpha & 5 & 1-\alpha\end{array}\right|=0,C_{1} \rightarrow C_{2}+C_{2}+C_{3}$
Taking $(9-\alpha)$ common from the first column, we get $\begin{array}{l}\Rightarrow \quad(9-\alpha)\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 3 & 5 \\ 1 & 1-\alpha & 3 \\ 1 & 5 & 1-\alpha\end{array}\right|$=0 \\ \Rightarrow & (9-\alpha)$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & -\alpha-2 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & -\alpha-4\end{array}$ \mid=0\right. \\ \Rightarrow & (9-\alpha)$\left|\begin{array}{cc}\alpha+2 & 2 \\ -2 & \alpha+4\end{array}\right|$=0 \\ \Rightarrow & (9-\alpha)$\left(\alpha^{2}+6 \alpha+8+4\right)$=0 \\ (\alpha-9)$\left(\alpha^{2}+6 \alpha+12\right)$=0\end{array}$
 ⇒ \alpha=9$ is the only real value of \alpha.

questions.q: If $A=\left[\begin{array}{cc}2-k & 2 \\ 1 & 3-k\end{array}\right]$ is a singular matrix, then the value of $5 k-k^2$ is
questions.solution:
A matrix $A$ is singular if its determinant is zero, so $\det(A) = 0$.

Given $A = \begin{bmatrix} 2-k & 2 \\ 1 & 3-k \end{bmatrix}$, the determinant is calculated as:

$\det(A) = (2-k)(3-k) - (2)(1) = 0$

Expanding the expression:

$6 - 2k - 3k + k^2 - 2 = 0$

$k^2 - 5k + 4 = 0$

Rearranging the terms to find the value of $5k - k^2$:

$k^2 - 5k = -4$

Multiplying by $-1$ gives:

$5k - k^2 = 4$

Answer: 4

questions.q: The least positive value of $t$, so that the lines $x=t+\alpha, y+16=0 \quad$ and $\quad y=\alpha x$ are concurrent, is
questions.solution:
Consider the given equation of lines,

$\begin{array}{r}$x-(t+$\alpha)=$0 \\
y+16=0
\end{array}

and

-$\alpha$x+y=0

Since, these lines are concurrent, therefore the system of equations is consistent.
Now,

$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}$1 & 0 & -(t+$\alpha)$\\
0 & 1 & 16 \\
-$\alpha$& 1 & 0
\end{array}\right|=0

$\begin{array}{lr}
\Rightarrow$& 1(0-16)-(t+$\alpha)($0+$\alpha)=$0 \\
\Rightarrow & -16-$\alpha($t+$\alpha)=$0 \\
\Rightarrow & $\alpha($t+$\alpha)+$16=0 \\
\Rightarrow & $\alpha^{2}+$t $\alpha+$16=0
\end{array}

Clearly, $\alpha$ should be real. $\therefore t^{2}-4 \times 16 \geq 0 \Rightarrow t^{2}-64 \geq 0$
Hence, least positive value of $t$ is 8.

options: only finite number of non-zero solutions
questions.solution: We have, $\begin{aligned}& 8x-3 y-5 z=0 \\ & 5 x-8 y+3 z=0 \\ & 3 x+5 y-8 z=0 \\ &D=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}8 & -3 & -5 \\ 5 & -8 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & -8 \end{array}\right| \\ &=8(64-15)+3(-40-9)-5(25+24) \\ =& 8 \times49+3 \times(-49)-5 \times49 \\ =& 0 \end{aligned} $\therefore$ The system has infinitely many non-zero solutions.$

questions.q:
The number of real values of $t$ such that the system of homogeneous equations $\begin{aligned}
t x+(t+1) y+(t-1) z & =0 \\
(t+1) x+t y+(t+2) z & =0 \\
(t-1) x+(t+2) y+t z & =0
\end{aligned}$ has non-trivial solutions is
questions.solution:
Given,

$\begin{aligned}$& t x+(t+1) y+(t-1) z=0 \\
& (t+1) x+t y+(t+2) z=0 \\
& (t-1) x+(t+2) y+t z=0
\end{aligned}

Here,
Coefficient matrix, $A=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}t & t+1 & t-1 \\ t+1 & t & t+2 \\ t-1 & t+2 & t\end{array}\right]$ If $|A|=0$, then system of equations has non-trivial solution and it has infinite solutions.

|A|=$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}$t & t+1 & t-1 \\
t+1 & t & t+2 \\
t-1 & t+2 & t
\end{array}\right|=0

Apply operation $R_2 \rightarrow R_2-R_1, R_3 \rightarrow R_3-R_1$, we get

=$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}$t & t+1 & t-1 \\
1 & -1 & 3 \\
-1 & 1 & 1
\end{array}\right|=0

Apply $C_2 \rightarrow C_2-C_1, C_3 \rightarrow C_3-C_1$, we get

$\left|\begin{array}{crr}$t & 1 & -1 \\
1 & -2 & 2 \\
-1 & 2 & 2
\end{array}\right|=0

Expanding along $R_1$, we get

$\begin{array}{rlrl}$& & t(-4-4)-1(2+2)-1(2-2)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow & & -8 t-4=0 \\
\therefore & & t=$\frac{-1}{2}
\end{array}$So, no option is correct.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: The number of distinct real roots of $\left|$\begin{array}{lll}$\sin x$ & $\cos x$ & $\cos x$ \\ $\cos x$ & $\sin x$ & $\cos x$ \\ $\cos x$ & $\cos x$ & $\sin x\end{array}$\right|=0$ in the interval $-$\frac{\pi}{4} \leq x \leq \frac{\pi}{4} i$s
questions.solution:
Given, $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}\sin x & \cos x & \cos x \\ \cos x & \sin x & \cos x \\ \cos x & \cos x & \sin x\end{array}\right|=0\sin x\left(\sin ^{2} x-\cos ^{2} x\right)-\cos x\left(\sin x \cos x-\cos ^{2} x \right ) + \cos x \left(\cos ^{2} x-\sin x \cos x\right)=0\Rightarrow \sin x(\sin x-\cos x)(\sin x+\cos x)-\cos ^{2} x(\sin x-\cos x)-\cos ^{2} x(\sin x-\cos x)=0\Rightarrow(\sin x-\cos x)\left(\sin ^{2} x+\sin x \cos x-2 \cos ^{2} x\right)=0\Rightarrow(\sin x-\cos x)\left(\sin ^{2} x+2 \sin x\right.\left.\cos x-\sin x \cos x-2 \cos ^{2} x\right)=0\Rightarrow(\sin x-\cos x)^{2}(\sin x+2 \cos x)=0\Rightarrow \sin x-\cos x=0$ or $\sin x+2 \cos x=0\Rightarrow \quad \tan x=1$ or $\tan x=-2$
But $\quad x \in\left[-\frac{\pi}{4}, \frac{\pi}{4}\right]\Rightarrow$ Only one solution i.e. $x=\frac{\pi}{4}$

questions.q: The determinant $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & (x-3) & (x-3)^{2} \\ 1 & (x-4) & (x-4)^{2} \\ 1 & (x-5) & (x-5)^{2}\end{array}$\right|
questions.solution:
The given determinant vanishes, i.e.,



$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & x-3 & (x-3)^{2} \\

1 & x-4 & (x-4)^{2} \\

1 & x-5 & (x-5)^{2}

\end{array}$\right|=0



Expanding along $\mathrm{C}_{1}$,$ we get



$\begin{array}{l}

(x-4)(x-5)^{2}-(x-5)(x-4)^{2}-$\left\{(x-3)(x-5)^{2}\right. \\

\left.-(x-5)(x-3)^{2}\right\}$+(x-3)(x-4)^{2} \\

-(x-4)(x-3)^{2}=0 \\

\Rightarrow(x-4)(x-5)(x-5-x+4) \\

-(x-3)(x-5)(x-5-x+3) \\

+(x-3)(x-4)(x-4-x+3)=0

\end{array}$



\Rightarrow-(x-4)(x-5)+2(x-3)(x-5)-(x-3)



$(x-4)=0$

\Rightarrow-x^{2}+9 x-20+2 x^{2}-16 x+30-x^{2}+7 x-12=0



$\Rightarrow-32+30=0 \Rightarrow-2=0Which is not possible, hence no value of $\mathrm{x} satisfies the given condition.$

questions.q: If $x^{2} = \left|\begin{cases}sin\theta & cos\theta & 0 \\ - cos\theta & sin\theta & 1 \\ sin\theta & cos\theta & 2\end{cases}\right|$ then the value of $4x^{2} + xsin\dfrac{3\pi}{2} + 5$& is
questions.solution:
Given,& $x^{2} = \left|\begin{cases}sin\theta & cos\theta & 0 \\ - cos\theta & sin\theta & 1 \\ sin\theta & cos\theta & 2\end{cases}\right|$

On expanding $\left|\begin{cases}sin\theta & cos\theta & 0 \\ - cos\theta & sin\theta & 1 \\ sin\theta & cos\theta & 2\end{cases}\right|$ along ${C}_{3}$, we get

$x^{2} = 0 - 1\left|\begin{cases}sin\theta & cos\theta \\ sin\theta & cos\theta\end{cases}\right| + 2\left|\begin{cases}sin\theta & cos\theta \\ - cos\theta & sin\theta\end{cases}\right| = - 1 \left($ sin\thetacos$\theta -$ sin\thetacos$\theta\right) +2\left({sin}^{2}\theta + {cos}^{2}\theta\right)

$= - 1 $\times0 + 2 \times1$

$⇒ x^{2} = 2 ⇒ x = $\pm \sqrt{2}

If $ x = \sqrt{2}, then

4x^{2} + xsin\dfrac{3\pi}{2} +5 = 4 \times $\$left(\sqrt{2}\right)$$2 - $$\sqrt{2} +$$5$

$= 8 - $$\sqrt{2} +$$5 = $$\left(13 - \sqrt{2}\right)$

If $x = - $$\sqrt{2},$ then

4x^{2} + xsin\dfrac{3\pi}{2} +5 = 4 \times \left(- \sqrt{2}\right)2 + \sqrt{2} +5$

$= 8 + \sqrt{2} +5 = \left(13 + \sqrt{2}\right)$$

$

then the value of $a b c$ is$

Since, $\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}, \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}}$, and $\overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}$ are non-coplanar vectors,
therefore $[\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \overrightarrow{\mathbf{b}} \overrightarrow{\mathbf{c}}] \neq 0\Rightarrow \Delta=\left|\begin{array}{lll}1 & a & a^{2} \\ 1 & b & b^{2} \\ 1 & c & c^{2}\end{array}\right| \neq 0\Rightarrow\Delta \neq 0$
$\begin{array}{l}$$\text{ Now, }$& $\left(\begin{array}{lll}$a & a^{2} & 1+a^{3} \\
b & b^{2} & 1+b^{3} \\
c & c^{2} & 1+c^{3}
\end{array} \mid=0\right. \\
\Rightarrow$\left|\begin{array}{lll}$a & a^{2} & 1 \\
b & b^{2} & 1 \\
c & c^{2} & 1
\end{array}\right|+$\left|\begin{array}{lll}$a & a^{2} & a^{3} \\
b & b^{2} & b^{3} \\
c & c^{2} & c^{3}
\end{array}\right|=0 \\
\Rightarrow & \quad $\Delta($1+a b c)=0
\end{array}

\Rightarrow 
a b c=-1

questions.q:
If the system of equations
$(k+1)^3 x+(k+2)^3 y =(k+3)^3(k+1) x+(k+2) y =k+3x+y =1$
is consistent, then the value of $k$ is
questions.solution:
System of equations
$(k+1)^3 x+(k+2)^3 y=(k+3)^3(k+1) x+(k+2) y=(k+3)x+y=1$ is consistent.
Since, the given system of equations are consistent. Then $D=0$ and Also, $\left(D_1=D_2=D_3=0\right)$ have infinitely many solutions. By Crammer Rule
$D=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}(k+1)^3 & (k+2)^3 & (k+3)^3 \\(k+1) & (k+2) & (k+3) \\1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right|=0\because \quad C_2 \rightarrow C_2-C_1C_3 \rightarrow C_3-C_1D=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}(k+1)^3 & (k+2)^3-(k+1)^3 & (k+3)^3-(k+1)^3 \\ (k+1) & (k+2)-(k+1) & (k+3)-(k+1) \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right|=0D=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}(k+1)^3 & \left(3 k^2+9 k+7\right) & \left(6 k^2+24 k+26\right) \\ (k+1) & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right|=0$
Expand with $r$ to $R_32\left(3 k^2+9 k+7\right)-2\left(3 k^2+12 k+13\right)=0\Rightarrow 3 k^2+9 k+7-3 k^2-12 k-13=0\Rightarrow \quad-3 k-6=0 \Rightarrow 3 k=-6\Rightarrow \quad k=-2$

questions.q: Let $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}$ and $\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}$ be the roots of $a x^{2}+b x+c=0$ and $\mathrm{px}^{2}+\mathrm{qx}+\mathrm{r}=0$ respectively. If the system of equations $\alpha_{1} \mathrm{y}+\alpha_{2} \mathrm{z}=0$ and $\beta_{1} \mathrm{y}+\beta_{2} \mathrm{z}=0$ has a non-trivial solution, then
questions.solution:
Since $\alpha_{1}, \alpha_{2}$ and $\beta_{1}, \beta_{2}$ are the roots of ax $^{2}+b x+c=0$ and $p x^{2}+q x+r=0$ respectively

therefore



\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}=$\frac{-b}{a}, \alpha_{1} \alpha_{2}=\frac{c}{a}$and $\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}=\frac{-q}{p}, \beta_{1} \beta_{2}=\frac{r}{p}$

Since the given system of equation has a non-trivial solution



\therefore$\left|\begin{array}{ll}

\alpha_{1}$& \alpha_{2} \\

\beta_{1} & \beta_{2}

\end{array}\right|=0 $\text{ i.e. } \alpha_{1} \beta_{2}-\alpha_{2} \beta_{1}=$0



or $\quad \frac{\alpha_{1}}{\beta_{1}}=\frac{\alpha_{2}}{\beta_{2}}=\frac{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}{\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}}=\sqrt{\frac{\alpha_{1} \alpha_{2}}{\beta_{1} \beta_{2}}}\Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{pb}}{\mathrm{qa}}=\sqrt{\frac{\mathrm{pc}}{\mathrm{ra}}} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrmb^{2}}{\mathrmq^{2}}=\frac{\mathrm{ac}}{\mathrm{pr}}$

questions.solution: We have, $|A|=\left|\begin{array}{ccc}1 & \cos \theta & 0 \\ -\cos \theta & 1 & \cos \theta \\ -1 & -\cos \theta & 1\end{array}\right|=1[1-(-\cos \theta)(\cos \theta)]-\cos \theta[-\cos \theta+\cos \theta]+0\left(\cos ^{2} \theta+1\right)=1+\cos ^{2} \theta$ Now, we know that $-1 \leq \cos \theta \leq 1\Rightarrow \quad 0 \leq \cos ^{2} \theta \leq 1\Rightarrow \quad 1 \leq 1+\cos ^{2} \theta \leq 2\Rightarrow \quad 1 \leq|A| \leq 2\therefore \quad|A| \in[1,2]$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: If \($\mathrm{a}  \gt$0, $\mathrm{~b}  \gt$0, $\mathrm{c}  \gt$0\) are respectively the \($\mathrm{pth}, \mathrm{q}$\) th, rth terms of GP., then the value of the determinant \($\left|\begin{array}{lll}\log \mathrm{a}$& $\mathrm{p}$& 1 \\ \log $\mathrm{b}$& $\mathrm{q}$& 1 \\ \log $\mathrm{c}$& $\mathrm{r}$& 1\end{array}\right|\) is
questions.solution:
Let \(A\) be the 1 st term and \($\mathrm{R}$\) the common ratio of G.P., then
\$(\begin{aligned} \text{$ and } a=T_p=A R^{p-1} \\ $\text{$ and } \therefore $\log$$\mathrm{a}=\log \mathrm{A}+$($\mathrm{p}-$$1) $$\log$$\mathrm{R}
\end{aligned}$\)
Similarly, \(\log $\mathrm{b}=\log \mathrm{A}+(\mathrm{q}-$1) \log $\mathrm{R}$\)
and \(\log $\mathrm{c}=\log \mathrm{A}+(\mathrm{r}-$1) \log $\mathrm{R}$\)
\(\therefore $\Delta=\left|$\begin{array}{lll}
\logA+(p-1) \log R \text{ and } p \text{ and } 1 \\
\log A+(q-1) \log R \text{ and } q \text{ and } 1 \\
\log A+(r-1) \log R \text{ and } r \text{ and } 1
\end{array}$\right|\)
Split into two determinants and in the first take \(\log A\) common and in the second take \(\log $\mathrm{R}$\) common
\(\Delta=\logA\left|$\begin{array}{lll}1 \text{ and } p \text{ and } 1 \\
1 \text{ and } q \text{ and } 1 \\
1 \text{ and } r \text{ and } 1
\end{array}$\right|+\log R\left|$\begin{array}{lll}p-1 \text{ and } p \text{ and } 1 \\
q-1 \text{ and } q \text{ and } 1 \\
r-1 \text{ and } r \text{ and } 1
\end{array}$\right|\)
Apply \(\mathrm{C}}_{1} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}}_{2} \rightarrow \mathrm{C}}_{3}\) in the second
\$(\Delta=$0+$\log R\left|$$\begin{array}{lll}0 & p & 1 \\
0 & q & 1 \\
0 & r & 1
\end{array}$$\right|=0\)

questions.q:
Let $a, b, c$ be such that $b(a+c) \times 0$
If $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a & a+1 & a-1 \\ -b & b+1 & b-1 \\ c & c-1 & c+1\end{array}\right|+\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a+1 & b+1 & c-1 \\ a-1 & b-1 & c+1 \\ (-1)^{n+2} a & (-1)^{n+1} b & (-1)^{n} c\end{array}\right|=0$
then the value of $n$ is
questions.solution:
We have,
$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a & a+1 & a-1 \\ -b & b+1 & b-1 \\ c & c-1 & c+1\end{array}\right|$ + $\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a+1 & b+1 & c-1 \\ a-1 & b-1 & c+1 \\ (-1)^{n+2} a & (-1)^{n+1} b & (-1)^{n} c\end{array}\right|=0\Rightarrow\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a & a+1 & a-1 \\ -b & b+1 & b-1 \\ c & c-1 & c+1\end{array}\right|+\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a+1 & a-1 & (-1)^{n+2} a \\ b+1 & b-1 & (-1)^{n+1} b \\ c-1 & c+1 & (-1)^{n} c\end{array}\right|=0\Rightarrow\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a & a+1 & a-1 \\ -b & b+1 & b-1 \\ c & c-1 & c+1\end{array}\right|+\left|\begin{array}{ccc}(-1)^{n+2} a & a+1 & a-1 \\ (-1)^{n+1} b & b+1 & b-1 \\ (-1)^{n} c & c-1 & c+1\end{array}\right|=0\Rightarrow\left|\begin{array}{ccc}a\left(1+(-1)^{n+2}\right) & a+1 & a-1 \\ b\left(-1+(-1)^{n+1}\right) & b+1 & b-1 \\ c\left(1+(-1)^{n}\right) & c-1 & c+1\end{array}\right|=0\therefore n$ is any odd integer.

questions.q: If $A=\left|\begin{array}{lll}x & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & x & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & x\end{array}\right|$ and $B=\left|\begin{array}{cc}x & 1 \\ 1 & x\end{array}\right|$, then $\frac{d A}{d x}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$\begin{array}{ll}
\text{ Given, } & A=\left|\begin{array}{lll}
x & 1 & 1 \\
1 & x & 1 \\

 $\begin{aligned}2 x+3|y|+5[z] & =0 \\

and
According to Cramer's rule,

 \begin{aligned}\Delta& =$\left|\begin{array}{ccc}2 & 3 & 5 \\

\(\begin{aligned}
& \text{Since, }\left|\begin{array}{ll}f(x) & f^{\prime}(x) \\

On, integrating both sides, we get

 \text{ and }  \because \quad f(0)=1 \text{ and }f^{\prime}(0)=2 \\

 \text{ and }  \log _e\left(f^{\prime}(x)\right)=\log _e(f(x))+\log _e 2 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad f^{\prime}(x)=2 f(x) \\

& \because \quad f(0)=1 \text{, so }c=0 \\

questions.solution:
Given& $tanA + 3cosB + 6sinC = 1; 3tanA + cosB + 4sinC = 4$ and& $5tanA + 3cosB - 8sinC = - 2 .$

Let $tanA = x, cosB = y \text{$ and } sinC = z, then the given equations become$

Let $P = $\left[ $\begin{cases}$1 \text{ and $} 3\text{$ and } 6 \\ 3 $\text{ and }$ 1 $\text{ and }$ 4 \\ 5 $\text{ and }$ 3 $\text{ and }$ -8\end{cases}\right], X = $\left[\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right]$ and $\text{ and }$Q = $\left[\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 4 \\ - 2\end{array}\right] .$

Then,$ the system of equations can be written asPX = Q .$

Hence, we have $X = P^{- 1}Q .$

Now $\left|P\right|$ = $\left|\begin{cases}1 & 3 & 6 \\ 3 & 1 & 4 \\ 5 & 3 & - 8\end{cases}$\right|$

$⇒ $\left| P\right|$ = 1 $\left(-8 - 12\right)$ - 3 $\left(-24 - 20\right)$$ + 6 $$\left(9 - 5\right)$$

$⇒ $\left| P\right|$ = - 20 + 132 + 24 = 136 .$

The cofactors$ of the elements of the matrixP$ are$

${A}_{11} = - 8 - 12 = - 20, {A}_{12} = - \left(-24 - 20\right) = 44, {A}_{13} = 9 - 5 = 4,$

${A}_{21} = - \left(-24 - 18\right) = 42, {A}_{22} = - 8 - 30 = - 38, {A}_{23} = - \left(3 - 15\right) = 12,$

${A}_{31} = 12 - 6 = 6, {A}_{32} = - \left(4 - 18\right) = 14, {A}_{33} = 1 - 9 = - 8 .$ Thus, the adjoint matrix of $P$ is$

$adjP = $\left[\begin{cases}-20 \text{ and } 42 \text{ and } 6 \\ 44 \text{ and } - 38 \text{ and } 14 \\ 4 \text{ and } 12 \text{ and } - 8\end{cases}\right] .$

And$P^{- 1} = $adjP $\left| P\right|$,$

$⇒ P^{- 1} = $\dfrac{1}{136}$\left[\begin{cases}-$20 \text{ and $} 42\text{$ and } 6 \\ 44 $\text{$ and } -38 $\text{$ and } 14 \\ 4 $\text{$ and } 12 $\text{ and $} -8\end{cases}\right] .$

The solution$ of the given system is$

\left[ $\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}$$ \right] = $$\dfrac{1}{136}$$\left[$$\begin{cases}-20 & 42 & 6 \\ 44 & - 38 & 14 \\ 4 & 12 & - 8\end{cases}$$\right]$\ $\left[$\begin{array}{ll}1 \\ 4 \\ - 2\end{array}$\right]$$

$⇒ $\left[\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right] = \dfrac{1}{136}\left[\begin{array}{ll}-20 \times1 + 42 \times4 + 6 \times\left(-2\right) \\ 44 \times1 + \left(-38\right)\times4 + 14 \times \left(-2\right) \\ 4 \times1 + 12 \times4 + \left(-8\right)\times \left(-2\right)\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ \left[\begin{array}{ll}x \\ y \\ z\end{array}\right] = \dfrac{1}{136}\left[\begin{array}{ll}136 \\ 136 \\ 68\end{array}\right]$

$⇒ x = tanA = 1, y = cosB = - 1 and $\text{$ and }$z = sinC = $\dfrac{1}{2}$ .$

Also, A and $C lie in \left[0, $\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)$ and Blies in $\left[0, 2\pi\right] .$

Thus$ tanA = 1, ⇒ A = $$\dfrac{\pi}{4}$$,$cosB = - 1, ⇒ B = $\pi$ and $\text{$ and }$ sinC = $$\dfrac{1}{2}$$,$C = $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$$ .$

Now $B - 2A - C = \pi -2 \times \dfrac{\pi}{4}$ - $\dfrac{\pi}{6}$ = $\dfrac{\pi}{3} .$

Let& $p$ and $p + 2$~be prime numbers and let
$\Delta = \left|\begin{cases}p ! & \left(p + 1\right) ! & \left(p + 2\right) ! \\ \left(p + 1\right) ! & \left(p + 2\right) ! & \left(p + 3\right) ! \\ \left(p + 2\right) ! & \left(p + 3\right) ! & \left(p + 4\right) !\end{cases}\right|$
Then the sum of the maximum values of $\alpha$ and $\beta$, such that $p^{α}$~and $\left(p + 2\right)\beta$~divide $\Delta$, is _______.
questions.solution:
Given,

$\Delta = \left|\begin{cases}P ! & \left(P + 1\right) ! & \left(P + 2\right) ! \\ \left(P + 1\right) ! & \left(P + 2\right) ! & \left(P + 3\right) ! \\ \left(P + 2\right) ! & \left(P + 3\right) ! & \left(P + 4\right) !\end{cases}\right|$

Now using the factorial concept and taking common terms we get,

$⇒ \Delta = P ! \left(P + 1\right) ! \left(P + 2\right) ! \left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ P + 1 & P + 2 & P + 3 \\ \left(P + 2\right)\left(P + 1\right) & \left(P + 3\right)\left(P + 2\right) & \left(P + 4\right)\left(P + 3\right)\end{cases}\right|$

Now on solving determinant we get, $\left|\begin{cases}1 & 1 & 1 \\ P + 1 & P + 2 & P + 3 \\ \left(P + 2\right)\left(P + 1\right) & \left(P + 3\right)\left(P + 2\right) & \left(P + 4\right)\left(P + 3\right)\end{cases}\right|$

Using operation~${C}_{1} \to {C}_{1} - {C}_{2} & {C}_{2} \to {C}_{2} - {C}_{3}$

$\left|\begin{cases}0 & 0 & 1 \\ - 1 & - 1 & P + 3 \\ - 2P - 4 & - 2P - 6 & \left(P + 4\right)\left(P + 3\right)\end{cases}\right|$

$= 2P + 6 - \left(2P + 4\right) = 2$

Now putting the value of determinant we get,

$⇒ \Delta = 2P ! \left(P + 1\right) ! \left(P + 2\right) !$

$⇒ \Delta = 2P^{3}\left(P - 1\right) ! \left(P + 1\right)\left(P - 1\right) ! \left(P + 2\right)\left(P + 1\right)\left(P - 1\right) !$

Which is divisible by~$P^{α}$~and& $\left(P + 2\right)\beta$

So,~$\alpha = 3, \beta = 1$

questions.q: 164. The solution of the differential equation $\sec ^{2} x \tan y d x+\sec ^{2} y \tan x d y=0$ is
questions.solution:
The given differential equation is $\sec^{2} x \tan y dx + \sec^{2} y \tan x dy = 0$.

Rearranging the terms, we get $\sec^{2} y \tan x dy = -\sec^{2} x \tan y dx$.

Separating the variables, we have $\dfrac{\sec^{2} y}{\tan y} dy = -\dfrac{\sec^{2} x}{\tan x} dx$.

Integrating both sides, $\int \dfrac{\sec^{2} y}{\tan y} dy = -\int \dfrac{\sec^{2} x}{\tan x} dx$.

Let $u = \tan y$, then $du = \sec^{2} y dy$. Let $v = \tan x$, then $dv = \sec^{2} x dx$.

The equation becomes $\int \dfrac{1}{u} du = -\int \dfrac{1}{v} dv$.

Integrating, we get $\ln|u| = -\ln|v| + C_{0}$, which simplifies to $\ln|u| + \ln|v| = C_{0}$.

This implies $\ln|uv| = C_{0}$, or $uv = e^{C_{0}} = C$.

Substituting back $u = \tan y$ and $v = \tan x$, we obtain $\tan y \cdot \tan x = C$.

Answer: $\tan y \cdot \tan x=C$

questions.q: $The general solution of the differential equation \left(\tan ^{-1} y-x\right) d y=\left(1+y^{2}\right) d x$ is
questions.solution:
The given differential equation can be written as $\frac{d x}{d y}+\frac{x}{1+y^{2}}=\frac{\tan ^{-1} y}{1+y^{2}} \ldots$ (i)

Now, eq. (i) is a linear differential equation of the form $\frac{d x}{d y}+\mathrm{P}_{1} x=\mathrm{Q}_{1}$

where $\mathrm{P}_{1}=\frac{1}{1+y^{2}}$ and $\mathrm{Q}_{1}=\frac{\tan ^{-1} y}{1+y^{2}}$

Therefore, I.F $=e^{\int \frac{1}{1+y^{2}} d y}=e^{\tan ^{-1} y}$

Thus, the solution of the given differential equation is given by $x e^{\tan ^{-1} y}=\int\left(\frac{\tan ^{-1} y}{1+y^{2}}\right) e^{\tan ^{-1} y} \mathrm{dy}+\mathrm{C} \ldots$ (ii)

Let $\mathrm{I}=\int\left(\frac{\tan ^{-1} y}{1+y^{2}}\right) e^{\tan ^{-1} y} \mathrm{dy}$

On substituting $\tan ^{-1} y=t$, so that

$\left(\frac{1}{1+y^{2}}\right) \mathrm{dy}=\mathrm{dt}$, we get

$I=\int t e^{t} d t=t e^{t}-\int 1 \cdot e^{t} d t=t e^{t}-e^{t}=e^{t}(t-1)$ or $\mathrm{I}=e^{\tan ^{-1} y}   \left(\tan ^{-1}y-1\right)$

On substituting the value of 1 in equation (i1), we get

$x \cdote^{\tan ^{-1} y}=\cdote^{\tan ^{-1} y}\left(\tan ^{-1}$y-1\right)+  $\mathrm{C}or $x=$\left(\tan ^{-1}y-1\right)$+$\mathrm{C}  e^{$\tan ^{-1} y}

which is the general solution of the given differntial equation.

questions.q:
In a certain culture of bacteria, the rate of increase is proportional to the number
present. It is found that the number doubles in 4 hours. Then the number of times
the bacteria are increased in 12 hours is
questions.solution:
Let $x$ be the number of bacteria in certain culture at time $t$. Then rate of increase is $\frac{d x}{d t}$ which is proportional to $x$.
$$\begin{array}{l}
\therefore \frac{\mathrm{dx}}{\mathrm{dt}} \propto \mathrm{x} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{dx}}{\mathrm{dt}}=\mathrm{Kx} \Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{dx}}{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{Kdt} \Rightarrow \int \frac{\mathrm{dx}}{\mathrm{x}}=\mathrm{K} \int \mathrm{dt} \\
\therefore \log \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{Kt}+\mathrm{c} ...(1)\\
\text{ Initially when } \mathrm{t}=0, \operatorname{let} \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{x}_{0} \\
\therefore \log \mathrm{x}=0+\mathrm{c} \Rightarrow \mathrm{c}=\log \mathrm{x}_{0} \\
\therefore \text{ from }(1) \log \mathrm{x}=\mathrm{kt}+\log \mathrm{x}_{0} \\
\therefore \log \left(\frac{\mathrm{x}}{\mathrm{x}_{0}}\right)=\mathrm{Kt}...(2)
\end{array}$
Given number doubles in 4 hrs i.e. when $ t=4, x=2 x_{0}\therefore $\log\left(\frac{2 \mathrm{x}_{0}}{\mathrm{x}_{0}}\right)=4 \mathrm{ K} \Rightarrow \mathrm{K}=\frac{1}{4} \log2\therefore$ from (2) $\log\left(\frac{x}{x_{0}}\right)=\frac{t}{4} \log2 
When \mathrm{t}= 12\log \left(\frac{x}{x_{0}}\right)=\frac{12}{4} \log2=3 \log 2=\log 2^{3}=\log 8\therefore \frac{x}{x_{0}}=8 \Rightarrow x=8 x_{0}$
This problem can be alternatively solved as follows :
Let the intial number of bacteria be \mathrm{x}$$.
$\therefore$ Number of bacteria after 4 $\mathrm{hrs}=$2 $\mathrm{x}$
Number of bacteria after 8 $\mathrm{hrs}=$2(2 $\mathrm{x}$)=4 $\mathrm{x}$
Number of bacteria after 12 $\mathrm{hrs}=$2(4 $\mathrm{x}$)=8 $\mathrm{x}$

questions.q: The solution of the equation $\left(x-4 y^3\right) \frac{d y}{d x}-y=0,(y \gt 0)$ is
questions.solution:
Here, the differential equation

$\begin{aligned}& \left( x-4 y³\right) \frac{d y}{d x}- y=0,(y>0) \\
& \Rightarrow \quad\left( x-4 y³\right) \frac{d y}{d x}= y \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d x}{d y}=\frac{x-4 y^3}{y}\\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d x}{d y}=\frac{x}{y}-4 y² \quad \Rightarrow \quad \frac{d x}{d y}-\frac{x}{y}=-4 y² \\
& \therefore \quad P=-\frac{1}{y} \cdot Q=-4 y²
\end{aligned}

Integrating factor,

\text{ I.F. }=$ e^{$\int P d y}=e^{\int-\frac{1}{y}$ d y}=e^{-$\log y}=e^{\log$ y-1}=$\frac{1}{y}$ Now, the solution is given by

$\begin{aligned}& x \cdot(\text{ I.F. })=\int(\text{ I.F. }) \cdot Q d y+C \\
& \frac{x}{y}=\int \frac{1}{y} \times\left(-4 y²\right) d y+C \\
& \frac{x}{y}=\int-4 y d y+C \\
& \frac{x}{y}=-4 \frac{y^2}{2}+ C
\end{aligned}

\begin{aligned}& x=-2 y³+C y \\
& x+2 y³=C y
\end{aligned}

$\therefore \quad$ This is the required solution.$

$⇒ 3f\left(x\right) = f\left(x\right) + xf^{'}\left(x\right) - x^{2}$

$⇒ 0 + C = \dfrac{1}{3} ⇒ C = \dfrac{1}{3}$

$⇒ f\left(e\right) =\dfrac{4e^{2}}{3}$

Neither I nor II is true

questions.solution:
I. $d y+2 x y d x=2 e^{-x^2} d x\Rightarrow \quad \frac{d y}{d x}+2 x y=2 e^{-x^2}$
This is a linear differential equation in $y$
Here, $P=2 x, Q=2 e^{-x^2}\therefore \text{ I.F. }=e^{\int P d x}=e^{\int 2 x d x}=e^{x^2}\therefore$ Complete solution is
$\begin{aligned}
& y e^{x^2}=2 \int e^{-x^2} e^{x^2} d x+c \\
\Rightarrow \quad y e^{x^2} & =2 x+c
\end{aligned}$
II. $y e^{x^2}-2 x=c$
On differentiating w.r.t $x$, we get
$y e^{x^2} \cdot 2 x+e^{x^2}\frac{d y}{d x}$-$2=0$\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow & e^{x^2} $\frac{d y}{d x}$ & =2-2 x y e^{x^2} \\
\Rightarrow &$\frac{d y}{d x}$& =2 e^{-x^2}-2 x y
\end{aligned}$\therefore \mathrm{I}is true$ and II is false.

Differentiate both sides with respect to $xy^{\prime}(x)=\frac{e^{-2 x}}{2}(1-2 x)  <  0 \forall x \in   $\$left(\frac{1}{2},1\right)$

Hence, $y(x)$ is decreasing in  $\$left($\frac{1}{2}$,1\right)$$

Taking log on both sides, we get
$\begin{aligned}
& 2 y \log 2 x=\log \left(4 \mathrme^{2 x-2 y}\right) \\
& \Rightarrow 2 y \log 2 x=\log 4+\log \mathrme^{2 x-2 y} \\
& \Rightarrow 2 y \log 2 x=\log 4+2 x-2 y \\
& \Rightarrow 2 y \log 2 x+2 y=\log 4+2 x \\
& \Rightarrow 2(y \log 2 x+y)=2 \log 2+2 x \\
& \Rightarrow y \log 2 x+y=\log 2+x \\
& \Rightarrow y(1+\log 2 x)=x+\log 2 \\
& \Rightarrow y=\frac{x+\log 2}{1+\log 2 x}
\end{aligned}$
Differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\begin{gathered}
\frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}=\frac{(1+\log 2 x)(1+0)-(x+\log 2)\left(\frac{1}{2 x}\right) \cdot 2}{(1+\log 2 x)^2} \\
\Rightarrow \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}=\frac{(1+\log 2 x)-\frac{1}{x}(x+\log 2)}{(1+\log 2 x)^2} \\
\Rightarrow(1+\log 2 x)^2 \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}=1+\log 2 x-1-\frac{\log 2}{x} \\
\Rightarrow(1+\log 2 x)^2 \frac{\mathrm{d} y}{\mathrm{ d} x}=\log 2 x-\frac{\log 2}{x} \\
=\frac{x \log 2 x-\log 2}{x}
\end{gathered}$

questions.q: The equation of normal to the curve $y=(1+x)^{y}+\sin ^{-1}  \left(\sin ^{2}x\right)$ at $x=0 is$
questions.solution:
Given the curve $y = (1+x)^{y} + \sin^{-1}(\sin^{2}x)$.

At $x = 0$, $y = (1+0)^{y} + \sin^{-1}(\sin^{2}0) = 1^{y} + 0 = 1$. Thus, the point of contact is $(0, 1)$.

To find the slope of the tangent, differentiate the equation with respect to $x$:
Let $u = (1+x)^{y}$. Then $\ln u = y \ln(1+x)$.
Differentiating with respect to $x$: $\dfrac{1}{u} \dfrac{du}{dx} = \dfrac{dy}{dx} \ln(1+x) + \dfrac{y}{1+x}$.
So, $\dfrac{du}{dx} = (1+x)^{y} \left[ \dfrac{dy}{dx} \ln($1+x) + $\dfrac{y}{1+x} \right].
At $(0, 1)$, \dfrac{du}{dx} =$1^{1} [ $\dfrac{dy}{dx} \ln($1) + $\dfrac{1}{1} ] =$1$.

Now differentiate $\sin^{-1}(\sin^{2}x)$ with respect to $x$:
\dfrac{d}{dx} [\sin^{-1}(\sin^{2}$x)] = $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1 - (\sin^{2}x)^{2}}} \cdot$2 \sin x \cos x = $\dfrac{\sin 2x}{\sqrt{1 - \sin^{4}x}}.
At $x = 0$, this derivative is \dfrac{0}{1} =$0$.

Therefore, \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{du}{dx} +$0 = 1 + 0 = 1$.
The slope of the tangent $m = 1$.

The slope of the normal $m_{\perp} = -$\dfrac{1}{m} = -$1$.
The equation of the normal at $(0, 1)$ is $y - 1 = -1(x - 0)$.
$y - 1 = -x \Rightarrow x + y = 1$.

Answer: $x+y=1

questions.solution:
Let $x = tan\theta$
${y}_{1} = \tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{sec\theta - 1}{tan\theta}\right) = \tan^{- 1}\left(tan\dfrac{θ}{2}\right) = \dfrac{θ}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}\tan^{- 1}x$
$x = sinϕ, {y}_{2} = \tan^{- 1}\left(\dfrac{2sinϕcosϕ}{cos2ϕ}\right) = \tan^{- 1} ( tan2ϕ ) = 2ϕ = 2\sin^{- 1}x$

$\dfrac{d{y}_{1}}{d{y}_{2}} = \dfrac{d{y}_{1} / dx}{d{y}_{2} / dx} = \dfrac{1\left(1 + x^{2}\right) \cdot \dfrac{1}{2}}{2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{1 - x^{2}}}$
$= \dfrac{1 - x^{2}}{4\left(1 + x^{2}\right)} = \dfrac{1 - \dfrac{1}{4}}{4\left(1 + \dfrac{1}{4}\right)} = \dfrac{3}{10}$

We have,

$\begin{aligned}$& z=\sec (y-a x)+\tan (y+a x) \\

questions.solution:
Given,

$2x^{y} + 3y^{x} = 20$

Now differentiating both sides w.r.t $x,$ we get

$2x^{y}\left(y^{'}lnx + \dfrac{y}{x}\right) + 3y^{x}\left(lny + \dfrac{x}{y} \cdot y^{'}\right) = 0 \left\{\text{here}ln = \log_{\mathrm{e}}\right\}$

Putting $x = 2 \text{ and } y = 2,$ we get

$⇒ 8\left(ln2 \cdot y^{'} + 1\right) + 12\left(lny + y^{'}\right) = 0$

$⇒ 8\left(ln2 \cdot y^{'} + 1\right) + 12 \left(lny + y^{'}\right) = 0$

$⇒ y^{'} = - $\$left(\dfrac{3ln2 + 2}{2ln2 + 3}\right)$

$⇒ y^{'} = - $\$left(\dfrac{2 + ln8}{3 + ln4}\right)

$

3(2 $\sqrt{2})^$2 $\cdot \frac{d y}{d x}-$3 $\cdot \frac{d y}{d x}+$1=0 \Rightarrow $\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{-1}{21}$Again on substituting $x=-10 \sqrt{2}, y=2 \sqrt{2}$ in Eq. (ii), we get

questions.q: $y=e^{a \sin ^{-1} x} \Rightarrow\left(1-x^2\right) y_{n+2}-(2 n+1) x y_{n+1}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given, $\quad y=e^{a \sin ^{-1} x}$
On differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\begin{aligned}
& y_1=e^{a \sin ^{-1} x} a \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} \\
\Rightarrow \quad & y_1 \sqrt{1-x^2}=a y \\
\Rightarrow \quad & \left(1-x^2\right) y_1^2=a^2 y^2
\end{aligned}$
Again, differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get
$\begin{aligned}
\left(1-x^2\right) 2 y_1 y_2-2 x y_1^2 & =a^2 2 y y_1 \\
\Rightarrow \quad\left(1-x^2\right) y_2-x y_1-a^2 y & =0
\end{aligned}$
Using Leibnitz's rule,
$\begin{aligned}
& \left(1-x^2\right) y_{n+2}+{ }^n C_1 y_{n+1}(-2 x)+{ }^n C_2 y_n(-2) \\
& -x y_{n+1}-{ }^n C_1 y_n-a^2 y_n=0 \\
& \Rightarrow\left(1-x^2\right) y_{n+2}+x y_{n+1}(-2 n-1) \\
& +y_n\left[-n(n-1)-n-a^2\right]=0 \\
& \Rightarrow\left(1-x^2\right) y_{n+2}-(2 n+1) x y_{n+1}=\left(n^2+a^2\right) y_n \\
&
\end{aligned}$

$⇒ y = x - 1 + $\dfrac{1}{15} \left(3\cos^{5}x - 5\cos^{3}x\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} =1 + \dfrac{1}{15}\left(15$\cos^{4}x$ \left(-$ sinx\right) + 15\cos^{2}xsinx\right)$

$⇒ $\dfrac{dy}{dx} =1 + \left(\cos^{4} x\left(- sinx\right)$ +$ \cos^{2}xsinx\right)$

$⇒ y^{'}\left(\dfrac{π}{6}\right) =$1 + $\left(\cos^{4}\left(\dfrac{π}{6}\right) \left(- sin \left(\dfrac{π}{6}\right)\right) + $\cos^{2}$\left($\dfrac{π}{6}$\right)$sin $\left($\dfrac{π}{6}$\right)$\right)$

$⇒ y^{'}\left(\dfrac{π}{6}\right) =$1 + $\left(\dfrac{ \left(\sqrt{3}\right)$4}${24}\left(- $$\dfrac{1}{2}$\right) + \dfrac { $\left(\sqrt{3}\right)$22 }${22}\times \dfrac{1}${2}\right)$

$⇒ y^{'}$\left($\dfrac{π}{6}$\right)$ =1 - $\dfrac{9}{32}$ + $\dfrac{3}{8}$

$⇒ y^{'}$$\left($\dfrac{π}{6}$\right)$$ = $$\dfrac{32 - 9 + 12}{32}$

$⇒ y^{'}$$\left($\dfrac{π}{6}$\right)$$ = $$\dfrac{35}{32}$$

$⇒ 96y^{'}$\left($\dfrac{π}{6}$\right)$ =35 \times3$

questions.q: If $y\left(x\right) = {\left({x}^{x}\right)}^{x}, x > 0$ then $\dfrac{{d}^{2}x}{d{y}^{2}} + 20$ at $x = 1$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given,

$y\left(x\right) = {\left({x}^{x}\right)}^{x}$

Taking ${\log}_{e}$ both side

$lny\left(x\right) = {x}^{2} \cdot lnx$

Now differentiating both side w.r.t $x$ we get,

$\dfrac{1}{y\left(x\right)} \cdot {y}^{'}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{{x}^{2}}{x} + 2x \cdot lnx$

${y}^{'}\left(x\right) = y\left(x\right)\left[x + 2xlnx\right]$ .......(i)

Given $y\left(1\right) = 1$, so ${y}^{'}\left(1\right) = 1$

Now rewriting equation (i) again we get,

$\dfrac{dx}{dy} = \dfrac{1}{{x}^{{x}^{2} + 1}\left(1 + 2lnx\right)}$

Now $\dfrac{{d}^{2}x}{d{y}^{2}} = \dfrac{d}{dx}\left({\left({x}^{{x}^{2} + 1}\left(1 + 2lnx\right)\right)}^{- 1}\right)\dfrac{dx}{dy}$

$⇒ \dfrac{{d}^{2}x}{d{y}^{2}} = \dfrac{- {x}^{{x}^{2}}\left(1 + 2lnx\right)\left({x}^{2} + 3 + 2{x}^{2}lnx\right)}{{\left({x}^{{x}^{2}}\left(1 + 2lnx\right)\right)}^{3}} \times 1$

$⇒ {\left(\dfrac{{d}^{2}x}{d{y}^{2}}\right)}_{x = 1} = - 4$

So, ${\left(\dfrac{{d}^{2}x}{d{y}^{2}}\right)}_{x = 1} + 20 = - 4 + 20 = 16$

questions.q: $f ( x ) = \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}; g ( x ) = \dfrac{x + 1}{x^{2} + 1}; h ( x ) = 2x - 3$. Then the value of $f^{'}\left[h^{'}\left(g^{'} ( x )\right)\right] =$
questions.solution:
Given that

$f ( x ) = \sqrt{x^{2} + 1}; g ( x ) = \dfrac{x + 1}{x^{2} + 1}; h ( x ) = 2x - 3$

By using Chain rule

$f^{'}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{2x}{2\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}} = \dfrac{x}{x^{2} + 1}$

By using Quotient rule

$g^{'}\left(x\right) = \dfrac{\left[x^{2} + 1\right]\left(1\right) - \left[x\right]\left(2x\right)}{\left(x^{2} + 1\right)^{2}} = \dfrac{x^{3} - 2x^{2} + 1}{\left(x^{2} + 1\right)^{2}}$

$h^{'}\left(x\right) = 2$

$f^{'}\left[h^{'}\left(g^{'}\left(x\right)\right)\right] = f^{'} \left[h^{'} \left(\dfrac{x^{3} - 2x^{2} + 1}{ \left(x^{2} + 1\right)^{2}}\right)\right]

$= f^{'} $\left(2\right)$

$= \dfrac{2}{{2}^{2} + 1} = \dfrac{2}{5}$

questions.solution:
$f(x)=(\cos x)(\cos 2 x) \ldots(\cos n x)f^{\prime}(x)=-\sin x \cdot \cos 2 x \ldots \cos n x+\cos x \frac{d}{d x}\{\cos 2 x \cdot \cos 3 x \ldots \cos n x\}f^{\prime}(x)=-\sin x \cdot \cos 2 x \ldots \cos n x+\cos x[-2 \sin 2 x \cdot \cos 3 x \ldots \cos n x\left.+\cos 2 x \frac{d}{d x} \cos 3 x \cdot \cos 4 x \ldots \cos n x\right]f^{\prime}(x) \Rightarrow-(\sin x \cdot \cos 2 x \ldots \cos n x)-(2 \cos x \cdot \sin 2 x \cdot \cos 3 x \ldots \cos n x)+\cos x \cdot \cos 2 x \frac{d}{d x}(\cos 3 x \cdot \cos 4 x \cdot \cos n x)f^{\prime}(x) \Rightarrow-(\sin x \cdot \cos 2 x \ldots \cos n x)-(2 \cos x \cdot \sin 2 x \ldots \cos n x)-(3 \cos x \cdot \cos 2 x \cdot \sin 3 x \ldots \cos n x)-(n \cos x \cdot \cos 2 x \ldots \sin n x)$
So,
$\Rightarrow f^{\prime}(x)+\sum_{r=1}^n(r \tan r x) f(x)=f^{\prime}(x)+\{\tan x+2 \tan 2 x+3 \tan 3 x+\ldots+n \tan n x\} f(x)=f^{\prime}(x)+f(x) \tan x+2 f(x) \tan 2 x+\ldots+n f(x) \tan n x=f^{\prime}(x)+[(\sin x \cdot \cos 2 x \ldots \cos n x)+(2 \cos x \cdot \sin 2 x \ldots \cos n x)+\ldots+(n \cos x \cdot \cos 2 x \ldots \sin n x)]=f^{\prime}(x)-f^{\prime}(x)\Rightarrow 0$
Hence, $f^{\prime}(x)+\sum_{r=1}^n(r \tan r x) f(x)=0$

questions.q: The eccentric angle of a point on the ellipse $x^{2} + 3y^{2} = 6$ lying at a distance of $2$ units from its centre is
questions.solution:
The given equation of ellipse can be written in the form& $\dfrac{x2}{\left(\sqrt{6}\right)2} + \dfrac{y2}{\left(\sqrt{2}\right)2} = 1$.

Now let the eccentric angle of the point be~$\theta$, then its co-ordinates are~$\left(\sqrt{6}cos\theta, \sqrt{2}sin\theta\right)$.

Since the distance of the point from the centre is~$2$~units

$∴ \left(\sqrt{6}cos\theta - 0\right)2 + \left(\sqrt{2}sin\theta - 0\right)2 = 4$

$⇒ 6{cos}^{2}\theta + 2\left(1 - {cos}^{2}\theta\right) = 4 ⇒ 4{cos}^{2}\theta = 2$

$⇒ cos\theta = \pm \dfrac{1}{2} ∴ \theta = \dfrac{π}{4}$~or& $\dfrac{3\pi}{4}$

questions.q: An ellipse passes through the foci of the hyperbola, $9x^{2} - 4y^{2} = 36$ and its major and minor axes lie along the transverse and conjugate axes of the hyperbola respectively. If the product of eccentricities of the two conics is $\dfrac{1}{2},$ then which of the following points does not lie on the ellipse?
questions.solution:
Equation of the hyperbola
$\dfrac{x^{2}}{4} - \dfrac{y^{2}}{9} = 1$



Focus of hyperbola $\left({a}_{1}{e}_{1}, 0\right)$ and $( - {a}_{1}{e}_{1}, 0 )$

${a}_{1} = 2, {e}_{1} = \sqrt{1 + \dfrac{9}{4}} = \dfrac{\sqrt{13}}{2}$

$∴$ Foci would be $\left(+ \sqrt{13}, 0\right)$ and $\left(- \sqrt{13}, 0\right)$~

Product of eccentricity would be&

$\dfrac{\sqrt{13}}{2} ⋅ {e}_{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$∴ {e}_{2} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}}$ .

As the major & minor axis of the ellipse coincide with axis of hyperbola then the value of ${a}_{2}$~for ellipse would be $\sqrt{13}$ ,

${e}_{2} = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{{b}_{2}^{2}}{{a}_{2}^{2}}}$

$\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}} = \sqrt{1 - \dfrac{{b}_{2}^{2}}{13}}$

${b}_{2}^{2} = 12$

$∴$ Equation of the ellipse would be~

$\dfrac{x^{2}}{13} + \dfrac{y^{2}}{12} = 1 .$

Option (1) $\dfrac{39}{4 ⋅ ( 13 )} + \dfrac{3}{12} = 1$

Satisfies the equation, hence it lies on the ellipse.~

Option (2)& $\dfrac{13}{4 ( 13 )} + \dfrac{3}{4.12} = 1$

does not lie on the ellipse.

Option (3) $\dfrac{13}{2 ( 13 )} + \dfrac{6}{12} = 1$ satisfy.

Option (4) $\dfrac{13}{13} + 0 = 1$ satisfy.

So, option $\left(\dfrac{13}{2}, \dfrac{3}{2}\right)$ is the answer.

questions.q:
Let $\mathbb{R}$ be the set of all real numbers.

Statement I : The function $f: \left(- \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f\left(x\right) = secx + tanx$ is a one - one function.

Statement II : The function $f: [ 0, \infty ) \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f\left(x\right) = x^{2}$ is a one-one function.

Which of the above statements is(are) true?
options: Statement I is true, but Statement II is false
Statement II is true, but Statement I is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
questions.solution:
Given,

$\mathbb{R}$ be the set of all real numbers.

Now solving statement I : The function $f: \left(- \dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right) \to \mathbb{R}$ defined by $f\left(x\right) = secx + tanx$

Now differentiating the function with respect to $x$ we get,

$f^{'} \left(x\right) = secx \left( secx + tanx\right)$

Now we know that $secx$ is always positive in given domain and& $secx + tanx$ will also be positive as& $tanx$ is negative in& $\left(- \dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)$ but& $secx ≥ tanx$ in& $\left(- \dfrac{\pi}{2},0\right)$

So, $f^{'}\left(x\right) ≥ 0$ hence it is& a one - one function.

Now solving statement II : The function $f: [ 0, \infty ) \to \mathbb{R}$defined by

$f\left(x\right) = x^{2}$

Differentiating the function we get,

$f^{'}\left(x\right) = 2x$

$⇒ f^{'}\left(x\right) ≥ 0 ∀ x \in [ 0, \infty )$

Hence it is also a& one-one function.

So both are true.

(i) Centre of ellipse $(0,0)$ and centre of hyperbola is $(0,0)$

(iv) Vertices of ellipse are $(\pm a, 0) or (\pm 5,0)$. Vertices of hyperbola are $(\pm a, 0) or (\pm 5,0)$.
From the above discussions, their are common is centre and vertices.

\end{aligned}$
Focus of hyperbola is
$\begin{aligned}

questions.q:
If the normals drawn to the hyperbola \(x y=4\) at \($\left(\alpha_$i, \beta_i\right)(i=1,2,3,4)\) are concurrent at$ the point \((a, b)\), then
\(\frac{\left(\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3+\alpha_4\right)}{\left(\beta_1+\beta_2+\beta_3+\beta_4\right)}\left(\alpha_$1 \alpha_2 \alpha_3 \alpha_4\right)=\)
questions.solution:
The equation of normal to the given hyperbola \(x y=4\) at point \(\left(2 t, \frac{2}{t}\right)\) is
\(2 t⁴-x t³+y t-2=0\) ...(i)
\(\because\) Normal (i) passes through point \((a, b)\), so \(2 t⁴-a t³+b t-2=0\), the equation having roots are \(\frac{\alpha_1}{2}, \frac{\alpha_2}{2}, \frac{\alpha_3}{2}\) and \(\frac{\alpha_4}{2}\), so
\begin{gathered}$\frac{1}{2}\left(\alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3+\alpha_4\right)=\frac{a}{2} \Rightarrow \alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3+\alpha_4=a \\
\sum\left(\frac{\alpha_1 \alpha_2}{4}\right)=0 \\
\sum \frac{\alpha_1 \alpha_2 \alpha_3}{8}=\frac{-b}{2} \text{$ and $} \frac{\alpha_1 \alpha_2 \alpha_3 \alpha_4}{16}=-1 \\
\because \beta_1+\beta_2+\beta_3+\beta_4=\frac{4}{\alpha_1}+\frac{4}{\alpha_2}+\frac{4}{\alpha_3}+\frac{4}{\alpha_4}
\end{gathered} =4 \frac{\Sigma \alpha_1 \alpha_2 \alpha_3}{\alpha_1 \alpha_2 \alpha_3 \alpha_4}\)
\(=4 \frac{-b / 2 \times 8}{-16}=b\)
\begin{aligned}\frac{\left.\therefore \alpha_1+\alpha_2+\alpha_3+\alpha_4\right)}{\beta_1+\beta_2+\beta_3+\beta_4}& \left(\alpha_1 \alpha_2 \alpha_3 \alpha_4\right) \\
= & \frac{a(-16)}{b}=-16 \frac{a}{b}
\end{aligned}$
Hence, option (b) is correct.

questions.q: The locus of a variable point whose chord of contact w.r.t. the hyperbola $\dfrac{x2}{a2} - \dfrac{y2}{b2} =1$ subtends a right angle at the origin is
questions.solution:
Given,

The equation of the given hyperbola is& $\dfrac{x2}{a2} - \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1 ⋯ \left(1\right)$

Now let $\left(h, k\right)$ be the pole of a chord& $PQ$ of the hyperbola

Then the straight line& $PQ$ is the polar of the point& $\left(h, k\right)$ w.r.t. the hyperbola and so its equation is

$\dfrac{xh}{a2} - \dfrac{yk}{b2} =1 ⋯ \left(2\right)$

Now the center of the hyperbola is the origin, let it be point $C$,

Now making& $\left(1\right)$ homogeneous with the help of& $\left(2\right)$, the combined equation of& $CP$ and& $CQ$ is

$\dfrac{x2}{a2} - \dfrac{y2}{b2} =\left(\dfrac{xh}{a2} - \dfrac{yk}{b2}\right)2 ⋯ \left(3\right)$

Now the chord $PQ$ subtends a right angle at& $\left(0, 0\right)$

Therefore the lines $CP$ and& $CQ$ given by& $\left(3\right)$ are perpendicular and so in the equation& $\left(3\right)$, we have the coefficient of $x^{2} +$coefficient of $y^{2} = 0$

$⇒ \left(\dfrac{1}{a2} - \dfrac{h2}{a4}\right) + \left(\dfrac{- 1}{b2} - \dfrac{k2}{b4}\right) =0$

$⇒ \dfrac{h2}{a4} + \dfrac{k2}{b4} = \dfrac{1}{a2} - \dfrac{1}{b2}$

Thus locus is

$\dfrac{x2}{a4} + \dfrac{y2}{b4} = \dfrac{1}{a2} - \dfrac{1}{b2}$

&

&

( y-6 \sqrt{2})& =\frac{3}{2 \sqrt{2}}( x-9) \\
\Rightarrow \quad 2 \sqrt{2} y-24 & =3 x-27 \\

\Rightarrow \quad 2 \sqrt{2} y+24 & =-3 x+27 \\

$

questions.solution:
Given, $4 x^2-9 y^2=36$
After differentiating w.r.t. $x$, we get $\begin{aligned} \text{ 4.2.x-9.2.y. } \frac{d y}{d x}=$0 \\
&\Rightarrow $\text{ Slope$ of $tangent }=\frac{d y}{d x}=\frac{4 x}{9 y}
\end{aligned}$ So, slope of normal =$\frac{-9 y}{4 x}$Now, equation of $normal at point  \left(x_0, y_0\right) is given by $y-y_0=$\frac{-9 y_0}{4 x_0} \left(x-x_0\right) As normal intersects \mathrm{X} axis at A$, Then A \equiv $\left(\frac{13 x_0}{9},0\right)$ and $B \equiv\left(0,\frac{13 y_0}{4}\right)As$O A B P$ is a parallelogram
\therefore$ midpoint of $O B \equiv \left(0, $$\frac{13 y_0}{8}$\right) \equiv$Midpoint of A P$
So, $P(x, y) $\equiv  \left($\frac{-13 x_0}{9}$$, $$\frac{13 y_0}{4}$\right)\because $\left(x_0, y_0\right)$ lies on hyperbola, therefore 4 $\left(x_0\right)^2-9\left(y_0\right)^2=36$$ From equation (i): x_0=$$\frac{-9 x}{13}$ and y_0=$\frac{4 y}{13}$ From equation (ii), we get$9 x²-4 y²=169$
Hence, locus of point $P$ is : $9 x²-4 y²=169$

questions.solution:
Equation of the tangent at the point ' $\theta$ ' is $\begin{aligned}& \frac{x \sec \theta}{a}-\frac{y \tan \theta}{b}=1 \\
& \Rightarrow P=(a \cos \theta,0) \text{$ and $} Q=(0,-b \cot \theta)\\
& \text{ Let } \mathrm{R} \text{ be }(\mathrm{h}, \mathrm{k}) \Rightarrow \mathrm{h}= a \cos \theta, \mathrm{k}=- b \cot \theta\\
& \Rightarrow \quad \frac{k}{h}=\frac{-b}{a \sin \theta} \Rightarrow \sin \theta=\frac{-b h}{a k} \quad \text{ and }\\
& \cos \theta=\frac{h}{a}
\end{aligned}$ By squaring and adding, $\frac{b^2 h^2}{a^2 k^2}+\frac{h^2}{a^2}=1  \begin{aligned}& \Rightarrow \frac{b^2}{k^2}+1=\frac{a^2}{h^2}\\
& \Rightarrow \frac{a^2}{h^2}-\frac{b^2}{k^2}=1
\end{aligned} Now, given \mathrm{q}^{\mathrm{n}}$ of hyperbola is $\frac{x^2}{4}-\frac{y^2}{2}=1$
\Rightarrow a²=4, b²=2 $\therefore$ R lies on $\frac{a^2}{x^2}-\frac{b^2}{y^2}=1$ i.e., $\frac{4}{x^2}-\frac{2}{y^2}=1$

questions.solution:
The given equation of hyperbola is& $\dfrac{x2}{a2} - \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1, ae = 2, e = \dfrac{3}{2}$

$⇒ a = \dfrac{4}{3}$

$⇒ b^{2} = a^{2}e^{2} - a^{2} = 4 - \dfrac{16}{9} = \dfrac{20}{9}$

The tangent is perpendicular to~$2x + 3y = 6$.

Slope of tangent is~$m = \dfrac{- 1}{\dfrac{- 2}{3}} = \dfrac{3}{2}$

Equation of tangent, $m = \dfrac{3}{2}$

Equation of tangent is~$y = mx - \sqrt{a^{2}m^{2} - b^{2}}$
$⇒ y = \dfrac{3}{2}x - \sqrt{\dfrac{16}{9} \times \dfrac{9}{4} - \dfrac{20}{9}}$

( $∵$ Tangent is in ${1}^{st }$ quadrant$\left⇒ C < 0\right)$

$⇒ y = \dfrac{3}{2}x - \dfrac{4}{3}$

Converting the equation into intercept form:

$⇒ \dfrac{x}{\left(\dfrac{8}{9}\right)} + y\left(- \dfrac{4}{3}\right) = 1$

$⇒ \left|6a\right| + \left|5b\right| = \left|\dfrac{6 \times 8}{9}\right| + \left|\dfrac{5 \times \left(- 4\right)}{3}\right| = 12$

Hence this is the required option.

Given equation of hyperbola is

questions.q: Let $P \lleft(asec\theta,btan\theta\right)$and $Q  \left(asecϕ, btanϕ\right) where $\theta +ϕ = $\dfrac{\pi}{2}, be two points on$ the $hyperbola \dfrac{x2}{a2} - \dfrac{y2}{b2} =1.$ If& the ordinate of the point of intersection of normals at $P and Q$ is $- k \left(\dfrac{a^{2} + b^{2}}{2b}\right),$ then $k$& is equal to
questions.solution:
We have,

$\dfrac{x2}{a2} - \dfrac{y2}{b2} = 1 . . . \left(i\right)$

On differentiating w.r.t., $x,$ we get

$\dfrac{2x}{a2} - \dfrac{2y}{b2} \times \dfrac{dy}{dx} =0$

$⇒ \dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{b2}{a2}\left(\dfrac{x}{y}\right)$

$⇒ - \dfrac{dx}{dy} = - \dfrac{a2}{b2} \left(\dfrac{y}{x}\right)

Slope for normal at the point $ P \l$ left(asec\theta,btan\theta\right)$ is

$\left(- \dfrac{dx}{dy}\right)P = - \dfrac{a^{2}btan\theta}{b^{2}asec\theta} = - \ddfrac{a}{b}sin\theta

$∴$ Equation of normal at \lleft(asec\theta,btan\theta\right)$ is

$y - btan\theta = - \ddfrac{a}{b}sin\theta \left($ x - $asec\theta\right)

$⇒ $\l$ left(asin\theta\right)$ x + by = \left($ a^{2} + b^{2}\right)tan\theta

$⇒ ax + b cosec \thetay = \left($ a^{2} + b^{2}\right)sec\theta . . . $\left(ii\right)$

Similarly, equation of normal to $\dfrac{x2}{a2} - \dfrac{y2}{b2} =1$ at

$( asecϕ, btanϕ )$ is

$ax + by cosec ϕ = \left($ a^{2} + b^{2}\right)secϕ . . . $\left($ ii\right)$

On subtracting \left($ ii\right)$ from& \left(i\right)$, we get

$b ( cosec \theta -cosec ϕ ) y = \left(a^{2} + b^{2}\right) ( sec\theta -secϕ )$

$⇒ y = \dfrac{a^{2} + b^{2}}{b} \cdot\left(\dfrac{sec\theta - secϕ}{cosec \theta - cosec ϕ}\right)$

But $\dfrac{sec\theta - secϕ}{cosec \theta - cosec ϕ} = \dfrac{sec\theta - sec\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)}{cosec \theta - cosec $\$left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - \theta\right)$}$

\left[∵ ϕ + \theta = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$$

$= $\dfrac{sec\theta - cosec \theta}{cosec\theta - sec\theta} =$-1$

Thus,

$y = - \$left(\dfrac{a^{2} + b^{2}}{b}\right),$$i.e., $k = 2$.

$

questions.solution:
Given hyperbola is

$16x^{2} - 9y^{2} + 32x + 36y - 164 = 0$

$⇒ 16\left(x + 1\right)^{2} - 9\left(y - 2\right)^{2} = 164 + 16 - 36$

$⇒ 16 \left(x + 1\right)^{2} - 9 \left(y - 2\right)^{2} = 144.... \left(1\right)$

$⇒ $\dfrac{( x + 1{)}^{2}}{9} - \dfrac{( y - 2{)}^{2}}{16} =1$

Compare the above equation with& $⇒ \dfrac{( x - h{)}^{2}}{a2} - \dfrac{( y - k{)}^{2}}{b2} =$1$

We get, $h = - 1, k = 2, a^{2} = 9 and $\text{$ and }$b^{2} = 16$

$∴$ Eccentricity, $e = $\sqrt{1 + \dfrac{16}{9}}$= $\dfrac{5}{3}$

We know that, focii are $\left(h + ae, k\right)$ and& $\left(h - ae, k\right)$

Hence, focii are $( 4, 2 )$ and& $( - 6, 2 )$

Let the centroid be $( h, k )$ & A ( \alpha, \beta )$be point on hyperbola$

So $h = $$\dfrac{\alpha - 6 + 4}{3}$$,k = $$\dfrac{\beta + 2 + 2}{3}$$

$⇒ \alpha =3h + 2, \beta =3k - 4$

Put the values of $\alpha, \beta in $the equation \left(1\right),$

16$\left(\left(3h + 2\right)$ + 1\right)^{2} - $9$$\left(\left(3k - 4\right)$$ - 2\right)^{2} = 144$

$⇒ 144 ( h + 1{)}^{2} - 81 ( k - 2{)}^{2} = 144$

$⇒ $16$\left(h^{2} + 2h + 1\right)$ - $9$$\left(k^{2} - 4k + 4\right)$$ = 16$

$⇒ 16h^{2} - 9k^{2} + 32h + 36k - 36 = 0$

So, the locus of the centroid is $

$16x^{2} - 9y^{2} + 32x + 36y - 36 = 0$

$

$⇒ f $$\left(n\right)$$ = tan $$\left[\tan^{-1}\left($\dfrac{2 - 1}{1 + 2 \times 1}$\right)$ + \tan^{-1}$\left($\dfrac{3 - 2}{1 + 3 \times 2}$\right)$ + \tan^{-1}$\left($\dfrac{4 - 3}{1 + 4 \times 3}$\right)$ +... + \tan^{-1}$\left(\dfrac{ \left(n + 1\right)$ - n}{1 + n ( n + 1 )}\right)\right]$

Using $\tan^{-1}a$ - $\tan^{-1}b$ = $\tan^{-1}$\left($\dfrac{a - b}{1 + ab}$\right)$,$

$⇒ f $\left(n\right)$ = tan $\left[\tan^{-1}\left(2\right)$ - $\tan^{-1}$$\left(1\right)$$ + $\tan^{-1}$\left(3\right)$ - $\tan^{-1}$$\left(2\right)$$ + \tan^{-1}$$\left(4\right)$$ - \tan^{-1}$$\left(3\right)$$ +... + \tan^{-1}$$\left(n + 1\right)$$ - \tan^{- 1}$$\left(n\right)$\right]$

questions.q: The set of values of $x$ such that $\tan ^{-1}  \left(\frac{x}{x-2}\right)-\tan ^{-1} \left(\frac{x}{2 x-1}\right)=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right)is$
questions.solution:
$We have,
\begin{aligned}
& \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{x-2}\right)-\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{x}{2 x-1}\right)=\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{2}{3}\right) \\
& \tan ^{-1} \frac{\left(\frac{x}{x-2}-\frac{x}{2 x-1}\right)}{1+\left(\frac{x}{x-2}\right)\left(\frac{x}{2 x-1}\right)}=\tan ^{-1} \frac{2}{3} \\
& \Rightarrow \frac{2 x^2-x-x^2+2 x}{2 x^2-4 x-x+2+x^2}=\frac{2}{3} \Rightarrow \frac{x^2+x}{3 x^2-5 x+2}=\frac{2}{3} \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 3 x^2+3 x=6 x^2-10 x+4 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad 3 x^2-13 x+4=0 \Rightarrow(3 x-1)(x-4)=0 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad x=\frac{1}{3}, 4, \quad x \in\left\{\frac{1}{3}, 4\right\}
\end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
Given equation
$\sin \left[2 \cos ^{-1}\left\{\cot \left(2 \tan ^{-1} x\right)\right\}\right]=0\Rightarrow 2 \cos ^{-1}\left\{\cot \left(2 \tan ^{-1} x\right)\right\}=n \pi, n \in \mathbf{Z}\Rightarrow \cos ^{-1}\left\{\cot \left(2 \tan ^{-1} x\right)\right\}=\frac{n \pi}{2}\because \quad \cos ^{-1} x \in[0, \pi]\therefore \quad \cos ^{-1}\left\{\cot \left(2 \tan ^{-1} x\right)\right\}=0, \frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\Rightarrow \cot \left(2 \tan ^{-1} x\right)=1,0,-1 \Rightarrow 2 \tan ^{-1} x=m \pi+\frac{\pi}{4}m \pi+\frac{\pi}{2}$ or $m \pi-\frac{\pi}{4}, m \in \mathbf{Z}\Rightarrow \tan ^{-1} x=\frac{m \pi}{2} \pm \frac{\pi}{8}$ or $\frac{m \pi}{2}+\frac{\pi}{4}, m \in \mathbf{Z}\because \quad \tan ^{-1} x \in\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\therefore \tan ^{-1} x= \pm \frac{\pi}{8}, \frac{\pi}{2}-\frac{\pi}{8},-\frac{\pi}{2}+\frac{\pi}{8}, \pm \frac{\pi}{4}\therefore \quad x= \pm \tan \frac{\pi}{8}, \pm \cot \frac{\pi}{8}, \pm \tan \frac{\pi}{4}\Rightarrow \quad x= \pm(\sqrt{2}-1), \pm \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}-1}, \pm 1= \pm(\sqrt{2}-1), \pm(\sqrt{2}+1), \pm 1$
The roots which are greater than or equal to one are $\sqrt{2}+1,1$.

questions.q:
Consider the statements
(I) If $f(x)=\sin  \left(\cot ^{-1}\left(\cos   \left(\tan ^{-1}x\right)\right)\right)$, then
$$f(0)=\frac{1}{2}
($$II) $\sin \left(4 \tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{5}-\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{239}\right)=1$
Then the correct option among the following is
options: Both I and II are false
Both I and II are true
I is true, but II is false
I is false, but II is true
questions.solution:
(I) We have,
$\begin{aligned} f(x) & =\sin \left(\cot ^{-1}\left(\cos \left(\tan ^{-1} x\right)\right)\right) \\ & =\sin \cot ^{-1} \cos \cos ^{-1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}} \\ & =\sin \cot ^{-1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}} \\ & =\sin \sin ^{-1} \sqrt{\frac{1+x^2}{2+x^2}}=\sqrt{\frac{1+x^2}{2+x^2}}\end{aligned}\therefore \quad f(0)=\sqrt{\frac{1+0}{2+0}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
So, Statement $\mathrm{I}$ is false.
(II) We have,
$\begin{aligned} \sin \left(4 \tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{5}-\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{239}\right) & =\sin \left(2 \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{\frac{2}{5}}{1-\frac{1}{25}}\right)-\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{239}\right) \\ = & \sin \left(2 \tan ^{-1} \frac{5}{12}-\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{239}\right) \\ = & \sin \left(\tan ^{-1} \frac{\frac{10}{12}}{1-\frac{25}{144}}-\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{239}\right) \\ = & \sin \left(\tan ^{-1} \frac{120}{119}-\tan ^{-1} \frac{1}{239}\right) \\ = & \sin \left(\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{119}{1+\frac{120}{119} \times \frac{1}{239}}\right)\right) \\ = & \sin \tan ^{-1}\left[\frac{28680-119}{28441+120}\right]=\sin \tan ^{-1} \frac{28561}{28561} \\ = & \sin \tan ^{-1} 1=\sin \cdot \frac{\pi}{4}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}$
Statement II is false.

questions.q: If $\sum_{n=1}^k \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{n^2+3 n+3}\right)=\tan ^{-1} \alpha$, then $\alpha=$
questions.solution:
$We have,
\begin{aligned}
\sum_{n=1}^k \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{n^2+3 n+3}\right) =\tan ^{-1} \alpha \\
\sum_{n=1}^k \tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{(n+2)-(n+1)}{1+(n+2)(n+1)}\right) =\tan ^{-1} \alpha \\
\Rightarrow \quad \sum_{n=1}^k\left(\tan ^{-1}(n+2)-\tan ^{-1}(n+1)\right) =\tan ^{-1} \alpha \\
\Rightarrow \quad\left(\tan ^{-1} 3-\tan ^{-1} 2\right)+\left(\tan ^{-1} 4-\tan ^{-1} 2\right) \ldots & \tan ^{-1}(k+2)-\tan ^{-1}(k+1) \\
\tan ^{-1}(k+2)-\tan ^{-1} 2 =\tan ^{-1} \alpha \\
\tan ^{-1}\left(\frac{k+2-2}{1+(k+2)(2)}\right) =\tan ^{-1} \alpha \\
\frac{k}{1+2 k+4}=\alpha \Rightarrow \alpha =\frac{k}{2 k+5}
\end{aligned}$

$= \dfrac{3\pi}{2}$
$⇒ m = \dfrac{3}{2} = 1.5$

\Rightarrow & & x y+\sqrt{1-x^2} \sqrt{1-y^2}& =2 x y \\
\Rightarrow & & x²+y² & =1
\end{aligned}  [on squaring]

questions.solution:
Consider the given expression,

$\lim_{\text{x} \to \infty} {\left(\dfrac{\text{p} \dfrac{1}{\text{x}} + \text{q} \dfrac{1}{\text{x}} + \text{r} \dfrac{1}{\text{x}} + \text{s} \dfrac{1}{\text{x}}}{4}\right)}^{3 \text{x}}$ [where, $\text{p,}\text{q,}\text{r,}\text{s > 0]}$

Put, $\dfrac{1}{\text{x}} = \text{z}$, so that $\text{x} \to \infty ⇒ \text{z} \to 0$

$= \lim_{\text{z} \to 0} \left(\dfrac{p^{z} + q^{z} + r^{z} + s^{z}}{4}\right) \dfrac{3}{\text{z}}$

which is in the form ${1}^{∞}$.

${=e}^{\lim_{z \to 0}\left(\dfrac{p^{z} + q^{z} + r^{z} + s^{z}}{4} - 1\right)\dfrac{3}{z}}$
$= e^{\lim_{\text{z} \to 0} \left(\dfrac{p^{z} - 1}{\text{z}} + \dfrac{q^{z} - 1}{\text{z}} + \dfrac{r^{z} - 1}{\text{z}} + \dfrac{s^{z} - 1}{\text{z}}\right) \dfrac{3}{4}}$

$= e^{\dfrac{3}{4} \left(\log_{\mathrm{e}} \text{p} + \log_{\mathrm{e}} \text{q} + \log_{\mathrm{e}} \text{r} + \log_{\mathrm{e}} \text{s}\right)}$

$= e^{\dfrac{3}{4}\log_{\mathrm{e}}\left(\text{pqrs}\right)} = \left(\text{pqrs}\right)\dfrac{3}{4}$

questions.solution:
Given, $f:[-2,2] \rightarrow R$
f(x)=\left$\${$\begin{array}{cc}
\frac{\sqrt{1+c x}-\sqrt{1-c x}}{x},& -2 \leq x < 0 \\
\frac{x+3}{x+1}$,& 0 \leq x \leq 2
\end{array}$\right.

Now, $\quad$ LHL =\lim$_{x \rightarrow$ 0^{-}} f(x)
\begin{aligned}
&$=\lim$ _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{\sqrt{1-c h}-\sqrt{1+c h}}{-h}\\
 \times \frac{\sqrt{1-c h}+\sqrt{1+c h}}{\sqrt{1-c h}+\sqrt{1+c h}}\\
&$=\lim$ _{h \rightarrow 0} \frac{(1-c h)-(1+c h)}{-h(\sqrt{1-0}+\sqrt{1+0})}\\
&=\lim$_{h \rightarrow 0} $\frac{-2 c h}{-h(1+1)}=c
\end{aligned}$ and $\mathrm{RHL}=\lim _{x \rightarrow 0^{+}} f(x)

\begin{aligned}
& =\lim _{h \rightarrow  0}$ f(0+h)=$\lim _{h \rightarrow  0} \frac{0+h+3}{0+h+1}$\\
& =$\lim _{h \rightarrow  0} \frac{h+3}{h+1}=\frac{0+3}{0+1}=3$
\end{aligned}$

Since, $ f$ is continuous at $x=0$.

\therefore \mathrm{LHL}$=$\mathrm{RHL}$ \Rightarrow $\mathrm{c}=$3$

 =\lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{n} \sum_{r=1}^ n \log \lleft(1+\frac{r}{n}\right)=\int_0^1 \log (1+x) d x \\

The function $f(x)$ has a simple discontinuity at a point other than a

\end{aligned} [Using L' Hospital rule] \begin{array}{ll}

questions.solution:
Let $f\left(x\right) = \dfrac{\left[x\right] + \left[{2}^{2}x\right] + \left[{3}^{2}x\right] +... + \left[n^{2}x\right]}{{1}^{2} + {2}^{2} + {3}^{2} +... + n^{2}}$

Now, we have,

$f\left(x\right) \le \dfrac{x + {2}^{2}x + {3}^{2}x +... + n^{2}x}{{1}^{2} + {2}^{2} + {3}^{2} +... + n^{2}} = x$

and, $f\left(x\right) > \dfrac{\left(x - 1\right) + \left({2}^{2}x - 1\right) + \left({3}^{2}x - 1\right) +... + \left(n^{2}x - 1\right)}{{1}^{2} + {2}^{2} + {3}^{2} +... + n^{2}}$

$= \dfrac{xΣn^{2} - n}{Σn^{2}} = x - \dfrac{6}{ \left(n + 1\right)\left(2n + 1\right)} \left(∵ x - 1 \le \left[x\right] < x, ∀ x \in R\right)$

Thus, we have,

$x - \dfrac{6}{\left(n + 1\right)\left(2n + 1\right)} < f\left(x\right) \le x$

Now, we have,

$\lim_{n \to \infty}x - \dfrac{6}{\left(n + 1\right)\left(2n + 1\right)} = x & \lim_{n \to \infty}x = x$

Hence, by Sandwich Theorem, we have

$\lim_{n \to \infty}f\left(x\right) = x$

If the trace of $A$ is $- 4$ and $AB = \left[\begin{cases}- 1 & 0 & 17 \\ - 3 & 10 & 25 \\ 28 & - 8 & 3\end{cases}\right]$ then $a + b + c + d =$
questions.solution:
Given:

$A = \left[\begin{cases}a & 3 & 5 \\ 5 & - 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & - 4\end{cases}\right]$

$B = \left[\begin{cases}b & 1 & 4 \\ 4 & c & 1 \\ - 3 & 1 & d\end{cases}\right]$

Since, the trace of $A$ is $- 4$, so

$a - 1 - 4 = - 4$

$⇒ a = 1$

Also,

$AB = \left[\begin{cases}- 1 & 0 & 17 \\ - 3 & 10 & 25 \\ 28 & - 8 & 3\end{cases}\right]$

$⇒ \left[\begin{cases}1 & 3 & 5 \\ 5 & - 1 & 3 \\ 2 & 3 & - 4\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{cases}b & 1 & 4 \\ 4 & c & 1 \\ - 3 & 1 & d\end{cases}\right] = \left[\begin{cases}- 1 & 0 & 17 \\ - 3 & 10 & 25 \\ 28 & - 8 & 3\end{cases}\right]$

$⇒ \left[\begin{cases}b - 3 & 6 + 3c & 7 + 5d \\ 5b - 13 & 8 - c & 19 + 3d \\ 2b + 24 & 3c - 2 & 11 - 4d\end{cases}\right] = \left[\begin{cases}- 1 & 0 & 17 \\ - 3 & 10 & 25 \\ 28 & - 8 & 3\end{cases}\right]$

$∴ b - 3 = - 1 ⇒ b = 2$

$6 + 3c = 0 ⇒ c = - 2$

$7 + 5d = 17 ⇒ d = 2$

Hence, $a + b + c + d = 1 + 2 - 2 + 2 = 3$

questions.solution:
Given, A and Bare symmetric matrix of $same order. \Rightarrow \quad A=A^{\prime}, B=B^{\prime} (i)$(A+B)^{\prime}=A^{\prime}+B^{\prime}=A+B \quad$ [from Eq. (i)] $\Rightarrow(A+B)$ is symmetric.
(ii) $(A-B)^{\prime}-\Lambda^{\prime}-B^{\prime}-\Lambda-B$ [from Eq. (i)] $\Rightarrow(A-B)$is symmetric. \text{ (iii) } \begin{aligned}
(A B+B A)^{\prime} &=(A B)^{\prime}+(B A)^{\prime} \\
&=B^{\prime} A^{\prime}+A^{\prime} B^{\prime} \\
&=B A+A B \quad\lfloor\text{$ from $Eq. (i) }]\\
&=(A B+B A)
\end{aligned} \Rightarrow(A B+B A)$ is symmetric. $\text{ (iv) } \begin{aligned}
(A B-B A)^{\prime} &=(A B)^{\prime}-(B A)^{\prime} \\
&=B^{\prime} A^{\prime}-A^{\prime} B^{\prime} \\
&=B A-A B \quad \text{ [from Eq. (i)] }\\
&=-(A B-B A)
\end{aligned} \Rightarrow(A B-B A)$ is skew-symmetric matrix.

questions.q: If the matrix $\left[\begin{array}{rr}2 & 3 \\ 5 & -1\end{array}$\right]=A+B$, where A$ is symmetric and $B$ is skew-symmetric, then $B$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given,
$\left[\begin{array}{rr}
2 & 3 \\
5 & -1
\end{array}\right]=A+B$
We know that, every square matrix can be expressed uniquely as the sum of symmetric and skew-symmetric matrix.
Let
$C=\left[\begin{array}{rr}

5 & -1
\end{array}\right]$
Since, $A$ is symmetric and $B$ is skew-symmetric matrix.
$\begin{aligned}
\therefore \quad C &=\frac{1}{2}\left(C+C^{\prime}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\left(C-C^{\prime}\right)=A+B \\

2 & 3 \\
5 & -1
\end{array}\right)-\left(\begin{array}{rr}
2 & 5 \\
3 & -1
\end{array}\right)\right\} \\
&=\frac{1}{2}\left(\begin{array}{rr}
0 & -2 \\
2 & 0
\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}{rr}
0 & -1 \\
1 & 0

\end{aligned}$

$A^{2} = \left[\begin{cases}0 & i \\ i & 0\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{cases}0 & i \\ i & 0\end{cases}\right] = \left[\begin{cases}- 1 & 0 \\ 0 & - 1\end{cases}\right] = - I$
$A^{3} = A^{2} A = - I ⋅ A = - A$
$A^{4} = {\left(A^{2}\right)}^{2} = I$
$A^{5} = A, A^{6} = - I, A^{7} = - A, A^{8} = I \ldots.$ So on
$I + A + A^{2} + A^{3} = I + A - I - A = 0$
$A^{4} + A^{5} + A^{6} + A^{7} = 0 \ldots \ldots \ldots \ldots A^{104} + A^{105} + A^{106} + A^{107} = 0$
$A^{108} + A^{109} + A^{110} = I + A - I = A$
$⇒ I + A + A^{2} +. \ldots \ldots. + A^{110} = A$

questions.q: If $A = \left[\begin{cases}0 & - tan   \left(\dfrac{θ}{2}\right)$\\ tan $\left(\dfrac{θ}{2}\right) & 0\end{cases}\right]$ and $\left({I}_{2} +$ A\right)$\left({I}_{2} -A\right)- 1 = \left[ \begin{cases}a & - b \\ b & a\end{cases} \right],$ then 13$\left(a^{2} + b^{2}\right)$ is equal to _____ .
questions.solution:
$A = \left[\begin{cases}0 & - tan\dfrac{θ}{2} \\ tan\dfrac{θ}{2} & 0\end{cases}\right]$

$⇒ I + A = \left[\begin{cases}1 & - tan\dfrac{θ}{2} \\ tan\dfrac{θ}{2} & 1\end{cases}\right]$

$⇒ I - A = \left[\begin{cases}1 & tan\dfrac{θ}{2} \\ - tan\dfrac{θ}{2} & 1\end{cases}\right]\left\{∴ | I - A | = \sec^{2}\theta / 2\right\}$

$⇒ \left(I - A\right)- 1 = \dfrac{1}{\sec^{2}\dfrac{θ}{2}}\left[\begin{cases}1 & - tan\dfrac{θ}{2} \\ tan\dfrac{θ}{2} & 1\end{cases}\right]$

$⇒ \left(I + A\right)\left(I - A\right)- 1 = \dfrac{1}{\sec^{2}\dfrac{θ}{2}}\left[\begin{cases}1 & - tan\dfrac{θ}{2} \\ tan\dfrac{θ}{2} & 1\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{cases}1 & - tan\dfrac{θ}{2} \\ tan\dfrac{θ}{2} & 1\end{cases}\right]$

$= \dfrac{1}{\sec^{2}\dfrac{θ}{2}}\left[\begin{cases}1 - \tan^{2}\dfrac{θ}{2} & - 2tan\dfrac{θ}{2} \\ 2tan\dfrac{θ}{2} & 1 - \tan^{2}\dfrac{θ}{2}\end{cases}\right]$

$a = \dfrac{1 - \tan^{2}\dfrac{θ}{2}}{\sec^{2}\dfrac{θ}{2}}$

$b = \dfrac{2tan\dfrac{θ}{2}}{\sec^{2}\dfrac{θ}{2}}$

$∴ a^{2} + b^{2} = 1$

$∴ 13\left(a^{2} + b^{2}\right) = 13$

questions.solution:
We have,

$A = \left[\begin{cases}a & b \\ c & d\end{cases}\right]$

$A^{2} = \left[\begin{cases}a & b \\ c & d\end{cases}\right]\left[\begin{cases}a & b \\ c & d\end{cases}\right]$

$A^{2} = \left[\begin{cases}a^{2} + bc & ab + bd \\ ac + cd & bc + d^{2}\end{cases}\right]$

Given, $A^{2} = A$ and $ad - bc = 0$

$∴ \left[\begin{cases}a^{2} + bc & ab + bd \\ ac + cd & bc + d^{2}\end{cases}\right] = \left[\begin{cases}a & b \\ c & d\end{cases}\right]$

$ab + bd = b$

$b\left(a + d\right) = b$

$⇒ a + d = 1$

Given curve is

\end{array}$

On comparing$ with a x^{2}+2 h x y+b y^{2}+2 g x+2 f y+c=0,$ we get
$a=49-16 \lambda^{2}, b=\left(49-9 \lambda^{2}\right), h=-12 \lambda^{2}$
Condition for parabola is ab $=h^{2}$.

$\begin{array}{l}
\therefore \quad \left(49-16 \lambda^{2}\right) \left(49-9 \lambda^{2}\right)$=$\left(-12 \lambda^{2}\right)^{2} \\
\Rightarrow \quad 2401-441 \lambda^{2}-784 \lambda^{2}+144 \lambda^{4}=144 \lambda^{4} \\
\Rightarrow \quad 2401-1225 \lambda^{2}=0 \\
\Rightarrow \quad \lambda^{2}=\frac{2401}{1225}$\end{array}$\Rightarrow \quad \lambda^{2}=\frac{(49)^{2}}{(35)^{2}}\Rightarrow \quad \lambda=\pm \frac{49}{35}\Rightarrow \quad \lambda=\pm \frac{7}{5}$
