questions.solution: Let the two tangents to the parabola \(y^{2}=4 a x\) be \(P T\) and \(Q T\) which are at right angle to one another at \($\mathrm{T}(\mathrm{h}, \mathrm{k})$\). Then we have a find the locus of \($\mathrm{T}(\mathrm{h}, \mathrm{k})$\). We know that \(y=m x+$\frac{a}{m}$\), where \(m\) is the slope is the equation of tangent to the parabola \(\mathrmy^{2}=4 $\mathrm{ax}$\) for all \($\mathrm{m}$\). Since this tangent to the parabola will pass through \($\mathrm{T}(\mathrm{h}, \mathrm{k})$\), so \($\mathrm{k}=\mathrm{mh}+\frac{\mathrm{a}}{\mathrm{m}}$; $\text{ or } \mathrmm^{2} \mathrm{~h}-\mathrm{mk}+\mathrm{a}=$0\) This is a quadratic equation in \(m\), so will have two roots, say \(m_{1}\) and \(m_{2}\), then \($\mathrm{m}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}=\frac{\mathrm{k}}{\mathrm{h}}$\), and \($\mathrm{m}_{1} \cdot \mathrm{m}_{2}=\frac{\mathrm{a}}{\mathrm{h}}$\) Given that the two tangents intersect at right angle so \($\mathrm{m}_{1} \cdot \mathrm{m}_{2}=-$1 $\text{ or } \frac{\mathrm{a}}{\mathrm{h}}=-$1 $\text{ or } \mathrm{h}+\mathrm{a}=$0\) The locus of \($\mathrm{T}(\mathrm{h}, \mathrm{k})$\) is \($\mathrm{x}+\mathrm{a}=$0\), which is the equation of directrix.

questions.q: If the line $y - 2 = 0$ is the directrix of the parabola $x^{2} - ky + 32 = 0, k \ne 0$ and the parabola intersects the circle $x^{2} + y^{2} = 8$ at two real distinct points, then the absolute value of $k$& is
questions.solution:
$x^{2} - ky + 32 = 0$
$⇒ x^{2} = k \left($ y - $\dfrac{32}{k}\right)
Put, $ x = X, y - $\dfrac{32}{k} =$ Y$
The equation of directrix is $Y + $\dfrac{k}{4} =0$
i.e. $y - \dfrac{32}{k} + \dfrac{k}{4} =0$
But, $y - 2 = 0$ is the directrix.
$⇒ \dfrac{32}{k} - \dfrac{k}{4} =2$
$⇒ k^{2} + 8k - 128 = 0$
$⇒ k = - 16$ or $k = 8$
For $k = 8,$ the parabola is $x^{2} = 8 \left(y - 4\right)$ which does not intersect the circle.
For $k = - 16,$ the parabola is $x^{2} = - 16 \left(y + 2\right)$ which intersects the circle at two real distinct points.
$⇒$ Absolute value of $k = \left|-16\right| = 16$

questions.q: How many numbers lying between 999 and 10000 can be formed with the help of the digits $0,2,3,6,7,8$, when the digits are not repeated?
questions.solution: The numbers between 999 and 10000 are all 4-digit numbers. The number of 4 - digit numbers formed by digits $0,2,3,6,7,8$ is ${ }^{6} \mathrm{P}_{4}=360$. But here those numbers are also involved which begin from 0. So, we take those numbers as three-digit numbers. Taking initial digit 0 , the number of ways to fill remaining 3 places from five digits $2,3,6,7,8$ are ${ }^{5} \mathrm{P}_{3}=60$ So, the required numbers $=360-60=300$.

Number of rectangles in a chess board
(including squares) \(=\Sigma n³\)
\(=\frac{n^2(n+1)^2}{4}\)
Number of squares in a chess board
\(=\Sigma n²=\frac{n(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6}\)
So, Number of rectangles which are not squares
$$\begin{aligned}&=\Sigma n³-\Sigma n² \\
&=\frac{n^2(n+1)^2}{4}-  n \frac{(n+1)(2 n+1)}{6}=350 \\
& \Rightarrow \quad n\left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}-\frac{2 n+1}{3}\right)=350
\end{aligned}$$\)
$$\begin{aligned}
\Rightarrow& & n \left(\frac{n+1}{2}\right)  \ left(\frac{3 n²+3 n-4 n-2}{6}\right)& =350 \\
\Rightarrow &   n(n+1)\left(3 n²-n-2\right) & =350 \times6 \times2 \\
\Rightarrow &   n(n+1)\left(3 n²-3 n+2 n-2\right)& =350 \times6 \times2 \\
\Rightarrow & & n(n+1)(3 n(n-1)+2(n-1) & =350 \times6 \times2 \\
\Rightarrow & & n(n+1)(n-1)(3 n+2) & =350 \times6 \times2 \\
\Rightarrow & & (n-1) n(n+1)(3 n+2) & =5 \times6 \times7 \times20
\end{aligned}$$\)
By comparison we get
\(\therefore \quad n=6\)
Hence, total number of black and white squares
\(=n \timesn=6 \times6=36\)
Half of there are
\(\text{white }=\frac{36}{2}=18 \text{ squares. }\)

questions.solution: $\because a_{n}=$ number of all $n$ digit +ve integers formed by the digits 0,1 or both such that no consecutive digits in them are 0 . and $b_{n}=$ number of such $n$ digit integers ending with 1 $c_{n}=$ number of such $n$ digit integers ending with 0 Clearly, $a_{n}=b_{n}+c_{n}\left(\because a_{n}\right.$ can end with 0 or 1) Also $b_{n}=a_{n-1} and c_{n}=a_{n-2}[\because$ if last digit is 0 , second last has to be 1] $\therefore$ We get $a_{n}=a_{n-1}+a_{n-2}, n \geq 3$ Also $a_{1}=1, a_{2}=2$, Now by this recurring formula, we get $\begin{aligned} a_{3} &=a_{2}+a_{1}=3 \\ a_{4} &=a_{3}+a_{2}=3+2=5 \\ a_{5} &=a_{4}+a_{3}=5+3=8 \\ \text{ Also } b_{6} &=a_{5}=8 \end{aligned}$

questions.q:
Six cards and six envelopes are numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and cards are to be placed in envelopes so that

each envelope contains exactly one card and no card is placed in the envelope bearing the same number and

more over the card numbered 1 is always placed in envelope numbered 2. Then the number of ways it can

be done is
questions.solution:
Total number of placements of 6 cards into 6 envelopes when no card is placed in the envelope bearing the same number.
$= 6 ! ( 1 - \dfrac{1}{1 !} + \dfrac{1}{2 !} - \dfrac{1}{3 !} + \dfrac{1}{4 !} - \dfrac{1}{5 !} + \dfrac{1}{6 !} )$
$= 6 ! ( \dfrac{1}{2 !} - \dfrac{1}{3 !} + \dfrac{1}{4 !} - \dfrac{1}{5 !} + \dfrac{1}{6 !} )$
$= 360 - 120 + 30 - 6 + 5 = 265$
Number of ways the card numbered 1 is placed among the above placements = 5 (envelope number 2, 3, 4, 5, 6)
So the required number of ways when card& 1 is placed& in the envelope& numbered 2 = 265 / 5 = 53

questions.q: Consider $4$ boxes, where each box contains $3$ red balls and $2$ blue balls. Assume that all $20$ balls are distinct. In how many different ways can $10$ balls be chosen from these $4$ boxes so that from each box at least one red ball and one blue ball are chosen?
questions.solution:
Let the four boxes be Box-1, Box-2, Box-3 and Box-4. Each of the box has $3$ red balls and $2$ blue balls.

$10$ balls can be chosen in:

Case I - When exactly one box gives four balls

Case II - When exactly two boxes gives three balls

Required number of ways$=$ Number of ways in Case I $+$ Number of ways in Case II.

$= C1 4 \left[C1 2 + C1 3\right]\left(C1 3 C1 2\right)^{3} + C2 4 \left[C2 3 C1 2 + C1 3 C2 2\right]2\left[C1 3 C1 2\right]2$

$= 4\left(5\right)\left(6\right)^{3} + 6\left(3 \times 2 + 3\right)^{2}\left(6\right)^{2}$

$= 4320 + 17496 = 21816$

Given $P(A)=0.5, P(B)=0.4, P(A \cap B)=0.3$,
then $P  \left(A^{\prime} / B^{\prime}\right) is equal to$
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}$P$\left($A^{\prime} \mid B^{\prime}\right)=& $\frac{P\left(A^{\prime} \cap B^{\prime}\right)}{P\left(B^{\prime}\right)}$\\
&=$\frac{P(A \cup B)^{\prime}}{P\left(B^{\prime}\right)}$\\
&=$\frac{1-P(A \cup B)}{1-P(B)}$\\
&=$\frac{1-[P(A)+P(B)-P(A \cap B)]}{1-P(B)}$\\
&=$\frac{1-[0.5+0.4-0.3]}{1-0.4}$\\
&=$\frac{0.4}{0.6}$\\
&=$\frac{2}{3}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: Three critics review a book. For the three critics the odds in favor of the book are $2: 5$, $3: 4$ and $4: 3$ respectively. The probability that the majority is in favor of the book, is given by
questions.solution:
The probability that the first critic favors the book is $\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A})=\frac{2}{2+5}=\frac{2}{7}\therefore \quad \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrmA^{\prime}\right)=1-\frac{2}{7}=\frac{5}{7}$
The probability that the second critic favors the book is $\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{B})=\frac{3}{3+4}=\frac{3}{7}\therefore \quad \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrmB^{\prime}\right)=1-\frac{3}{7}=\frac{4}{7}$
The probability that the third critic favors the book is $\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{C})=\frac{4}{4+3}=\frac{4}{7}\therefore \quad \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrmC^{\prime}\right)=1-\frac{4}{7}=\frac{3}{7}\therefore \quad$ Majority will be in favor of the book if at least two critics favor the book.
Hence, the probability is
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B} \cap \mathrmC^{\prime}\right)+\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrmB^{\prime} \cap \mathrm{C}\right) \\
& \quad+\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrmA^{\prime} \cap \mathrm{B} \cap \mathrm{C}\right)+\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A} \cap \mathrm{B} \cap \mathrm{C}) \\
& =\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A}) \cdot \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{B}) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrmC^{\prime}\right)+\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A}) \cdot \mathrm{P}\left(\mathrmB^{\prime}\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{C}) \\
& \quad+\mathrm{P}\left(\mathrmA^{\prime}\right) \cdot \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{B}) \cdot \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{C})+\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{A}) \cdot \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{B}) \cdot \mathrm{P}(\mathrm{C}) \\
& =\frac{2}{7} \times \frac{3}{7} \times \frac{3}{7}+\frac{2}{7} \times \frac{4}{7} \times \frac{4}{7}+\frac{5}{7} \times \frac{3}{7} \times \frac{4}{7}+\frac{2}{7} \times \frac{3}{7} \times \frac{4}{7} \\
& =\frac{18}{343}+\frac{32}{343}+\frac{60}{343}+\frac{24}{343}=\frac{134}{343}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If $4$ letter words are formed using letters of the word ‘MORADABAD’, then the probability that D comes exactly once in the $4$ letter word is
questions.solution:
Total cases $= 4$ letter word is formed by using either $3$ identical letter and $1$ distinct letter or $2$ alike of one kind and $2$ alike of ${2}^{nd}$ kind or $2$ alike, $2$ distinct or $4$ distinct
Number of ways for $3$ alike and $1$ distinct $= {C 1}_{1} \times {C 5}_{1} \times \dfrac{4 !}{3 !} = 20$
Number of ways for $2$ alike and $2$ alike $= {C 2}_{2} \times \dfrac{4 !}{2 ! 2 !} = 6$
Number of ways for $2$ alike and $2$ distinct $= {C 2}_{1} \times {C 5}_{2} \times \dfrac{4 !}{2 !} = 240$
Number of ways for $4$ distinct $= {C 6}_{4} \times 4 ! = 360$
The total number of ways $= 20 + 6 + 240 + 360 = 626$
For favorable cases, the following possibilities are there (one D is always included)
Number of ways for $3$ alike $= C1 1 \times \dfrac{4 !}{3 !} = 4$
Number of ways for $2$ alike $+ 1$ distinct $= C1 1 \times C1 4 \times \dfrac{4 !}{2 !} = 48$
Number of ways for $3$ distinct $= C3 5 \times 4 ! = 240$
The total number of ways for favorable cases $= 240 + 48 + 4 = 292$
Hence, the required probability $= \dfrac{292}{626} = \dfrac{146}{313}$

questions.q:
Let $H_1, H_2, \ldots, H_n$ be mutually exclusive events with $P\left(H_i\right) > 0, i=1,2, \ldots, n$. Let $E$ be any other event with $0 <  P(E) <  1$.
Statement I $P  \left(H_i / E\right) > P   \left(E / H_i\right)$ P  $\left(H_i\right)$ for $i=1,2, \ldots, n$.
Statement II \sum_{i=1}^n P$\left(H_i\right)=1$
options: Statement I is true, Statement II is true; Statement II is a correct explanation for Statement I
Statement I is true, Statement II is true; Statement II is not a correct explanation for Statement II
Statement I is true, Statement II is false
Statement I is false, Statement II is true
questions.solution:
Statement : I If $P\left(H_i \cap E\right)=0$ for some $i$, then

P $\left(\frac{H_i}{E}\right)=$ P $\left(\frac{E}{H_i}\right)=0

If $ P $\left(H_i \cap E\right)$ \neq 0$ for $\forall i=1,2, \ldots . n$, then

\begin{aligned}P\left(\frac{H_i}{E}\right)& =\frac{P\left(H_i \cap E\right)}{P\left(H_i\right)} \times \frac{P\left(H_i\right)}{P(E)}\\
& \left.=\frac{P\left(\frac{E}{H_i}\right) \times P\left(H_i\right)}{P(E)}>P\left(\frac{E}{H_i}\right) \cdotP\left(H_i\right) \quad \text{ [as }0 < P(E) < 1\right]
\end{aligned}

Hence, Statement I may not always be true.
Statement II
Clearly, $ H_1 \cup H_2 \cup \ldots . \cup H_n=S$ (sample space)

\Rightarrow \quad P \left(H_1\right)+P \left(H_2\right)+\ldots+P \left(H_n\right)=1 .

Hence, Statement II is true.$

& P(B)=\frac{3}{4}, \text{ not possible }

$\begin{array}{l} a+b+c=2,-a-3 b=5 \\

On solving above equations, we get $ a=-\frac{35}{4}, b=\frac{5}{4}$ and $c=\frac{38}{4}$
Hence, exactly one choice for each of b and c

Since, he quadratic expression $\left(x + a\right) \left(x + 1991\right) + 1$ can be factorised as $\left(x + b\$ \right) $\left( x + c\right)$, therefore

$\left(x + a\right) \left(x + 1991\right) + 1 = \left( x + b\\right) \left( x + c\right)

This implies that \left(x + a\right) \left(x + 1991\right) + 1$ has roots& $- b & - c$ i.e., integer roots. So, discriminant of $x^{2} + \left(1991 + a\right)x + 1991a + 1 = 0$must be perfect square.

$\left(1991 + a\right)$2 - 4 $\left(1991a + 1\right)$ = m^{2}$

$⇒ $\left(1991 - a\right)$2 = m^{2} + 4$

$⇒ $\left(1991 - a\right)$2 - m^{2} = 4$

$⇒ $\left(1991 - a - m\right) \left(1991 - a + m\right) = 4$

Since, both $\left(1991 - a - m\right)$ and $\left(1991 - a + m\right) are integers, therefore possible choices are

\left(1991 - a - m\right) \left(1991 - a + m\right) = 1 \times4$

$\left(1991 - a - m\right) \left(1991 - a + m\right)$ = - 1 \times $\left(- 4\right)$

$\left(1991 - a - m\right) \left(1991 - a + m\right)$ = 2 \times2$

\left(1991 - a - m\right) \left(1991 - a + m\right) = - 2 \times \left(-2\right)

Only possible result is $m = 0$, so

$a = 1989, 1993$

Here, general term ${T}_{k} = \dfrac{1}{( k + 2 )\sqrt{k} + k\sqrt{k + 2}}$

Now, ${T}_{1} = \dfrac{1}{2}( \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}} ),$

${T}_{1} + {T}_{2} + . .. {T}_{k} = \dfrac{1}{2}( 1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{k + 1}} - \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{k + 2}} )$

Now, if $k \to \infty$

$\mathop{∑}_{k = 1}^{\infty}{T}_{k} = \dfrac{1}{2}( 1 + \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} - 0 - 0 )$

$= \dfrac{\sqrt{1} + \sqrt{2}}{2\sqrt{2}}$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q: Let the relation $R_{1}$ be defined on $R$ as $a R_{1}b$ if $1+a b > 0.$ Then
options: $R_{1}$ is reflexive and transitive but not symmetric
$R_{1}$ is reflexive and symmetric but not transitive.
questions.solution:
We observe the following properties:
Reflexivity : Let a be an arbitrary element of $R$, Then, $a \in R\Rightarrow 1+a \cdot a=1+a^{2} \gt 0 \quad\left[\because a^{2} \gt 0\right.$ for all $\left.a \in R\right]\Rightarrow \quad(a, a) \in R_{1}\left[\right.$ By def. of $\left.R_{1}\right]$ 
Thus, $(a, a) \in R_{1}$ for all $a \in R$. So, $R_{1}$ is reflexive on $R$. 
Symmetry : Let $(a, b) \in R$ Then, $(a, b) \in R_{1}\Rightarrow \quad 1+a b \gt 0[\because a b=b a$ for all $]\Rightarrow \quad 1+b a \gt 0 \Rightarrow(b, a) \in R_{1}$
Thus, $(a, b) \in R_{1} \neq(b, a) \in R,$ for all $a, b \in R$ 
So, $R_{1}$ is symmetric on $R$. 
Transitivity : we observe that $\left(1, \frac{1}{2}\right) \in R_{1}$ and $\left(\frac{1}{2},-1\right) \in R_{1}$ but (1,-1)$\notin R_{1}$ because
$1+1 \times(-1)=0 \gg 0$
So, $R_{1}$ is not transitive on $R$.

questions.q:
If the mean of 10 observations is 50 and the sum of the squares of the deviations of the
observations from the mean is 250, then the coefficient of variation of thoseobservations is
questions.solution:
Given, number of observation, $n=10$,
Mean, $\bar{x}=50$ and $\sum|x i-\bar{x}|^2=250$
Variance, $\sigma^2=\sum_{i=1}^n \frac{\left|x_i-\bar{x}\right|^2}{n}\begin{gathered}
\Rightarrow \sigma^2=\sum_{i=1}^{10} \frac{\left|x_i-\bar{x}^2\right|}{10} \\
=\frac{250}{10}=25 \Rightarrow \sigma=5
\end{gathered}\therefore$ Cofficient of variation,
$\text{ C.V. }=\frac{\sigma}{x} \times 100=\frac{5}{50} \times 100=10$

questions.q: Let an angle of a triangle is $60 °$. If the variance of the angles of the triangle is $4614 °$, then the other two angles are
questions.solution:
Let three angles of triangle be& $x, y & z$.

As sum of three angles of triangle$= 180 °$.

$⇒ x + y + z = 180 °$

$⇒ 60 ° + y + z = 180 °$ (Given one angle is& ${60}^{∘}$)

$⇒ y + z = 120 ° \ldots \left(1\right)$

Now, it is given that variance of the angles of triangle is equal to $4614 °$.

$∴ \dfrac{x^{2} + y^{2} + z^{2}}{3} =4614 °$

$⇒ \dfrac{\left({60}^{∘}\right)2 + y^{2} + z^{2}}{3} =4614 °$

$⇒ y^{2} + z^{2} = 10242 °$

$⇒ \left(y + z\right)2 - 2yz = 10242 °$

$⇒ 14400 ° - 2yz = 10242 °$ (Using& $\left(1\right)$)

$⇒ yz = 2079 ° \ldots \left(2\right)$

Now, $\left(y + z\right)2 = \left(y - z\right)2 + 4yz$

$⇒ \left(120\right) ° = \left($ y - z\right)2 + 4 \times2079 °$ (Using& \left(1\right) & \left(2\right)$)

$⇒ \left($ y - z\right)2 = 14400 ° - 8316 ° = 6084 °$

$⇒ y - z = 78 ° \ldots $\left(3\right)$

Solving equations $\left(1\right) & \left(3\right)$, we get,

$y = 99 ° & z = 21 °$

Thus, other two angles are $99 ° & 21 °$.

questions.q: The coefficient of variation and standard deviation of an ungrouped data are 60 and 21 respectively. If 15 is added to every observation of the data, then the coefficient of variation of the new data is
questions.solution:
According to the given information, Coefficient of variance $(\mathrm{CV})=\frac{\sigma}{\mu} \times 100$
Where $\sigma$ is standard deviation and $\mu$ is mean of an ungrouped data.
$\because \quad \frac{\sigma}{\mu} \times 100=60$ and $\sigma=21$
So, $\quad \mu=\frac{21 \times 10}{6}=35$
After adding 15 to each observation of the data, the new mean $\mu^{\prime}=35+15=50$ but
$\Sigma\left|\mu^{\prime}-x_i^{\prime}\right|=\Sigma\left|\mu-x_i\right|$, [where $x_i^{\prime}=x_i+15$ ]
Now, $\sigma=\sqrt{\frac{\sum\left(\mu-x_i\right)^2}{n}}=21\Rightarrow \Sigma\left(\mu-x_i\right)^2=(21)^2 \times n$
So, new standard deviation $\sigma^{\prime}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum\left(\mu^{\prime}-x_i^{\prime}\right)^2}{n}}=\sqrt{\frac{(21)^2 \times n}{n}}=21 $\therefore$ New coefficient of variance =\frac{\sigma^{\prime}}{\mu^{\prime}} \times100=\frac{21}{50} \times100=21 \times2=42 Hence, option (b) is correct.$

questions.q: Let the mean of $50$ observations is $15$ and the standard deviation is $2$. However, one observation was wrongly recorded. The sum of the correct and incorrect observations is $70$. If the mean of the correct set of observations is $16$, then the variance of the correct set is equal to
questions.solution:
By using the formula of& mean we get, $= \dfrac{∑ {x}_{i}}{50} = 15 ⇒ ∑ {x}_{i} = 750$

Now variance$= \dfrac{∑ {x}_i^{2}}{50} - {15}^{2} = {2}^{2} ⇒ ∑ {x}_i^{2} = 11450$

$⇒ \mathop{∑ {x}_{i}}_{new} = 50 \times 16 = 800$

So, $\mathop{∑ {x}_{i}}_{new} - ∑ {x}_{i} = 800 - 750 = 50$

Hence, if wrong observation was $x$ then corrected one is $x + 50$.
$⇒ x + \left(x + 50\right) = 70 ⇒ x = 10$

Therefore, the correct observation $= 60$.

Now, $\mathop{∑ {xi}^{2}}_{new} = 11450 - \left(10\right)^{2} + \left(60\right)^{2} = 14950$

Therefore, variance of the correct set $= \dfrac{14950}{50} - \left(16\right)^{2} = 299 - 256 = 43$.

\Rightarrow & d^{2}=2 \Rightarrow|d|=\sqrt{2}

questions.q: The mean and variance of $10$ observations were calculated as $15$ and $15$ respectively by a student who took by mistake $25$ instead of $15$& for one observation. Then, the correct standard deviation is _______.
questions.solution:
Given,

$n = 10$~and mean& $\overset{¯}{x} = \dfrac{∑ {x}_{i}}{10} = 15$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{10}{x}_{i} = 150$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{9}{x}_{i} + 25 = 150$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{9}{x}_{i} = 125$

Now new sum will be~$\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{9}{x}_{i} + 15 = 140$

So, actual mean~$= \dfrac{140}{10} = 14 = \overset{¯}{x}new$

Now finding variance~

$\dfrac{∑ {x}_i^{2}}{10} - \left(\overset{¯}{x}\right)2 = 15$

$⇒ \dfrac{∑ {x}_i^{2}}{10} - {15}^{2} = 15$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{10}{x}_i^{2} = 2400$

Removing observation of~$25$~we get,

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{9}{x}_i^{2} + 625 = 2400$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{9}{x}_i^{2} = 1775$

Now adding observation~$15$~we get,

$\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{9}{x}_i^{2} + {15}^{2} = 2000 = \left(∑ {x}_i^{2}\right)actual$

Now calculating actual standard deviation we get,

${σ}_{actual}^{2} = \dfrac{\left(∑ {x}_i^{2}\right)actual}{10} - \left(\overset{¯}{x}new\right)2$

$= \dfrac{2000}{10} - {14}^{2}$

$= 200 - 196 = 4$

Calculating standard deviation,~$\left(S . D\right)actual = \sqrt{4} = 2$

So, $\dfrac{∑ {x}_i^{2}}{20} -\left(\dfrac{∑ {x}_{i}}{20}\right)2 = 9 ⋯ \left(ii\right)$

$⇒ \dfrac{∑ {x}_i^{2}}{20} - \left(15\right)2 = 9 ⋯ \left($ ii\right)$

$⇒ ∑ {x}_i^{2} = 234 \times20 = 4680$

Given mean of \left({x}_{1} + \alpha\right)2, \left({x}_{2} + \alpha\right)2, \ldots , \left({x}_{20} + \alpha\right)2$ is& $178$

So, $\dfrac{∑ \left({x}_{i} + \alpha\right)2}${20} =$178 ⇒ ∑ \left({x}_{i} + \alpha\right)2 = 3560$

$⇒ ∑ {x}_i^{2} + 2\alpha∑ {x}_{i} + ∑ {α}^{2} = 3560$

$⇒ 4680 + 600\alpha +20{α}^{2} = 3560$

$⇒ {α}^{2} + 30\alpha +56 = 0$

$⇒ \left(\alpha +28\right)\left(\alpha +2\right) = 0$

\alpha = -2, - 28$

Square of maximum value of \alpha is& 4$

questions.q:
Consider the following frequency distribution:

Class: $0 - 6$ $6 - 12$ $12 - 18$ $18 - 24$ $24 - 30$
Frequency: $a$ $b$ $12$ $9$ $5$

If mean $= \dfrac{309}{22}$ and median $= 14,$ then the value $( a - b{)}^{2}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Class Frequency Mid-point $\left({x}_{i}\right)$ ${f}_{i}{x}_{i}$
$0 - 6$ $a$ $\dfrac{0 + 6}{2} = 3$ $3a$
$6 - 12$ $b$ $\dfrac{6 + 12}{2} = 9$ $9b$
$12 - 18$ $12$ $\dfrac{12 + 18}{2} = 15$ $180$
$18 - 24$ $9$ $\dfrac{18 + 24}{2} = 21$ $189$
$24 - 30$ $5$ $\dfrac{24 + 30}{2} = 27$ $135$
$N = \left(26 + a + b\right)$ $\left(504 + 3a + 9b\right)$

We know that, mean$= \dfrac{∑ {f}_{i}{x}_{i}}{∑ {f}_{i}}$

Given, mean$= \dfrac{309}{22}$

$⇒ \dfrac{3a + 9b + 180 + 189 + 135}{a + b + 26} = \dfrac{309}{22}$

$⇒ \dfrac{504 + 3a + 9b}{a + b + 26} = \dfrac{309}{22}$

$⇒ 66a + 198b + 11088 = 309a + 309b + 8034$

$⇒ 243a + 111b = 3054$

$⇒ 81a + 37b = 1018 . . . \left(1\right)$

Now, median$= 14,$ which lies in the interval $12 - 18,$ thus $12 - 18$ is the median class and we have $= l + \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{N}{2} - c\right) \times h}{f},$

Where, $l$ is the lower limit of the median class i.e. $l = 12, c$ is the cumulative frequency of the class above the median class i.e. $c = a + b, f$ is the frequency of the median class i.e. $f = 12$ and $h$ is the length of the interval i.e. $h = 6 .$

Thus, we have $12 + \left(\dfrac{\left(\dfrac{a + b + 26}{2}\right) - ( a + b )}{12}\right) \times 6 = 14$

$⇒ \dfrac{\left(\dfrac{a + b + 26 - 2a - 2b}{2}\right)}{2} = 14 - 12$

$⇒ \dfrac{26 - a - b}{4} = 2$

$⇒ 26 - a - b = 8$

$⇒ a + b = 18 . . . \left(2\right)$

On solving the equations $\left(1\right)$ and $\left(2\right),$ we get $a = 8, b = 10 .$

$∴ {\left(a - b\right)}^{2} = {\left(8 - 10\right)}^{2} = 4 .$

Incorrect $\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{n}{x}_i^{2} = 100 ( 26 .01 + 1600 ) = 162601$

If the standard deviation of these observations is $1$, then the value of $\left|\alpha - \beta\right|$ is _______.
questions.solution:
$\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{18}\left({x}_{i} - \alpha\right) = 36, \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{18}\left({x}_{i} - \beta\right)2 = 90$

$⇒ \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{18}{x}_{i} = 18\left(\alpha + 2\right), \mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{18}{x}_i^{2} - 2\beta\mathop{∑}_{i = 1}^{18}{x}_{i} + 18{β}^{2} = 90$

Hence $∑ {x}_i^{2} = 90 - 18{β}^{2} + 36\beta \left(\alpha +2\right)$

Given $\dfrac{∑ {x}_i^{2}}{18} -\left(\dfrac{∑ {x}_{i}}{18}\right)2 = 1$

$⇒ 90 - 18{β}^{2} + 36\beta\left(\alpha +2\right) - 18\left(\alpha +2\right)2 = 18$

$⇒ 5 - {β}^{2} + 2\alpha\beta +4\beta - {α}^{2} -4\alpha -4 = 1$

$⇒ \left(\alpha - \beta\right)2 + 4\left(\alpha - \beta\right) =0 ⇒ \left|\alpha - \beta\right| =0$ or $4$

As \alpha and \beta are distinct $| \alpha - \beta | =4$

questions.solution:

Diagonal of a square are perpendicular and bisect each other
Let the equation of the other diagonal be $y=m x+\mathrm{c}$ where $\mathrm{m}$ is the slope of the line and $\mathrm{c}$ is the $y-$ intercept.
Since this line passes through $(-4,5)$
\therefore \quad 5=-4 $\mathrm{ m}+\mathrm{c}$ Since this line is at right angle to the line 7 x-y+8=0 $\text{ or }$ y=7 x+8 $\text{, having slope }=7 \text{, } \therefore \quad7 \times \mathrm{m}=-1 \text{ or } \mathrm{m}=\frac{-1}{7}$ Putting this value of $m$ in equation (i) we get 5=-4 $\times\left(\frac{-1}{7}\right)+\mathrm{c}$ or $5=\frac{4}{7}+\mathrm{c} \quad$ or $\quad \mathrm{c}=5-\frac{4}{7}=\frac{31}{7}$
Hence equation of the other diagonal is y=-$\frac{1}{7} \mathrm{x}+\frac{31}{7} \text{ or }7 \mathrm{y}=-\mathrm{x}+31 or $ x+7 y-31=0$ or $x+7 y=31$.$

The given straight lines are $3x + 4y = 5 and 4x - 3y = 15$. Clearly, these straight lines are perpendicular to each other $\left({m}_{1}{m}_{2} = - 1\right)$ and intersect at A$. Now, $B and C$ are points on these lines such that $AB = AC and BC$ passes through \left(1, 2\right).

From figure it is clear that $∠ B = ∠ C = 45 °$

Let slope of $BC$ be $m$. Then,

$tan45 ° = $\left|\dfrac{m + \dfrac{3}{4}}{1 - \dfrac{3}{4}m}\right|$

$⇒ \pm 1 = \dfrac{4m + 3}{4 - 3m}$

$4m + 3 = \pm \left(4 - 3m\right)

$4m + 3 = 4 - 3m$

or $4m + 3 = - 4 + 3m$

$m = $\dfrac{1}{7}$

or $m = - 7$

Hence, equation of $BC$ is

$y - 2 = \dfrac{1}{7}\left(x - 1\right)

or $y - 2 = - 7 $\left(x - 1\right)$

$⇒ 7y - 14 = x - 1$

or $y - 2 = - 7x + 7$

$⇒ x - 7y + 13 = 0$

or $7x + y - 9 = 0$

Hence, option (c) is correct.

Point $Q$ can be obtained by using parametric form of a straight line, $⇒ Q ≡ \left(\sqrt{3} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}\text{r}}{2}, 2 - \dfrac{\text{r}}{2}\right)$ 

Also, point $Q$ is on $\sqrt{3} \text{x} - 4 \text{y} + 8$  so it will satisfy this equation, hence, 

$\sqrt{3}\left(\sqrt{3} - \dfrac{\sqrt{3}\text{r}}{2}\right) - 4\left(2 - \dfrac{\text{r}}{2}\right) + 8 = 0$

$3 - \dfrac{3}{2} \text{r} - 8 + 2 \text{r} + 8 = 0$

$\text{⇒r}\left(2 - \dfrac{3}{2}\right) = - 3 ⇒ r = - 6$

Hence, the length of $PQ = 6$

questions.q: Consider the set ${A}_{n}$ of points $\left(x, y\right)$ such that $0 \le x \le n, 0y \le n$ where $n, x, y$ are integers. Let ${S}_{n}$ be the set of all lines passing through at least two distinct points from ${A}_{n}.$ Suppose we choose a line $l$ at random from ${S}_{n}.$ Let ${P}_{n}$ be the probability that $l$ is tangent to the circle $x^{2} + y^{2} = n^{2}  \left(1 +   \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{n}\right)2\right)Then, the $limit \lim_{n \to \infty$}{P}_{n}$ is

Equation of line passing through two points $\left({x}_{1}, {y}_{1}\right)$ and $\left({x}_{2}, {y}_{2}\right)$ is

$y - {y}_{1} = \dfrac{{y}_{2} - {y}_{1}}{{x}_{2} - {x}_{1}} \left(x - {x}_{1}\right)$

$⇒ \left({x}_{2} - {x}_{1}\right)y + \left({y}_{1} - {y}_{2}\right)x + {y}_{1}\left({x}_{1} - {x}_{2}\right) + {x}_{1}\left({y}_{2} - {y}_{1}\right) =0$

$⇒ ax + by + c = 0,$ where $a, b, c \in I$

$a = {y}_{1} - {y}_{2}, b = {x}_{2} - {x}_{1}$

$c \in y \left({x}_{1} - {x}_{2}\right) + {x}_{1} \left({y}_{2} - {y}_{1}\right)

Perpendicular distance from origin to line

$ax + by + c = 0$ is \dfrac{c}{a^{2} + b^{2}}$ and $\dfrac{c2}{a^{2} + b^{2}}$ is rational.

Case I $n$ is not perfect square and square $f$ radius $= $n^{2}\l$left(1 \left(1 - \dfrac{1}{n}\right)2\right) =$ rational

$⇒r^{2} \ne \dfrac{c2}{a^{2} + b^{2}}$

$⇒ ax + by + c = 0$ never be tangent to give $n$ circle

$⇒ \lim_{n \to $\infty$}{P}_{n} = 0$

Case II If $n$ is perfect square. In this case number of tangents passing through two points from given set are few, but total number of lines are in much quantity when $n$ approaches to infinite.
$⇒\lim_{n \to $\infty$}{P}_{n} = 0$

questions.q: Consider a triangle $\Delta$ whose two sides lie on the $x$-axis and the line $x + y + 1 = 0$. If the orthocenter of $\Delta$ is $(1,1)$, then the equation of the circle passing through the vertices of the triangle $\Delta$ is
questions.solution: Let& $A$ is the point of intersection of the given lines& $y = 0, x + y + 1 = 0$ Their point of intersection $A$ is& $\left(- 1, 0\right)$ Let $B$ is the other point on the line& $x + y + 1 = 0$, Now, the perpendicular from $B$ on the $x$-axis will pass through the orthocenter. So, the equation of perpendicular from $B$ on the $x$-axis is& $x = 1$ Thus, the coordinates of $B$ are& $\left(1, - 2\right)$ Let the third vertex is $\left(h, k\right)$ Slope of the line perpendicular to $x + y + 1 = 0$ is& $1$ So, the perpendicular from $\left(h, k\right)$ to line& $x + y + 1 = 0$ has slope& $1$ and passes through the orthocenter& $\left(1, 1\right)$ Thus, its equation is $y = x$ Now, $y = x$ and& $x$-axis intersects at the origin. Hence, the vertices of the triangle are $( - 1, 0 ) , ( 1, - 2 ) & ( 0, 0 )$ Let the equation of the circle is $x^{2} + y^{2} + 2gx + 2fy = 0( 0, 0 ) \to c = 0( - 1, 0 ) \to 1 - 2g = 0 ⇒ g = \dfrac{1}{2}( 1, - 2 ) \to 5 + 1 - 4f = 0 ⇒ f = \dfrac{3}{2}$ Hence, the equation of the circumcircle is& $x^{2} + y^{2} + x + 3y = 0$. Aliter We know, the image of the orthocentre about the sides of a triangle lies on circumcircle. The image of $( 1, 1 )$ about $y = 0$ is $( 1, - 1 )$ The image of $\left(1, 1\right)$ about $x + y + 1 = 0$ is $( - 2, - 2 )$ & intersection of $y = 0, x + y + 1 = 0$ is $( - 1, 0 ) .$ Let the equation of circle is $x^{2} + y^{2} + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$ All the three points $( 1, - 1 ) , \left(-2, - 2\right) & \left(-1, 0\right) lies on this circle $( 1, - 1 ) \to 2 + 2g - 2f + c = 0 . . . $\left( i\right)$( - 1, 0 ) \to 1 - 2g + c = 0 . . . $\left(ii\right)$( - 2, - 2 ) \to 8 - 4g - 4f + c = 0 . . . $\left(iii\right)$ By using the equations $\left(i\right)$, $\left(ii\right) & \left( iii\right), we get $g = $\dfrac{1}{2},$ f = $\dfrac{3}{2},$ c = 0$ Hence, the equation of the circle is $x^{2} + y^{2} + x + 3y = 0

questions.q: If the planes $\overset{→}{r} \cdot \left(2\overset{^}{i} - \lambda\overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k}\right) = 0$ and $\overset{→}{r} \cdot \left(\lambda\overset{^}{i} + 5\overset{^}{j} - \overset{^}{k}\right) = 5$ are perpendicular to each other, then the value of ${λ}^{2} + \lambda$ is
questions.solution:
We have,

$\overset{→}{r} \cdot \left(\lambda\overset{^}{i} + 5\overset{^}{j} - \overset{^}{k}\right) = 5$

$\overset{→}{r} \cdot \left(2\overset{^}{i} - \lambda\overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k}\right) = 0$

We know that two planes~$\overset{→}{r} \cdot \overset{→}{n}1 = {d}_{1}$~and& $\overset{→}{r} \cdot \overset{→}{n}2 = {d}_{2}$~are perpendicular if

$\overset{→}{n}1 \cdot \overset{→}{n}2 = 0$

Therefore,

$\left(\lambda\overset{^}{i} + 5\overset{^}{j} - \overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \left(2\overset{^}{i} - \lambda\overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k}\right) = 0$

$⇒ 2\lambda - 5\lambda - 3 = 0$

$⇒ - 3\lambda - 3 = 0$

$⇒ \lambda = - 1$

Therefore,~${λ}^{2} + \lambda = 0$

questions.q: Find the coordinates of the point where the line joining the points (2,-3,1) and (3,-4,-5) cuts the plane $2 x+y+z=7$

questions.q: Let ${L}_{1}$ (respectively ${L}_{2}$ ) be the line passing through $2\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{k}$ (respectively $2\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - 3\overset{^}{k}$) and parallel to $3\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 2\overset{^}{k}$ (respectively $\overset{^}{i} - 2\overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}$). Then the shortest distance between the lines ${L}_{1}$ and ${L}_{2}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given that line& ${L}_{1}$~passes through& $2\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{k}$~and parallel to& $3\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 2\overset{^}{k}$

and~line& ${L}_{2}$~passes through& $2\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - 3\overset{^}{k}$~and parallel to& $\overset{^}{i} - 2\overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}$.

Then,~${a}_{1} = 2\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{k}$,~${b}_{1} = 3\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 2\overset{^}{k}$~and& ${a}_{2} = 2\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - 3\overset{^}{k}$,~${b}_{2} = \overset{^}{i} - 2\overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}$

Shortest distance between lines is given by,~$d = \left(\overset{→}{b}1 \times \overset{→}{b}2\right) \cdot \left(\overset{→}{a}2 - \overset{→}{a}1\right)\left|\overset{→}{b}1 \times \overset{→}{b}2\right|$.

Now,~$\left(\overset{→}{b}1 \times \overset{→}{b}2\right) = \left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 3 & - 1 & 2 \\ 1 & - 2 & 1\end{cases}\right| = 3\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} - 5\overset{^}{k}$

$⇒ \left|\overset{→}{b}1 \times \overset{→}{b}2\right| = \sqrt{{3}^{2} + \left(- 1\right)2 + \left(- 5\right)2} = \sqrt{35}$

And,~$\left(\overset{→}{a}2 - \overset{→}{a}1\right) = \overset{^}{j} - 2\overset{^}{k}$

Putting these values, we get~$d = \dfrac{\left(3\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} - 5\overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \left(\overset{^}{j} - 2\overset{^}{k}\right)}{35} = \dfrac{- 1 + 10}{35} = \dfrac{9}{35}$

If the vector $\overset{→}{TA}$ is perpendicular to both $\overset{→}{PR} and \overset{→}{QS}$ and the length of vector $\overset{→}{TA}$~is $\sqrt{5}$ units, then the modulus of a position vector of $A$ is :
questions.solution:
$P \left(3, - 1, 2\right)

$Q $\left(1, 2, - 4\right)$

$\overset{→}{PR} ‖ 4\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 2\overset{^}{k}$

$\overset{→}{QS} ‖ - 2\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - 2\overset{^}{k}$

Dr's of normal to the plane containing $P, T and Q$ will be proportional to :

$\left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i}& \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 4 & - 1 & 2 \\ - 2 & 1 & - 2\end{cases}\right| =4\overset{^}{j} + 2\overset{^}{k}$

$∴ \dfrac{ℓ}{0} = \dfrac{m}{4} = \dfrac{n}{2}$

For point, $T$ : \overset{→}{PT} = $\dfrac{x - 3}{4} = \dfrac{y + 1}{- 1} = \dfrac{z - 2}{2} =$\lambda$

$\overset{→}{QT} = $\dfrac{x - 1}{- 2} = \dfrac{y - 2}{1} = \dfrac{z + 4}{- 2} =$\mu$

$T ≡ $\left(4\lambda + 3, - \lambda - 1, 2\lambda + 2\right)$

$Q ≡ \left(2\mu + 1, \mu + 2, - 2\mu - 4\right)

$4\lambda + 3 = - 2\mu + 1 ⇒ 2\lambda + \mu = - 1$

$\lambda + \mu = - 3 ⇒ \lambda = 2$

and $\mu = - 5, \lambda + \mu = - 3 ⇒ \lambda = 2$

So point $T: $\left(11, - 3, 6\right)$

$\overset{→}{OA} = \left(11\overset{^}{i} - 3\overset{^}{j} + 6\overset{^}{k}\right)$ \pm $\left(\dfrac{2\overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}}{5}\right)$\sqrt{5}

\overset{→}{OA} = $\left(11\overset{^}{i} - 3\overset{^}{j} + 6\overset{^}{k}\right)$ \pm $\left(2\overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}\right)$

$\overset{→}{OA} = 11\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 7\overset{^}{k}$ or $9\overset{^}{i} - 5\overset{^}{j} + 5\overset{^}{k}$

$\left|\overset{→}{OA}\right| =\sqrt{121 + 1 + 49} = \sqrt{171} or $\sqrt{81 + 25 + 25} = \sqrt{131}$

${l}_{1}: \dfrac{x - 2}{2} = \dfrac{y - 6}{1} = \dfrac{z - 2}{- 2}$

Let the shortest distance between& ${l}_{1}$ and the line& $\dfrac{x + 1}{2} = \dfrac{y + 4}{- 3} = \dfrac{z}{2}$ is& S.D.

S.D.& $= \left|\overset{→}{AB} \cdot \overset{→}{MN}\left|\overset{→}{MN}\right|\right|$

Here, $\overset{→}{AB} = 3\overset{^}{i} + 10\overset{^}{j} + 2\overset{^}{k}$

$\overset{→}{MN} = \left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 2 & 1 & - 2 \\ 2 & - 3 & 2\end{cases}\right| = - 4\overset{^}{i} - 8\overset{^}{j} - 8\overset{^}{k}$

So, shortest distance (S.D.)

$= \left|\dfrac{- 108}{12}\right| = \left|- 9\right| = 9$& units

questions.q:
Let $Q$ and $R$ be the feet of perpendiculars from the point $P \left(a, a, a\right)$ on the lines $x = y, z = 1$ and $x = - y, z = - 1$ respectively. If $∠ QPR$ is a right angle, then $12a^{2} is equal to ________

$
questions.solution:
Given,

Equation of line $x = y, z = 1$

$\dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{y}{1} = \dfrac{z - 1}{0} = r$

Now, let any point on the above line be $Q \left(r, r, 1\right)

Similarly, for line $x = - y, z = - 1$ we get,

\dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{y}{- 1} = \dfrac{z + 1}{0} =$k$

So, any point on the above line will be $R $\left(k, - k, - 1\right)$

Now, the direction ratio of $\overset{→}{PQ} = \left(a - r\right)\overset{^}{i} + \left(a - r\right)\overset{^}{j} + \left(a - 1\right)\overset{^}{k}$

Now, finding foot of perpendicular from $P$ on line $\dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{y}{1} = \dfrac{z - 1}{0}$using perpendicular condition we get,

$a - r + a - r + 0 = 0$

$⇒ 2a = 2r$

$⇒ a = r$

Hence, point $Q \left(a, a, 1\right)

And similarly, the $direction ratio of 

\overset{→}{PR} =$\left(a - k\right)$i + $\left(a + k\right)$\overset{^}{j} + $\left(a + 1\right)$\overset{^}{k}$

And again, finding foot of perpendicular from $P$ on line \dfrac{x}{1} = \dfrac{y}{- 1} = \dfrac{z + 1}{0}using perpendicular condition we get,

$a - k - a - k = 0 ⇒ k = 0$

Hence, point $R $\left($0, 0, - 1\right)$

Also, given $\overset{→}{PQ} ⊥ \overset{→}{PR}$

Now, using perpendicular condition we get,

\left($a - r\$\right)\left($a - k\right) + $\left($a - r\$\right)\left($a + k\right) + $\left($a - 1\$\right)\left($a + 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ $\left($a - a\$\right)\left($a - 0\right) + $\left($a - a\$\right)\left($a + 0\right) + $\left($a - 1\$\right)\left($a + 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ $\left($a - 1\$\right)\left($a + 1\right) = 0$

$⇒ a = 1 or - 1$

Hence, $12a^{2} = 12$

questions.q: A plane $P$ is parallel to two lines whose direction ratios are $- 2, 1, - 3$, and $- 1, 2, - 2$ and it contains the point $\left(2, 2, - 2\right)$. Let $P$ intersect the co-ordinate axes at the points $A, B, C$ making the intercepts $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$. If $V$ is the volume of the tetrahedron $OABC$, where~$O$ is the origin and $p = \alpha + \beta + \gamma$, then the ordered pair $\left(V, p\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Given a plane $P$ is parallel to two lines whose direction ratios are $- 2, 1, - 3$, and $- 1, 2, - 2$,

So normal of plane $P$ is given by,& $\left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ - 2 & 1 & - 3 \\ - 1 & 2 & - 2\end{cases}\right| =4\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} - 3\overset{^}{k}$

Now equation of plane $P$ which passes through $\left(2, 2, - 2\right)$ will be,

$4\left(x - 2\right) - \left(y - 2\right) - 3\left(z + 2\right) = 0$

$⇒ 4x - y - 3z - 12 = 0$

Now, coordinates of plane making intercepts at $X, Y & Z$ axis will be $A \left(3, 0, 0\right), B \left(0, - 12, 0\right), $C$\left(0, 0, - 4\right)$

$⇒ \alpha =3, \beta = -12, $\gamma = -$4$

$⇒ p = \alpha + \beta + \gamma = -13$

Now finding volume of tetrahedron $OABC$

$V = \left|\dfrac{1}{6}\overset{→}{OA} \cdot \left(\overset{→}{OB} \times \overset{→}{OC}\right)\right| =\left|\dfrac{1}{6}3\overset{^}{i} \cdot \left(\left(-12\overset{^}{j}\right)\times \left(-4\overset{^}{k}\right)\right)\right|$

$⇒ V = \left|\dfrac{1}{6}3\overset{^}{i} \cdot \left(48\overset{^}{i}\right)\right| = 8 \times3 = 24$

So, $\left(V, p\right) =\left(24, - 13\right)$

questions.q: A line $\dfrac{x - a}{2} = \dfrac{y - b}{3} = \dfrac{z - c}{4}$ intersects a plane $x - y + z = 4$ at a point where the line $\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y + 3}{5} = \dfrac{z + 1}{2}$ meets the plane. Also, a plane $ax - 2y + bz = 3$ meet them at the same point, then $11\left(a + b + c\right)$ is equal to
questions.solution:
Any general point on the line $\dfrac{x - 1}{2} = \dfrac{y + 3}{5} = \dfrac{z + 1}{2}$ is $\left(2\lambda + 1,5\lambda - 3,2\lambda - 1\right)$
It must satisfy $x - y + z = 4 ⇒ 2\lambda + 1 - 5\lambda + 3 + 2\lambda - 1 = 4$
$⇒ - \lambda + 3 = 4 ⇒ \lambda = - 1$
So, the point of intersection of the plane and the line is $\left(- 1, - 8, - 3\right)$
This point also lies on $ax - 2y + bz = 3 ⇒ - a + 16 - 3b = 3$
$⇒ a + 3b = 13 \ldots . \left(i\right)$
This point also satisfy $\dfrac{x - a}{2} = \dfrac{y - b}{3} = \dfrac{z - c}{4}$
$⇒ \dfrac{1 + a}{2} = \dfrac{8 + b}{3} = \dfrac{3 + c}{4} \ldots \left(ii\right)$
By taking $\dfrac{1 + a}{2} = \dfrac{8 + b}{3} ⇒ 3 + 3a = 16 + 2b$
$⇒ 3a - 2b = 13 \ldots \left(iii\right)$
From $\left(i\right)$ and $\left(iii\right)$
$a = \dfrac{65}{11}, b = \dfrac{26}{11}$
From $\left(ii\right)$
$\dfrac{1 + \dfrac{65}{11}}{2} = \dfrac{8 + \dfrac{26}{11}}{3} = \dfrac{3 + c}{4}$
$\dfrac{38}{11} = \dfrac{38}{11} = \dfrac{3 + c}{4} ⇒ c = \dfrac{119}{11}$
$⇒ 11\left(a + b + c\right) = 210$

Equation of plane is

$⇒ 3x - z - 2 = 0$

Since, \overset{→}{a} = \alpha\overset{^}{i} + \beta\overset{^}{j} + \gamma\overset{^}{k}$ is parallel& to $3x - z - 2 = 0$, therefore normal vector of plane is perpendicular to $\overset{→}{a}$, hence

$⇒ 3\alpha - \gamma = 0... \left(1\right)

Now,

$\overset{→}{a} ⊥ $\left(\overset{˙}{i} +2\overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k}\right)$

$⇒ \alpha +$+2\beta +$+3\gamma =0... \left(2\right)

And,

$\overset{→}{a} \cdot ( \overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} +2\overset{^}{k} ) = 0$

$⇒ \alpha + \beta +2\gamma =2... $\left(3\right)$

On solving $\left(1\right)$, $\left(2\right)$& $\left(3\right)$, we get

\alpha =1, \beta = -5, \gamma =3$

So, \left(\alpha - \beta + \gamma\right)2 = 81$

questions.solution:
Given the mirror image of& $P \left(a, b, c\right)$ is& $P^{'} \left($ a - 6, $\beta, \gamma\right)

The mid-point $ M = $\left(a - 3, \dfrac{\beta + b}{2}, \dfrac{\gamma + c}{2}\right)$$

Since $M$ lies on& $3x - 4y + 12z + 19 = 0$

$⇒ 3a - 9 - 4\$left(\dfrac{\beta + b}{2}\right) ++$12\$left(\dfrac{\gamma + c}{2}\right) +$$19 = 0$

$⇒ 6a - 18 - 4\beta -4b + 12\gamma +12c + 38 = 0$

$⇒ 6a - 4b + 12c - 4\beta ++12\gamma +20 = 0 ⋯ \left(1\right)$

Since $PP^{'}$ is parallel to normal of the plane then

$\dfrac{6}{3} = \dfrac{b - \beta}{- 4} = \dfrac{c - \gamma}{12}$

$⇒ b = \beta -8, c = \gamma +24$

Given $a + b + c = 5 ⇒ a + \beta -8 + \gamma +24 = 5$

$⇒ a = - \beta - \gamma -11$

Now putting these values in $\left(1\right)$ we get

$6\left(- \beta - \gamma -11\right) - 4\left(\beta -8\right) + 12\left(\gamma +24\right) - 4\beta ++12\gamma +20 = 0$

$⇒ 7\beta --9\gamma =170 - 33 = 137$

questions.solution:
Let the point on the circle be $\left(cos\theta, sin\theta, 0\right)$ and foot& of the perpendicular from a point on the circle $x^{2} + y^{2} = 1, z = 0$ to the plane $2x + 3y + z = 6$be $\left(h, k, w\right)$,

Now using foot of perpendicular formula we get,

$\dfrac{h - cos\theta}{2} = \dfrac{k - sin\theta}{3} = \dfrac{w - 0}{1}$

$= \dfrac{- 1 \lleft(2cos\theta ++3sin\theta -6\right)}{14} . . . . . . \left(1\right)

$⇒ h = $cos\theta + \dfrac{- 2\left(2cos\theta + 3sin\theta - 6\right)}{14}

$⇒ h = $\dfrac{10cos\theta - 6sin\theta + 12}{14}$ . . . . . $\left(2\right)$

Now again from $equation \left(1\right) we get,

$k = $sin\theta - \dfrac{3}{14}$ \lleft(2cos\theta ++3sin\theta -6\right)$

$k = $\dfrac{5sin\theta - 6cos\theta + 18}{14} . . . . . . \left(3\right)

Now eliminating $sin\theta$ and $cos\theta$ from equation& \left(1\right)$\text{ and $} \left(2\right) we get,

\left(5h + 6k - 12\right)2 + 4 \left(3h + 5k - 9\right)2 = 1$

$⇒ \left(5x + 6y - 12\right)2 + 4 \left(3x + 5y - 9\right)2 = 1

Again$ from equation $\left(1\right)$ w = =$\dfrac{- 1 \lleft(2cos\theta +$+3sin\theta -6\right)}${14} . . . \left(4\right)

Now$ from equation $\left(2\right)$, $\left(3\right)$\text{ and $}\left(4\right)$ we get,

$w = 6 - 2h - 3k$

$⇒ z = 6 - 2x - 3y$

$orx$\left(1 + \lambdac\right)$ - y$\left(c + \lambda\right)$ + z$\left(- b + a\lambda\right)$ = 0$ ...(iv)

If plane (iii) and (iv) are the same, then

$∴ $\dfrac{1 + c\lambda}{b} = \dfrac{- ( c + \lambda )}{a} = \dfrac{- b + a\lambda}{- 1}$or\lambda = - $\left(a + bc\right)\left(ac + b\right)

and $\lambda = - $\dfrac{( ab + c )}{ \left(1 - a^{2}\right)}$

Normal vector to the plane containing to given lines $\overset{\to}{n} = \left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & - 1\end{cases}\right| = - \overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}$

Direction ratios of normal vector $= - 1, 1, 1$.

Equation of plane will be $- 1\left(x - 1\right) + 1\left(y - 0\right) + 1\left(z - 0\right) = 0$

$⇒ x - y - z - 1 = 0$

If $\left(x, y, z\right)$ is foot of perpendicular drawn from $M\left(1, 0, 1\right)$ on the plane, then

$⇒ \dfrac{x - 1}{1} = \dfrac{y - 0}{- 1} = \dfrac{z - 1}{- 1} = \dfrac{- \left(1 - 0 - 1 - 1\right)}{3}$

$⇒ x = \dfrac{4}{3}, y = - \dfrac{1}{3}, z = \dfrac{2}{3}$

$⇒ \alpha + \beta + \gamma = \dfrac{4}{3} - \dfrac{1}{3} + \dfrac{2}{3} = \dfrac{5}{3}$

$⇒ 3\left(\alpha + \beta + \gamma\right) = 5$.

questions.solution: Let $\mathrm{ED}=h, \angle \mathrm{EAB}=\alpha\therefore \quad \angle \mathrm{EBD}=2 \alpha, \angle \mathrm{ECD}=3 \alpha$ Now, $\angle \mathrm{DBE}=\angle \mathrm{EAB}+\angle \mathrm{BEA}\Rightarrow \quad 2 \alpha=\alpha+\angle \mathrm{BEA}\Rightarrow \quad \angle \mathrm{BEA}=\alpha=\angle \mathrm{EAB}\Rightarrow \mathrm{AB}=\mathrm{EB}=a$ Similarly, $\angle \mathrm{EBC}=\alpha\operatorname{In} \Delta \mathrm{EBC}, \frac{\mathrm{BC}}{\sin \alpha}=\frac{\mathrm{EB}}{\sin \left(180^{{}^{\circ}}-3 \alpha\right)}\Rightarrow \frac{b}{\sin \alpha}=\frac{a}{\sin 3 \alpha} \Rightarrow \frac{a}{b}=\frac{\sin 3 \alpha}{\sin 3 \alpha}\Rightarrow \quad \frac{a}{b}=\frac{3 \sin \alpha-4 \sin ^{3} \alpha}{\sin \alpha}=3-4 \sin ^{2} \alpha\Rightarrow 4 \sin ^{2} \alpha=3-\frac{a}{b}=\frac{3 b-a}{b}\Rightarrow \sin \alpha=\sqrt{\frac{3 b-a}{4 b}}$ In $\Delta \mathrm{EBD}, \sin 2 \alpha=\frac{E D}{E B}\Rightarrow \quad \mathrm{ED}=\mathrm{a} \cdot 2 \sin \alpha \cdot \cos \alpha\Rightarrow h=2 a \sqrt{\frac{3 b-a}{4 b}}, \sqrt{1-\frac{3 b-a}{4 b}}=2 a \sqrt{\frac{3 b-a}{4 b}} \sqrt{\frac{b-a}{4 b}}=\frac{a}{2 b} \sqrt{(a+b)(3 b-a)}$

questions.solution:
We have, $\dfrac{sin\left(\lambda\alpha\right)}{sin\alpha} - \dfrac{cos\left(\lambda\alpha\right)}{cos\alpha} = \lambda - 1$

$sin\left(\lambda\alpha\right)cos\alpha - cos\left(\lambda\alpha\right)sin\alpha = \left(\lambda - 1\right)sin\alphacos\alpha$

$sin\left(\lambda - 1\right)\alpha = \left(\lambda - 1\right)sin\alphacos\alpha$

$sin\left(\lambda - 1\right)\alpha = \dfrac{\lambda - 1}{2}sin2\alpha$

It is possible, when $\lambda - 1 = 0 ⇒ \lambda = 1$

and $\dfrac{\lambda - 1}{2} = 1 ⇒ \lambda = 3$

$∴ \lambda$ has only two solution.

questions.q: If \(2 y \cos \theta=x \sin \theta\) and \(2 x \sec \theta-y \operatorname{cosec} \theta=3\), then \(x²+4 y²=\)
questions.solution:
We have \(2 \mathrm{y} \cos \theta=\mathrm{x} \sin \theta\)
or \(\frac{\cos \theta}{\mathrm{x}}=\frac{\sin \theta}{2 \mathrm{y}}=\mathrm{k}\) (say)
Then \(\cos \theta=\mathrm{kx}\) and \(\sin \theta=2 \mathrm{ky}\)...(1)
Again \(2 \mathrm{x} \sec \theta-\mathrm{y} \operatorname{cosec} \theta=3\)
or \(\frac{2 \mathrm{x}}{\cos \theta}-\frac{\mathrm{y}}{\sin \theta}=3\)
or \(\frac{2 \mathrm{x}}{\mathrm{kx}}-\frac{\mathrm{y}}{2 \mathrm{ky}}=3 \quad\) [from(1)]
or \(\frac{2}{\mathrm{k}}-\frac{1}{2 \mathrm{k}}=3\), giving \(\mathrm{k}=\frac{1}{2}\)
We now get \(\cos \theta=\frac{\mathrm{x}}{2}\) and \(\sin \theta=\mathrm{y}\)
Squaring and adding we get
\begin{aligned}& $\cos ^2 \theta+\sin$ ^2 \theta=$\frac{x^2}{4+y²}$\\
& \Rightarrow $\frac{x^2}{4}+$y^2=1, $\text{$ or } x^2+4 y²=4
\end{aligned}

questions.solution: Given, $\cot A=\frac{11}{60}\therefore \tan A=\frac{60}{11}$ and $\cos B=\frac{7}{25} \begin{aligned} & \because A \text{ and } B \notin Q_1 \\ & \therefore A \in Q_3 \text{ and } B \in Q_4 \\ & \therefore \tan B=-\frac{24}{7} \quad\left(\because \tan B=\text{ negative in } Q_4\right) \\ & \Rightarrow \frac{2 \tan \frac{B}{2}}{1-\tan ^2 \frac{B}{2}}=-\frac{24}{7} \\ & \Rightarrow 12 \tan ^2 \frac{B}{2}-7 \tan \frac{B}{2}-12=0 \\ & \Rightarrow\left(3 \tan ^{\frac{B}{2}}-4\right)\left(4 \tan \frac{B}{2}+3\right)=0 \\ & \Rightarrow \tan \frac{B}{2}=\frac{4}{3}(\text{ Rejected }) \text{ because } B \in Q_4 \text{ i.e. } \\ & \frac{3 \pi}{2} < B < 2 \pi \\ & \therefore \quad \frac{3 \pi}{4} < \frac{B}{2} < \pi \\ & \text{ i.e. } \quad \frac{B}{2} \in Q_2 \\ & \therefore \quad \tan \frac{B}{2}=\text{ negative } \\ & \text{ or } \quad \tan \frac{B}{2}=-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}\begin{aligned} & \text{ Now, } \tan \left(A+\frac{B}{2}\right)=\frac{\tan A+\tan \frac{B}{2}}{1-\tan A \cdot \tan \frac{B}{2}} \\ & =\frac{\frac{60}{11}-\frac{3}{4}}{1-\frac{60}{11}\left(-\frac{3}{4}\right)} \\ & =\frac{\frac{240-33}{44}}{\frac{224}{44}}=\frac{207}{224} \\ & \therefore\left(A+\frac{B}{2}\right) \in Q_1 \\ & \end{aligned}$

questions.solution:
${\left(\dfrac{sin\alpha}{cos\beta} + \dfrac{cos\alpha}{sin\beta} + \dfrac{cos\beta}{sin\alpha} + \dfrac{sin\beta}{cos\alpha}\right)}^{2}$

$= {\left(\dfrac{cos\left(\alpha - \beta\right)}{sin\betacos\beta} + \dfrac{cos\left(\alpha - \beta\right)}{sin\alphacos\alpha}\right)}^{2}$

$= {\left(2cos\left(\alpha - \beta\right)\left\{\dfrac{1}{sin2\beta} + \dfrac{1}{sin2\alpha}\right\}\right)}^{2}$

$= \dfrac{16}{9}{\left(\dfrac{2sin\left(\alpha + \beta\right) \cdot cos\left(\alpha - \beta\right)}{sin2\alpha \cdot sin2\beta}\right)}^{2}$

$= \dfrac{16}{9}{\left(\dfrac{4 \cdot \dfrac{1}{3} \cdot \dfrac{2}{3}}{cos\left(2\alpha - 2\beta\right) - cos\left(2\alpha + 2\beta\right)}\right)}^{2}$

$= \dfrac{16}{9}{\left(\dfrac{\dfrac{8}{9}}{\dfrac{8}{9} - 2 + \dfrac{2}{9}}\right)}^{2}$

$= \dfrac{16}{9}$

i.e. $\left[\dfrac{16}{9}\right] = 1$

questions.solution:
Given, $tanA = \dfrac{1}{x\left(x^{2} + x + 1\right)}, tanB = \dfrac{x}{x^{2} + x + 1}$ and $tanC = \left(x^{- 3} + x^{- 2} + x^{- 1}\right)\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1 + x + x^{2}}{x\sqrt{x}}$

We know that,

$tan\left(A + B\right) = \dfrac{tanA + tanB}{1 - tanAtanB}$

$⇒ tan\left(A + B\right) = \dfrac{\dfrac{1}{x\left(x^{2} + x + 1\right)} + \dfrac{x}{x^{2} + x + 1}}{1 - \dfrac{1}{x^{2} + x + 1}}$

$⇒ tan\left(A + B\right) = \dfrac{\left(1 + x\right)\left(\sqrt{x^{2} + x + 1}\right)}{\left(x^{2} + x\right)\left(\sqrt{x}\right)}$

$⇒ tan\left(A + B\right) = \dfrac{\left(1 + x\right)\left(\sqrt{x^{2} + x + 1}\right)}{\left(x^{2} + x\right)\left(\sqrt{x}\right)}$

$⇒ tan\left(A + B\right) = \dfrac{x^{2} + x + 1}{x\sqrt{x}}$

$⇒ tan\left(A + B\right) = tanC$

$⇒ A + B = C$

We have $|\overline{\mathrm{a}} \times \overline{\mathrm{b}}|=20$ and we have to find value of $\begin{aligned}& |(3 \overline{\mathrm{a}}+\overline{\mathrm{b}}) \times(2 \overline{\mathrm{a}}+3 \overline{\mathrm{b}})| \\

questions.q: Let $\overset{^}{a}$ and $\overset{^}{b}$ are& two non-collinear unit vectors. If $\overset{→}{u} = \overset{^}{a} - \left(\overset{^}{a} \cdot \overset{^}{b}\right)\overset{^}{b}$ and $\overset{→}{v} = \overset{^}{a} \times \overset{^}{b}$, then $| \overset{→}{v} |$ is equal to
questions.solution:
We have,& $\left|\overset{^}{a}\right| = \left|\overset{^}{b}\right| = 1$

Given,~$\overset{→}{v} = \overset{^}{a} \times \overset{^}{b} = \left|\overset{^}{a}\right|\left|\overset{^}{b}\right|sin\theta\overset{^}{n} = sin\theta\overset{^}{n}$

where,~$\theta$~is& the angle between $\overset{^}{a}$ and~$\overset{^}{b}$.~

$∴ \left|\overset{→}{v}\right| = sin\theta$

Now, $\overset{→}{u} = \overset{^}{a} - \left(\overset{^}{a} \cdot \overset{^}{b}\right)\overset{^}{b} = \overset{^}{a} - \left(\left|\overset{^}{a}\right|\left|\overset{^}{b}\right|cos\theta\right)\overset{^}{b}$

$\overset{→}{u} = \overset{^}{a} - \left(cos\theta\right)\overset{^}{b}$

$∴ \left|\overset{→}{u}\right| = \sqrt{\left|\overset{^}{a}\right|2 + \left|- cos\theta\left|\overset{^}{b}\right|\right|2 - 2\left|\overset{^}{a}\right|\left|- cos\theta\overset{^}{b}\right|cos\theta}$

$⇒ \left|\overset{→}{u}\right| = \sqrt{1 + {cos}^{2}\theta - 2{cos}^{2}\theta}$

$⇒ \left|\overset{→}{u}\right| = \sqrt{1 - {cos}^{2}\theta} = \sqrt{{sin}^{2}\theta}$

$∴ \left|\overset{→}{u}\right| = sin\theta$

So,~$\left|\overset{→}{v}\right| = \left|\overset{→}{u}\right|$

questions.q: If vectors $2 \mathrm{i}-\mathrm{j}+\mathrm{k}, \mathrm{i}+2 \mathrm{j}-3 \mathrm{k}$ and $3 \mathrm{i}+\mathrm{aj}+5 \mathrm{k}$ are coplanar, then the value of a is
questions.solution: If given vectors are coplanar, then there exists two scalar quantities $\mathrm{x}$ and $\mathrm{y}$ such that $2 \hat{i}-\hat{j}+\hat{k}=x(\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}-3 \hat{k})+y(3 \hat{i}+a \hat{j}+5 \hat{k})$ Comparing coefficient of $\hat{i}, \hat{j}$ and $\hat{k}$ on both sides of (1) we get $x+3 y=2,2 x+a y=-1,-3 x+5 y=1 \ldots(2)$ Solving first and third equations, we get $\mathrm{x}=1 / 2, \mathrm{y}=1 / 2$ Since the vectors are coplanar, therefore these values of $x$ and $y$ will satisfy the equation $2 x+a y=-1\therefore 2(1 / 2)+a(1 / 2)=-1 \Rightarrow a=-4$

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.q:
Let $\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}=a_1 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+a_2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+a_3 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$
Assertion (A) : The identity
$|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{i}}|^2+|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{j}}|^2+|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{k}}|^2=2|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}|^2$ holds for
$\vec{a}$.
Reason (R) : $\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{i}}=a_3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-a_2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$,
$\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{j}}=a_1 \hat{\mathbf{k}}-a_3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}, \overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{k}}=a_2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-a_1 \hat{\mathbf{j}}$
Which of the following is correct?
options: Both $(\mathrm{A})$ and $(\mathrm{R})$ are true and $(\mathrm{R})$ is the correct reason for (A)
Both $(A)$ and $(R)$ are true but $(R)$ is not the correct reason for (A)
questions.solution:
Given,
$\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}=a_1 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+a_2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+a_3 \hat{\mathbf{k}}$
Now, $|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{i}}|^2=(\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{i}}) \cdot(\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{i}})\begin{aligned} & =\left(a_3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-a_2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\right) \cdot\left(a_3 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-a_2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\right) \\ & =a_3^2+a_2^2\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{j}}|^2 & =\left(a_1 \hat{\mathbf{k}}-a_3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}\right) \cdot\left(a_1 \hat{\mathbf{k}}-a_3 \hat{\mathbf{i}}\right) \\ & =a_1^2+a_3^2\end{aligned}\begin{aligned}|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{k}}|^2 & =\left(a_1 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+a_1 \hat{\mathbf{j}}\right) \cdot\left(a_2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-a_1 \hat{\mathbf{j}}\right) \\ & =a_2{ }^2+a_1{ }^2\end{aligned}$
Now,
$\begin{aligned}|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{i}}|^2 & +|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{j}}|^2+|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{k}}|^2 \\ & =2\left(a_1^2+a_2^2+a_3^2\right) \\ & =2|\overrightarrow{\mathbf{a}}|^2\end{aligned}$
Hence, both $\mathrm{A}$ and $\mathrm{R}$ are true and $\mathrm{R}$ is correct reason for $\mathrm{A}$.

Equating the coefficient of $\hat{\mathbf{i}}\therefore \quad \lambda+\mu=0$

Squaring on both sides,

questions.q: Let \(\mathbf{m}\) be a vector of magnitude \(\sqrt{3}\) and perpendicular to the vectors \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}}\). Let \(\mathbf{n}\) be another vector of magnitude \(2 \sqrt{6}\) and perpendicular to the vectors \(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}\) and \(\hat{\mathbf{j}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\). The area (in sq. units) of the triangle formed with \(\mathbf{m}\) and \(\mathbf{n}\) as sides is
questions.solution:
Given,
\(\mathbf{m}=\sqrt{3} \times \text { unit vectors of }[(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}) \times(\hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}})]\)
$$\begin{aligned}
\because(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}})\times(\hat{\mathbf{j}}-\hat{\mathbf{k}})& =\left[\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\mathbf{i}}& \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
1 & 1 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & -1
\end{array} \right] \\
& =\hat{$\mathbf{i}$}(-1-0)-\hat{$\mathbf{j}$}(-1-0)+\hat{$\mathbf{k}$}($\mathbf{l}$) \\
& =-\hat{$\mathbf{i}$}+\hat{$\mathbf{j}$}+\hat{$\mathbf{k}$} \\
\therefore \quad $\mathbf{m}$ & =\sqrt{3} \times \frac{-\hat{$\mathbf{i}$}+\hat{$\mathbf{j}$}+\hat{$\mathbf{k}$}}{\sqrt{1+1+1}}$\\
& =\sqrt{3} \times \frac{-\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}}{\sqrt{3}}=-\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}
\end{aligned}$
and \(\mathbf{n}=2 \sqrt{6} \times\) unit vectors of \([(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}) \times(\hat{\mathbf{j}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{k}})]\)
 \begin{aligned}& \therefore(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-\hat{\mathbf{j}}) \times(\hat{\mathbf{j}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}) \\
&=\left[\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\mathbf{i}}& \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
2 & -1 & 0 \\
0 & 1 & 2
\end{array} \right] \\
&=\hat{$\mathbf{i}$}(-2-0)-\hat{$\mathbf{j}$}(4-0)+\hat{$\mathbf{k}$}(2+0)=-2 \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}-4 \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}+2 \hat{$\mathbf{k}$} \\
& $\mathbf{n}=2 \sqrt{6} \times \frac{-2 \hat{$\mathbf{i}$}-4 \hat{$\mathbf{j}$}+2 \hat{$\mathbf{k}$}}{\sqrt{4+16+4}}=2 \sqrt{6} \times \frac{-2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}}{2 \sqrt{6}}
\end{aligned}$
\(=-2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\)
Now, required area
 \begin{aligned}& =\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{m} \times \mathbf{n})=\frac{1}{2}|(-\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}) \times(-2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}-4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{k}})| \\
& =\frac{1}{2}\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\mathbf{i}}& \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
-1 & 1 & 1 \\
-2 & -4 & 2
\end{array}$$\right| \\
& =$\frac{1}{2} \times \mid \hat{$$\mathbf{i}$$}(2+4)-\hat{$$\mathbf{j}$$}(-2+2)+\hat{$$\mathbf{k}$$}(4+2|| \\
& =\frac{1}{2} \times|6 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+6 \hat{\mathbf{k}}|=\frac{1}{2} \sqrt{6^2+6^2}=\frac{1}{2} \times6 \times \sqrt{2}=3 \sqrt{2}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If the magnitude of the vector product of the vector \(\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}}\) with a unit vector along the sum of the vectors \(2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-5 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\) and \(\lambda \hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{k}}\) is equal to \(\sqrt{2}\), then the value of ' \(\lambda\) ' is
questions.solution:
$$\begin{aligned}\text {Let } \mathbf{a}& =\hat{\mathbf{i}}+\hat{\mathbf{j}}+\hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
\mathbf{b} & =2 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+4 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-5 \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
\mathbf{c} & =\lambda \hat{\mathbf{i}}+2 \hat{\mathbf{j}}+3 \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c} & =(2+\lambda) \hat{\mathbf{i}}+6 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}
\end{aligned} \)\hat{$\mathbf{d}$}=\) unit vector along \((\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c})=\frac{\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}}{|\mathbf{b}+\mathbf{c}|}\)
 \begin{aligned}=& \frac{(2+\lambda) \hat{\mathbf{i}}+6 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}}{\sqrt{(2+\lambda)^2+36+4}}\\ \mathbf{d} & =\frac{(2+\lambda) \hat{\mathbf{i}}+6 \hat{\mathbf{j}}-2 \hat{\mathbf{k}}}{\sqrt{\lambda^2+4 \lambda+44}}\end{aligned}$$\)$\begin{aligned}& \hat{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{d}}\\ & =\left|\begin{array}{ccc}\hat{\mathbf{i}}& \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\ 1 & 1 & 1 \\ \frac{(2+\lambda)}{\sqrt{\lambda^2+4 \lambda+44}}& \frac{6}{\sqrt{\lambda^2+4 \lambda+44}}& \frac{-2}{\sqrt{\lambda^2+4 \lambda+44}}\end{array} \right|$\end{aligned}$
\begin{aligned}& =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda^2+4 \lambda+44}}\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{\mathbf{i}}& \hat{\mathbf{j}} & \hat{\mathbf{k}} \\
1 & 1 & 1 \\
2+\lambda & 6 & -2
\end{array}\right| \\
& =\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda^2+4 \lambda+44}}|\hat{\mathbf{i}}(-8)-\hat{\mathbf{j}}(-2-2-\lambda)+\hat{\mathbf{k}}(6-2-\lambda)| \\
& \hat{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{d}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda^2+4 \lambda+44}}|-8 \hat{\mathbf{i}}+(4+\lambda) \mathbf{j}+(4-\lambda) \hat{\mathbf{k}}| \\
& |\hat{\mathbf{a}} \times \hat{\mathbf{d}}|=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda^2+4 \lambda+44}} \sqrt{64+(4+\lambda)^2+(4-\lambda)^2}\\
& \sqrt{2}=\frac{\sqrt{64+16+\lambda^2+16+\lambda^2}}{\sqrt{\lambda^2+4 \lambda+44}}
\end{aligned}\)
Squaring on both sides,
\(2=\frac{2 \lambda^2+96}{\lambda^2+4 \lambda+44}\)
\begin{aligned}2 \lambda^2+8 \lambda+88 & =2 \lambda^2+96 \\
8 \lambda & =8 \\
\lambda & =1
\end{aligned}\)
Hence, option (b) is correct.$

Let, $\vec{c}=a \hat{i}+b \hat{j}+c \hat{k}$
Given, $\vec{c} \times(\hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+5 \hat{k})=\overrightarrow{0} \begin{aligned}&\Rightarrow\left|\begin{array}{ccc}
\hat{i}& \hat{j} & \hat{k} \\
a & b & c \\
1 & 2 & 5

\end{aligned} Comparing both sides, we get 5 b-2 c=0 ; 5 a-c=0 ; 2 a-b=0 or 5 b=2 c ; 5 a=c ; 2 a=b$
Also given $|\vec{c}|^2=60$\Rightarrow a²+b²+c²=60 Putting$ the value of b and c$ in above eqn., we get $\begin{aligned}&a^2+(2 a)^2+(5 a)^2=60 \\
&\Rightarrow a²+4 a²+25 a²=60 \Rightarrow 30 a²=60 \\
&a^2=2 \\
&a=\pm \sqrt{2}; b=2 \sqrt{2}; c=5 \sqrt{2}
\end{aligned}$ Now, $\vec{c}=a \hat{i}+b \hat{j}+c \hat{k}$
\therefore $\vec{c}= \sqrt{2} \hat{i}+2 \sqrt{2} \hat{j}+5 \sqrt{2} \hat{k}$ Value of $\vec{c}$ \cdot(-7 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k})$ is \begin{aligned}&(\sqrt{2} \hat{i}+2 \sqrt{2} \hat{j}+5 \sqrt{2} \hat{k}) \cdot(-7 \hat{i}+2 \hat{j}+3 \hat{k}) \\
&=-7 \sqrt{2}+4 \sqrt{2}+15 \sqrt{2}=12 \sqrt{2}
\end{aligned}$

questions.q: If $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ and $\mathbf{d}$ are the unit vectors such that $(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d})=1$ and $\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{c}=\frac{1}{2}$, then
options: a, d are parallel and $\mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ are parallel
questions.solution:
Let angle between $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$ be $\theta_1, \mathbf{c}$ and $\mathbf{d}$ be $\theta_2$ and $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} and \mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d}$ be $\theta$. Since, $(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d})=1\Rightarrow \quad \sin \theta_1 \cdot \sin \theta_2 \cdot \cos \theta=1\Rightarrow \theta_1=90^{{}^{\circ}}, \theta_2=90^{{}^{\circ}}, \theta=0^{{}^{\circ}}\Rightarrow \mathbf{a} \perp \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c} \perp \mathbf{d},(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \|(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d})$ So, $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}=k(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d})$ and $\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}=k(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d})\Rightarrow \quad(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot \mathbf{c}=k(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d}) \cdot \mathbf{c} and (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot \mathbf{d}=k(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d}) \cdot \mathbf{d}\Rightarrow\left[$\begin{array}{lll}$\mathbf{a}$ & $\mathbf{b}$ & $\mathbf{c}$\end{array}$\right]=0$ and $\left[$\begin{array}{lll}$\mathbf{a}$ & $\mathbf{b}$ & $\mathbf{d}$\end{array}$\right]=0\Rightarrow \mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{c}$ and $\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{d}$ are coplanar vectors, so options (a) and (b) are incorrect. Let $\quad \mathbf{b} \| \mathbf{d} \Rightarrow \mathbf{b}=\pm \mathbf{d}$ As $\quad(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d})=1(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{b})=\pm 1\Rightarrow \quad[\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} \mathbf{c} \mathbf{b}]=\pm 1\Rightarrow \quad[\mathbf{c} \mathbf{b} \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}]=\pm 1\Rightarrow \quad \mathbf{c} \cdot[\mathbf{b} \times(\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b})]=\pm 1\Rightarrow \quad \mathbf{c} \cdot[\mathbf{a}-(\mathbf{b} \cdot \mathbf{a}) \mathbf{b}]=\pm 1\Rightarrow \quad \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{a}=\pm 1 \quad[\because \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}=0]$ which is a contradiction, so option (c) is correct.
Let option (d) be correct. $\begin{array}{ll} \Rightarrow& \mathbf{d}=\pm \mathbf{a} \text{$ and $} \mathbf{c}=\pm \mathbf{b}\\ \text{ As }& (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot(\mathbf{c} \times \mathbf{d})=1 \\ \Rightarrow & (\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}) \cdot(\mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a})=\pm1 \end{array}$ which is a contradiction, so option (d) is incorrect. Alternatively option (c) and (d) may be observed from the given figure.

If $\left(\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b}\right) \times \left(\overset{→}{c} \times \overset{→}{d}\right) = \dfrac{3}{26}\overset{^}{i} - \dfrac{2}{13}\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{6}{13}\overset{^}{k}$ and the angle between $\overset{→}{a} and \overset{→}{b}$ is $3{0}^{∘}$, then $\overset{→}{c}$ is equal to
questions.solution:
$\overset{→}{a} ⋅ \overset{→}{d} = \overset{→}{b} ⋅ \overset{→}{d} = \overset{→}{c} ⋅ \overset{→}{d} = 0$ (Given)

$\left|\overset{→}{a}\right| = \left|\overset{→}{b}\right| = \left|\overset{→}{c}\right| = \left|\overset{→}{d}\right| = 1\overset{→}{a} ⋅ \overset{→}{b} = \dfrac{3}{2}$
$\left(\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b}\right) \times \left(\overset{→}{c} \times \overset{→}{d}\right) = \dfrac{3}{26}\overset{^}{i} - \dfrac{2}{13}\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{6}{13}\overset{^}{k}$

$⇒ \left(\left(\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b}\right) ⋅ \overset{→}{d}\right)\overset{→}{c} - \left(\left(\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b}\right) ⋅ \overset{→}{c}\right)\overset{→}{d} = \dfrac{3}{26}\overset{^}{i} - \dfrac{2}{13}\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{6}{13}\overset{^}{k}$~ & ...$( 1 )$

$∵ \overset{→}{a}, \overset{→}{b}, \overset{→}{c}$ are coplanar $⇒ \left(\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b}\right) ⋅ \overset{→}{c} = 0$

$∵ \overset{→}{d}$ is perpendicular to $\overset{→}{a}, \overset{→}{b} ⇒ \overset{→}{d}$ must be parallel to $\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b}$

So, the angle between $\overset{→}{d} and \overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b}$ is either ${0}^{o} or 18{0}^{o}$

From $\left(1\right)$, we get,

$\pm \left|\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b}\right|\left|\overset{→}{d}\right|\overset{→}{c} = \dfrac{2}{26}\overset{^}{i} - \dfrac{2}{13}\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{6}{13}\overset{^}{k}$

$⇒ \pm \left|\overset{→}{a}\right|\left|\overset{→}{b}\right|sin ⁡ {30}^{o}\left|\overset{→}{d}\right|\overset{→}{c} = \dfrac{3}{26}\overset{^}{i} - \dfrac{2}{13}\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{6}{13}\overset{^}{k}$

$⇒ \pm \overset{→}{c}2 = \dfrac{3}{26}\overset{^}{i} - \dfrac{2}{13}\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{6}{13}\overset{^}{k} ⇒ \overset{→}{c} = \pm \left(3\overset{^}{i} - 4\overset{^}{j} + 12\overset{^}{k}\right)13$

questions.q: If $\overset{→}{x}$~and& $\overset{→}{y}$ are two non zero, non-collinear vectors satisfying~$\left(\left(a - 3\right){α}^{2} + \left(b - 4\right)\alpha + \left(c - 1\right)\right)\overset{→}{x}+ \left[\left(a - 3\right){β}^{2} + \left(b - 4\right)\beta + \left(c - 1\right)\right]\overset{→}{y}+ \left[\left(a - 3\right){γ}^{2} + \left(b - 4\right)\gamma + \left(c - 1\right)\right]\left(\overset{→}{x} \times \overset{→}{y}\right) = 0$~(where $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$ are three distinct numbers), then the value of $\dfrac{a^{2} + b^{2} + c^{2}}{4}$ is equal to ______. If your answer is K, mark 2K as answer after rounding off to nearest integer.
questions.solution:
Since, $\overset{\to}{x}, \overset{\to}{y}$ and $\overset{\to}{x} \times \overset{\to}{y}$ are $3$ non-coplanar vectors
Hence, $\left(a - 3\right){\alpha}^{2} + \left(b - 4\right)\alpha + \left(c - 1\right) = 0$
$\left(a - 3\right){\beta}^{2} + \left(b - 4\right)\beta + \left(c - 1\right) = 0$
$\left(a - 3\right){\gamma}^{2} + \left(b - 4\right)\gamma + \left(c - 1\right) = 0$
We can say that $\left(a - 3\right){x}^{2} + \left(b - 4\right)x + \left(c - 1\right) = 0$ has roots $\alpha, \beta, \gamma$
Since, quadratic has 3 roots so it becomes an identity
$⇒ a - 3 = 0, b - 4 = 0, c - 1 = 0$
$⇒ a = 3, b = 4, c = 1$
$⇒ \dfrac{{a}^{2} + {b}^{2} + {c}^{2}}{4} = \dfrac{26}{4} = 6 . 5$

questions.q: Let $\overset{\to}{\alpha} = 3\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j}$ and $\overset{→}{\beta} = 2\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k}.$ If $\overset{→}{\beta} = \overset{→}{\beta1} - \overset{→}{\beta2},$ where $\overset{→}{\beta1}$ is parallel to $\overset{\to}{\alpha}$ and $\overset{→}{\beta2}$ is perpendicular to $\overset{→}{\alpha},$ then $\overset{→}{\beta1} \times \overset{→}{\beta2}$ is equal to:
questions.solution:
If two vectors are parallel then they are proportional.

So, let $\overset{→}{{\beta}_{1}} = k\overset{→}{\alpha}$

Given $\overset{→}{\beta} = \overset{→}{{\beta}_{1}} - \overset{→}{{\beta}_{2}}$

$⇒ \overset{→}{\alpha} ⋅ \overset{→}{\beta} = \overset{→}{\alpha} ⋅ \overset{→}{\beta1} - \overset{→}{\alpha} ⋅ \overset{→}{\beta2}... \left(i\right)$

Now, $\overset{→}{\alpha} \cdot \overset{→}{\beta} = \left(3\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j}\right)\cdot \left(2\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k}\right)$

$= 6 - 1 = 5$

And, $\overset{→}{\alpha}$ is perpendicular& to $\overset{→}{\beta1},$ hence $\overset{→}{\alpha} ⋅ \overset{→}{\beta1} = 0$

And, $\overset{→}{\alpha} ⋅ \overset{→}{\beta2} = \overset{→}{\alpha} ⋅ \left(k\overset{→}{\alpha}\right) = $ k$\left(\overset{→}{\alpha}\right)2 = $ k$\left|\overset{→}{\alpha}\right|2$

Also, $\left|\overset{→}{\alpha}\right| =\sqrt{{3}^{2} + {1}^{2}} = \sqrt{10}$

Put, all these values in the equation $\left(i\right)$,$ to get 5 = k \times10$

$∴ k = \dfrac{1}{2}$

$∴ \overset{→$}{{\beta}_{1}$} = \dfrac{1}{2} (3\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} )$

$= \dfrac{3}{2}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{1}{2}\overset{^}{j}$

Now $\overset{→}{\beta2} = \overset{→}{\beta1} - \overset{→}{\beta} = - \dfrac{1}{2}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{3}{2}\overset{^}{j} -3\overset{^}{k}$

$∴ \overset{→}{\beta1} \times \overset{→}{\beta2} = \left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i}$& \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ $\dfrac{3}{2} \dfrac{1}{2}$& 0 \\ - $\dfrac{1}{2} \dfrac{3}{2}$& - 3\end{cases}\right|$

$= \overset{^}{i}$\left(- \dfrac{3}{2} -0\right) - \overset{^}{j} \left(- \dfrac{9}{2} -0\right) + \$ overset{^}{k}\$ left(\dfrac{9}{4} + \dfrac{1}{4}\right)$

$= - \dfrac{3}{2}\overset{^}{i} + \dfrac{9}{2}\overset{^}{j} + \dfrac{5}{2}\overset{^}{k}$

$= \dfrac{1}{2} ( -3\overset{^}{i} + 9\overset{^}{j} + 5\overset{^}{k} ).$

questions.q: If the vectors, $\overset{→}{p} = \left(a + 1\right)\overset{^}{i} + a\overset{^}{j} + a\overset{^}{k}, \overset{→}{q} = a\overset{^}{i} + \left(a + 1\right)\overset{^}{j} + a\overset{^}{k}$ and $\overset{→}{r} = a\overset{^}{i} + a\overset{^}{j} +   \left(a + 1\right)\overset{^}{k} \left(a \in \mathbb{R}\right)$ are coplanar and 3{ $\left(\overset{→}{p}. \overset{→}{q}\right)$}^{2} - \lambda{$\left|\overset{→}{r} \times \overset{→}{q}\right|$}^{2} = 0, then the $value of \lambda$ is ________
questions.solution:
$\left|\begin{cases}a + 1 & a & a \\ a & a + 1 & a \\ a & a & a + 1\end{cases}\right| = 0 ⇒ a + 1 + a + a = 0 ⇒ a = - \dfrac{1}{3}$
$\overset{→}{P} = \dfrac{2}{3}\overset{^}{i} - \dfrac{1}{3}\overset{^}{j} - \overset{^}{k}$
$\overset{→}{Q} = \dfrac{1}{3} \left(- \overset{^}{i} +2\overset{^}{j} - \overset{^}{k}\right)
$\overset{→}{R} = $\dfrac{1}{3}\left(- \overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 2\overset{^}{k}\right)
$\overset{→}{P} . \overset{→}{Q} = $\dfrac{1}{9}\left(- 2 - 2 + 1\right) = - \dfrac{1}{3}$
$\overset{→}{R} \times \overset{→}{Q} = \dfrac{1}{9}\left|\begin{cases}i & j & k \\ - 1 & 2 & - 1 \\ - 1 & - 1 & 2\end{cases}\right|$ = $\dfrac{1}{9}\left(i\left(4 - 1\right) - j \left(- 2 - 1\right) + k \left(1 + 2\right)\right) = \dfrac{1}{9}\left(3i + 3j + 3k\right)$ = $\dfrac{i + j + k}{3}
\left|\overset{→}{R} \times \overset{→}{Q}\right| = \dfrac{1}{3}\sqrt{3} ⇒ {\left|\overset{→}{R} \times \overset{→}{Q}\right|}^{2} = \dfrac{1}{3}3{\left(\overset{→}{P} . \overset{→}{Q}\right)}^{2} - \lambda{\left|\overset{→}{R} \times \overset{→}{Q}\right|}^{2} = 0$
$3 . \dfrac{1}{9} -\lambda . \dfrac{1}{3} =0 ⇒ \lambda = 1$

$\overset{→}{b} . \overset{→}{c} = 10 ⇒ \left|\overset{→}{b}\right|\left|\overset{→}{c}\right|cos ⁡ \left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = 10 ⇒ 5 . \left|\overset{→}{c}\right| . \dfrac{1}{2} = 10$

$⇒ $\sqrt{3} \times \left|\overset{→}{b}\right|\left|\overset{→}{c}\right|$ sin ⁡ $\dfrac{\pi}{3} \times1$

$⇒ \sqrt{3} \times5 \times4 \times \dfrac{3}{2} =30$

questions.q: Let $\overset{→}{a} = 3\overset{^}{i} + 2\overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}, \overset{→}{b} = 2\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k}$ and $\overset{→}{c}$ be a vector such that $\left(\overset{→}{a} + \overset{→}{b}\right) \times \overset{→}{c} = 2\left(\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b}\right) + 24\overset{^}{j} - 6\overset{^}{k}$ and $\left(\overset{→}{a} - \overset{→}{b} + \overset{^}{i}\right) . \overset{→}{c} = - 3$. Then $\left|\overset{→}{c}\right|2$ is equal to _______.
questions.solution:

$\overset{→}{a} = 3\overset{^}{i} + 2\overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}, \overset{→}{b} = 2\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k}$ and $\overset{→}{c}$ be a vector such that $\left(\overset{→}{a} + \overset{→}{b}\right)\times \overset{→}{c} = 2\left(\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b}\right)$+ 24\overset{^}{j} - 6\overset{^}{k}$ 

Now, finding \overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b} = \left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & - 1 & 3\end{cases}\right| = 7\overset{^}{i} - 7\overset{^}{j} - 7\overset{^}{k}$

Now, solving

$\left(\overset{→}{a} + \overset{→}{b}\right)\times \overset{→}{c} = 2\left(\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b}\right)$+ 24\overset{^}{j} - 6\overset{^}{k}$

$⇒ $\left(5\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} + 4\overset{^}{k}\right)\times \overset{→}{c} = 2\left(7\overset{^}{i} - 7\overset{^}{j} - 7\overset{^}{k}\right)$+ 24\overset{^}{j} - 6\overset{^}{k}$

$⇒ $\left|\begin{cases}\overset{^}{i} & \overset{^}{j} & \overset{^}{k} \\ 5 & 1 & 4 \\ x & y & z\end{cases}\right| =14\overset{^}{i} + 10\overset{^}{j} - 20\overset{^}{k}$

$⇒ \overset{^}{i}\left(z - 4y\right)$- \overset{^}{j}$\left(5z - 4x\right)$+ \overset{^}{k}$\left(5y - x\right) =14\overset{^}{i} + 10\overset{^}{j} - 20\overset{^}{k}$

Now, on comparing both side, 

$z - 4y = 14, 4x - 5z = 10, 5y - x = - 20.... \left(i\right)$

Now, solving 

$\left(\overset{→}{a} - \overset{→}{b} + \overset{^}{i}\right) \cdot \overset{→}{c} = -3$

$⇒ \left(2\overset{^}{i} + 3\overset{^}{j} - 2\overset{^}{k}\right) \cdot \overset{→}{c} = -3$

$⇒ 2x + 3y - 2z = - 3....... \left(ii\right)$

Now, solving the equation  $\left(i\right)$& $\left(ii\right)$ we get,

$∴ x = 5, y = - 3, z = 2$

$⇒ \left|\overset{→}{c}\right|2 = 25 + 9 + 4 = 38$

questions.q: If $\vec{a}, \vec{b}$ and $\vec{c}$ are unit vectors satisfying $|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{b}-\vec{c}|^{2}+|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}=9$, then $|2 \vec{a}+5 \vec{b}+5 \vec{c}|$ is
questions.solution:
$\begin{array}{l}

\because|\vec{a}|=|\vec{b}|=|\vec{c}|=1 \\

|\vec{a}-\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{b}-\vec{c}|^{2}+|\vec{c}-\vec{a}|^{2}=9 \\

\Rightarrow 2\left(|\vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{c}|^{2}\right)-2(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a})=9 \\

\Rightarrow \vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a}=\frac{-3}{2}

\end{array}$

Also,

$\begin{array}{l}

|\vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}|^{2}=|\vec{a}|^{2}+|\vec{b}|^{2}+|\vec{c}|^{2}+2(\vec{a} \cdot \vec{b}+\vec{b} \cdot \vec{c}+\vec{c} \cdot \vec{a}) \\

=1+1+1+2 \times\left(-\frac{3}{2}\right)=0 \\

\Rightarrow \vec{a}+\vec{b}+\vec{c}=0 \Rightarrow(\vec{b}+\vec{c})=-\vec{a} \\

\therefore|2 \vec{a}+5(\vec{b}+\vec{c})|=|2 \vec{a}-5 \vec{a}|=|-3 \vec{a}|=3

\end{array}$

questions.q: Let& $\overset{→}{a} = 3\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - \overset{^}{k}$~and& $\overset{→}{c} = 2\overset{^}{i} - 3\overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k} .$~If& $\overset{→}{b}$~is a vector such that& $\overset{→}{a} = \overset{→}{b} \times \overset{→}{c}$~and& $| \overset{→}{b}{|}^{2} = 50,$~then& $\left|72 - \left|\overset{→}{b} + \overset{→}{c}\right|$2\right|$~is equal to& $__________ .
questions.solution:
Given,

$\overset{→}{a} = 3\overset{^}{i} + \overset{^}{j} - \overset{^}{k}$~and& $\overset{→}{c} = 2\overset{^}{i} - 3\overset{^}{j} + 3\overset{^}{k} .$~

And& $\overset{→}{b}$~is a vector such that& $\overset{→}{a} = \overset{→}{b} \times \overset{→}{c}$~and& $| \overset{→}{b}{|}^{2} = 50,$

Now solving,~$| \overset{→}{a} | = | \overset{→}{b} \times \overset{→}{c} |$

$⇒ \sqrt{{3}^{2} + {1}^{2} + {1}^{2}} = | \overset{→}{b} | \cdot \sqrt{{2}^{2} + {3}^{2} + {3}^{2}} \cdot sin\theta$

$⇒ \sqrt{11} = \sqrt{50} \cdot \sqrt{22} \cdot sin\theta$

$∴ sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{10}$~or& $cos\theta = \dfrac{99}{10}$

Now solving,$\left|72 - \left|\overset{→}{b} + \overset{→}{c}\right|2\right|$~we get,

$\left|72 - \left|\overset{→}{b} + \overset{→}{c}\right|2\right|$

$= \left|72 - \left(\left|\overset{→}{b}\right|2 + \left|\overset{→}{c}\right|2 + 2\left|\overset{→}{b}\right|\left|\overset{→}{c}\right|cos\theta\right)\right|$

$= \left|72 - \left(50 + 22 + 2 \times 5\sqrt{2} . \sqrt{22}\dfrac{99}{10}\right)\right|$

$= \left|72 - \left(72 + \dfrac{2 \times 5 \times 2 \times 11 \times 3}{10}\right\right|$

$= \left|66\right| = 66$

Given: $\overset{→}{a} = \overset{^}{i} + 2\overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}$, $\overset{→}{b} = 3 \left(\overset{^}{i} - \overset{^}{j} + \overset{^}{k}\right), $\overset{→}{a} $\cdot \overset{→}{c} =3$ and $\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{c} = \overset{→}{b}.

Now, $\overset{→}{a} $\times \overset{→}{c} = \overset{→}{b}

$⇒ $\left(\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{c}\right) \cdot \overset{→}{b} = \left|\overset{→}{b}\right|2$

$⇒ \left(\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{c}\right) \cdot \overset{→}{b} = \left(3\sqrt{{1}^{2} + {1}^{2} + {1}^{2}}\right)2$

$⇒ \left(\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{c}\right) \cdot \overset{→}{b} =27$

$⇒ \overset{→}{a} \cdot \left(\overset{→}{c} \times \overset{→}{b}\right) =27 . . . \left(i\right)$

$\left\${$\text{as}$\overset{→}{a} \cdot $\left(\overset{→}{c} \times \overset{→}{b}\right) = \overset{→}{b} \cdot \left(\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{c}\right)\right\}$

Also, $\overset{→}{a} \cdot \overset{→}{b} =3 - 6 + 3 = 0$

$⇒ \overset{→}{a} \cdot \left(\left(\overset{→}{c} \times \overset{→}{b}\right) - \overset{→}{b} - \overset{→}{c}\right) = \overset{→}{a} \cdot \left(\overset{→}{c} \times \overset{→}{b}\right) - \overset{→}{a} \cdot \overset{→}{b} - \overset{→}{a} \cdot \overset{→}{c}$

$⇒ \overset{→}{a} \cdot \left(\left(\overset{→}{c} \times \overset{→}{b}\right) - \overset{→}{b} - \overset{→}{c}\right) =27 - 0 - 3$

$⇒ \overset{→}{a} \cdot \left(\left(\overset{→}{c} \times \overset{→}{b}\right) - \overset{→}{b} - \overset{→}{c}\right) =24$

$

questions.q:
Let $\overset{→}{a}, \overset{→}{b}, \overset{→}{c}$~be three non-coplanar vectors such that $\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b} = 4\overset{→}{c}, \overset{→}{b} \times \overset{→}{c} = 9\overset{→}{a}$~and& $\overset{→}{c} \times \overset{→}{a} = \alpha\overset{→}{b}, \alpha > 0$
If $\left|\overset{→}{a}\right| + \left|\overset{→}{b}\right| + \left|\overset{→}{c}\right| = 36$, then $\alpha$ is equal to _______.
questions.solution:
Taking cross product of $\overset{→}{c}$ both side we get,

$\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b} = 4\overset{→}{c} ⇒ \left(\overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b}\right) \times \overset{→}{c} = 0$

$⇒ \left(\overset{→}{a} \cdot \overset{→}{c}\right). \overset{→}{b} - \left(\overset{→}{b} \cdot \overset{→}{c}\right). \overset{→}{a} = 0$

$⇒ \left(\overset{→}{a} \cdot \overset{→}{c}\right). \overset{→}{b} = \left(\overset{→}{b} \cdot \overset{→}{c}\right). \overset{→}{a}$

Since vectors are non-coplanar& so,

$⇒ \left(\overset{→}{a} \cdot \overset{→}{c}\right) = \left(\overset{→}{b} \cdot \overset{→}{c}\right) =0...... \left(1\right)$

Similarly for $\overset{→}{b} \times \overset{→}{c} =9\overset{→}{a} ⇒ \overset{→}{a} \cdot \overset{→}{b} =0 = \overset{→}{a} \cdot \overset{→}{c}..... \left(2\right)

So, from equation \left(1\right)& \left(2\right) we can say that \overset{→}{a}, \overset{→}{b}, \overset{→}{c}$ are mutually $⊥set of $vectors.

Now taking modulus both side of \overset{→}{a} \times \overset{→}{b} =4\overset{→}{c}, \overset{→}{b} \times \overset{→}{c} =9\overset{→}{a} & \overset{→}{c} \times \overset{→}{a} = \alpha\overset{→}{b}$ we get,

$⇒ $\left|\overset{→}{a}\right|\left|\overset{→}{b}\right| ==4 \left|\overset{→}{c}\right|, \left|\overset{→}{b}\right|\left|\overset{→}{c}\right|$ ==9 $\left|\overset{→}{a}\right|$& $\left|\overset{→}{c}\right|\left|\overset{→}{a}\right|$ = \alpha$\left|\overset{→}{b}\right|$

$⇒ \left|\overset{→}{a}\right|\left|\overset{→}{c}\right|$ = $\dfrac{4}{9}\left|\overset{→}{c}\right|\left|\overset{→}{a}\right|$

$⇒ \left|\overset{→}{c}\right|\left|\overset{→}{a}\right|$ =$\dfrac{3}{2}

$∴$ If& \left|a\right| =$ \lambda, $\left|c\right|$ = $\dfrac{3\lambda}{2}& \left|b\right| = 6$

Now $\left|\overset{→}{a}\right|$ + $\left|\overset{→}{b}\right|$ + $\left|\overset{→}{c}\right|$ =36$

$⇒ \lambda + $\dfrac{3}{2}$ \lambda +6 = 36$

$⇒ \lambda = 12$

Now given \left|\overset{→}{c}\right|\left|\overset{→}{a}\right| = \alpha\left|\overset{→}{b}\right|

$⇒ \alpha = $\left|\overset{→}{c}\right|\left|\overset{→}{a}\right|\left|\overset{→}{b}\right|$ = $\dfrac{3 \times 12}{2}$ \times $\dfrac{12}{6}

$⇒ \alpha =36

For any vector $\overset{→}{a} = {a}_{1}\overset{^}{i} + {a}_{2}\overset{^}{j} + {a}_{3}\overset{^}{k}$, with $10 \left|{a}_{i}\right|< 1, i = 1, 2, 3$, consider the following statements:
$\left(A\right)$ : $max\left\{\left|{a}_{1}\right|$, $\left|{a}_{2}\right|$,$\left|{a}_{3}\right|\right\} \le \left|\overset{→}{a}\right|$
